News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

In August 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a bill – first floated in 2015 – to compensate the families of children born with microcephaly and other disabilities caused by Zika.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

But despite the national law, Ms Sena receives very little support.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Almost everybody born after 2016 has not been exposed to Zika at all... they are naive, and that piles up with the older people who did not get infected,” he told The Telegraph.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

For Erika Silva Costa and her ten-year-old daughter Stephany, the child with severe scoliosis, the struggle to secure that necessary care has reached a standstill.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Glasner made to wait for first win as Trafford thwarts Forest
News.content:
Leeds manager Daniel Farke said: “He has the potential to be one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League and that is why Thomas Tuchel has picked him for England.

“I like his natural confidence and aura, he knows that he’s good and he will be outstanding one day.

“He has major chances to be under the spotlight and we are very pleased with him so far.”

Forest manager Oliver Glasner will be pleased to see the back of Leeds. He was appointed by Forest for the primary reason of winning trophies after successful tenures with Crystal Palace and Eintracht Frankfurt, but this particular avenue is now closed for this season.

Four-time League Cup winners, Forest endured a difficult evening following the pre-match news that they have agreed a £45m deal with Chelsea for striker Liam Delap.

Forest have established a reputation for noisy transfer windows but are determined to focus on quality over quantity this year. With Delap to undergo a medical on Wednesday, Forest will then focus on signing a new right wing-back before the deadline.

Newcastle’s Jacob Murphy has been discussed, though a move is now regarded as unlikely. There are understood to be other targets under consideration.

Glasner has insisted he does not want Forest to panic, and it remains to be seen whether they do spring into life on the final day. He said: “I am not a magician or the messiah and we cannot ignore the reality that Leeds are ahead of us at the moment.

Sports.title: ‘Harmed us’ – Atletico Madrid lash out at Barcelona in scathing Julian Alvarez statement after president’s transfer plea
Sports.content:
ATLETICO MADRID have lashed out at Barcelona in a scathing attack over the Julian Alvarez transfer saga.

The Spanish side have been putting out fires for most of the summer owing to the ongoing battle to keep Alvarez at the club amid interest from Barcelona.



Blaugrana president Joan Laporta released a statement openly expressing the club’s wish to get a deal done.

In a video released on Barca’s social media pages on Wednesday, he said: “The truth is that we’re very interested in the player.



“We’d like our offer to be accepted and we say this with all due respect to Atletico Madrid.

“And we want them to know that if they are open to selling during the summer transfer window we would be willing to buy the player in accordance with the offer we’ve submitted to them.”

However, Atletico chief Miguel Angel Gil Martin swiftly issued a barbed response.

They told Marca: “The player is being victimised, but the only victim of the Julian case is us.

“They have harmed us economically and socially.

“There is zero per cent chance of selling him to Barca.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“This situation is not about money, it’s about dignity.

“There is zero per cent chance of selling it to Barca.

“There’s a campaign with many lies and half-truths.

“The only one who pays for this is Atlético.”



The situation inside Atletico is said to be “very tense” with Alvarez, 26, continuing to push for a move away.

Links between the former Manchester City star and Arsenal have gathered pace in recent weeks.

Alvarez was jeered by fans after coming on as a sub in their 2-2 draw against Villarreal in La Liga.

He was not in the squad for 2-0 win over Malaga days later and the situation is now “extremely tense”, Sky Sports have reported.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Alvarez is said to be “devastated” by both the hostile reception from supporters and being told he will not be allowed to join Barcelona, with the Gunners now emerging as the only other option on the table.



But for a deal to happen Arsenal will need to smash their transfer record by paying a £130million fee – some £25m more than the £105m they paid to land Declan Rice in 2023.

Sports.title: Man Utd ‘set bargain transfer price for Toby Collyer with Prem rival keen’ after midfielder told he can leave club
Sports.content:
MANCHESTER UNITED are prepared to sell Toby Collyer for just £3million, according to reports – and Hull City could offer him a Premier League lifeline.

The midfielder, 22, has been told he can quit the Red Devils before the transfer window slams shut next week.



Collyer was warned in pre-season that he does not have a future at United, who started the campaign with a woeful defeat to Hull on Saturday.

And chief Michael Carrick is willing to flog the academy graduate for a cut-price fee.



It has been claimed by talkSPORT that Hull believe Collyer is on the market for as little as £3m.

The Tigers are keen to hand the Old Trafford outcast a quickfire return to the MKM Stadium.

Collyer was part of the Hull squad which won promotion to the Premier League through the play-offs last season.

He joined the Tigers on loan in January and went on to make five appearances as they returned to the top-flight.

And Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic has a reunion with Collyer in his sights after adding him to his list of late targets.

But West Brom, where the United academy graduate spent the first half of last term before being recalled, have also been showing interest in a deal.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Carrick completed the mega-money signing of Carlos Baleba from Brighton on Tuesday.

The Cameroonian’s arrival, following the captures of Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, means Collyer has fallen even further down the pecking order.

He was not included in the matchday squad when the United Under-21s got their domestic season underway with a 5-0 thrashing of Ipswich earlier this week.

And the Red Devils are desperate to get Collyer off the books before next Tuesday’s deadline.



The ex-Brighton youngster has made 13 senior appearances in a United shirt.

But his most recent outing was in the 3-0 win over Leicester City in March 2025.

Sports.title: What TV channel is Tottenham vs Charlton’s Carabao Cup match on?
Sports.content:
TOTTENHAM begin their Carabao Cup campaign tonight against Charlton!

Roberto De Zerbi‘s side start in the second round after finishing 17th in the Premier League last season.



The Italian boss will be looking for a response from his team tonight after they were thrashed 3-0 by Brentford on the opening weekend last Sunday.

Spurs have been drawn against the Championship’s Charlton, who beat West Ham at the London Stadium last weekend in a huge shock.



Sandro Tonali and Co are hoping to join Brentford, Ipswich, Coventry and Leeds in the pot for the third round after the top-flight sides all won last night.

Last season, when Thomas Frank was still in charge in N17, Tottenham were beaten by Newcastle in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup.

What TV channel is Tottenham vs Charlton’s Carabao Cup match on?

With six Carabao Cup matches being played tonight on Sky Sports, the coverage is spread across multiple channels.

Everton‘s clash against Preston North End is taking centre stage on Sky Sports Main Event and Sky Sports Football.

Meanwhile, Spurs’ match will be aired on Sky Sports+.

Bradford vs Burnley and Newcastle vs West Brom are also being shown on Sky Sports+.



Every match will also be available to be streamed live on NOW TV.

Alternatively, SunSport‘s live blog will provide you with live updates from every single game across the night.

Sports.title: Man Utd ‘set to bid £43million for Eduardo Camavinga as they join Chelsea in transfer race for Real Madrid exile’
Sports.content:
MANCHESTER UNITED have launched a late move for Real Madrid star Eduardo Camavinga, according to reports in Spain.

Despite ex-United and new Real boss Jose Mourinho declaring their window shut, United’s planned opening bid of £43million might turn heads.



It’s Spanish outlet Cadena SER who claim the news to be true, in what would be a knee-jerk reaction from United.

They’ve already brought in Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and most-recently long-term target Carlos Baleba from Brighton.



But following an underwhelming performance against Hull, in which Tielemans and Santos were hooked at the same time, perhaps United are seeking further reinforcements.

Two-time Champions League winner Camavinga has fallen down the pecking order in the Spanish capital.



He’s been out of sorts for a few seasons and Mourinho seems to prefer Tchoumaeni, Valverde and new signing Bernardo Silva.

While Chelsea are also reportedly in the race, reports from Spain suggest United have £80million left to spend on Camavinga and Barcelona left-back Alejandro Balde.

Finding a left-back is unquestionably a more pressing issue for United than another midfielder.

It’s been one of their primary assignments all summer and despite long-term interest in Lewis Hall and recent links to Arsenal’s Myles Lewis-Skelly – Michael Carrick‘s team are still yet to get one in.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

And in another blow, it was reported today that Balde wants to stay at Barca, instead of make the move to Manchester.

The situation seems to be the same for Camavinga, who would reportedly rather stay at Los Blancos – it’s set to be a hectic end to the window for United and Carrick.

Sports.title: Man Utd legend Paul Scholes’ daughter shows off scars in bikini after she was hospitalised
Sports.content:
PAUL SCHOLES’ daughter Alicia has shown off her scars in a bikini snap after being hospitalised.

Alicia, 25, shared a number of holiday pictures after showing herself sunbathing by the pool at a luxury resort.



And she displayed scars around her abdomen in her showreel of photos this week.

Earlier this month she revealed she had been treated at Tameside General Hospital but didn’t declare the reason.



Alicia – who is the second youngest of Manchester United legend Scholes – made light of the scars as she posed for a mirror selfie.

In her caption, she wrote: “Took my 3 brand new shiny scars away.”



She received messages of support in the comments as one fan said: “So pretty.”

Another called her “so gorgeous”.

Alicia has more than 100,000 followers on Instagram and is often seen posting glamorous and revealing snaps.

She is one three children shared by Scholes and ex-wife Claire along with sons Arron and Aiden.



It comes after Alicia opened up about another medical issue after suffering a gruesome toe injury.



She shared pictures of a nasty-looking patch of skin missing from the side of her foot while on another trip with boyfriend Ayo Odukoya and said it was a treadmill-related incident.

And another close-up revealed one of her toes bloodied and badly grazed around the nail.

Alicia – who previously played netball for London Pulse – simply wrote alongside the painful-looking image: “ouch it hurts.”

Fortunately, the injury did not appear to completely ruin her trip as the netball player continued to share pictures from her getaway.

Her latest toe drama comes years after dad Scholes went viral for a rather different reason involving his daughter’s feet.



A bizarre clip shared online in 2021 appeared to show the Manchester United legend nibbling on Alicia’s toenails.

Sports.title: Chelsea in talks with Emiliano Martinez over transfer after they are offered Aston Villa’s World Cup winning keeper
Sports.content:
CHELSEA are considering a deal to sign Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez.

The Blues have been offered the Argentina international, 33, and are in talks with his camp following Robert Sanchez’s poor performance against Fulham on Monday night.



Martinez has been training separately from Unai Emery’s squad following the arrival of new No1 Zion Suzuki and is valued at around £8million by the Europa League winners.

Juventus were close to a deal for the former Arsenal keeper earlier this summer but that collapsed leaving him in limbo.



World Cup winner Martinez pushed to leave Villa Park a year ago, hoping for a move to Manchester United, though that never materialised.

Chelsea’s two current senior goalkeepers are Sanchez and Mike Penders, who spent last season with sister club Strasbourg.



The Blues have insisted they were happy to go into the season with that pair, but Sanchez’s display at Craven Cottage, which included a costly mistake for Josh King’s goal, appears to have changed that stance.

Xabi Alonso is yet to decide whether or not Sanchez or Penders will start their Carabao Cup game against Luton on Thursday night.

But he added that he has not felt it necessary to speak to his No1 about the mistakes against Fulham.

Alonso said: “No, normal conversations. We have talked more about team things, about what we did well, what we have to do better. So it was more about understanding the context.”



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

This could be the latest in a number of deals between Stamford Bridge and Villa Park this summer.

Chelsea have already signed Morgan Rogers for a British-record £117m from Villa.

Alejandro Garnacho moved the other way on loan while talks are progressing over a deal for Nicolas Jackson to join him in the Midlands.

Both clubs must comply with Premier League and Uefa rules around transfers this summer, with both operating under settlement agreements with the European governing body.



There is also Uefa’s swap rules to consider. If clubs sell players to each other within a 45-day period they are treated as a player swap – not as two separate transactions.

Jackson is not able to move on loan as Garnacho has already done so and the Premier League do not allow a club to loan two players from the same parent club at one time.

Sports.title: Man City set to bid for Enzo Fernandez despite missing transfer deadline as Chelsea line up replacement in Alex Scott
Sports.content:
MANCHESTER CITY are preparing an opening bid for Chelsea’s Enzo Fernandez.

The Blues value the midfielder, 25, at more than £120million after their self-imposed August 14 deadline for bids at that price came and went without an offer.



Despite that deadline, City’s interest remains with new boss Enzo Maresca keen on a reunion with the Argentine.

Speaking while on international duty in March, Fernandez criticised the Blues for Maresca’s departure from Stamford Bridge as their season spiralled out of control.



TRANSFER NEWS LIVE: ALL THE LATEST FROM THE SUMMER WINDOW

Chelsea will seek a replacement for Fernandez if an agreement is reached with City and, despite having a £64m bid rejected, they remain keen on Bournemouth’s Alex Scott.

The Cherries have insisted the midfielder, who has rejected the offer of a new contract, is not for sale but Chelsea are prepared to further test their resolve.



Maresca is overhauling City’s midfield, having already signed £116m Elliot Anderson and now added teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi in an £81m deal from Lille confirmed on Wednesday.

Rodri, Bernardo Silva and Tijjani Reijnders have all left while Nico Gonzalez is closing in on a move to Newcastle.

Bouaddi, 18, said: “This is a very special day for me and my family.

“Manchester City are, for me, the best club in the world. It’s a dream to be here and be able to call myself a City player.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

“I have spent most of my life working hard to become the best player I can be and reach the top of the game.

“I’ve watched City for many years, and I love their style of play. City always try and play quality football. And they have shown they are winners – this club feels like it’s built to win.”

Chelsea maintain they are happy to keep Fernandez if their valuation is not met, while new manager Xabi Alonso has stated he wants the midfielder to stay.

However, the former Benfica man, signed for a then British transfer record £106m in January 2023, was not named in the starting XI to face Fulham in the Premier League opener on Monday night.

Fernandez was introduced as a second-half substitute and cheered by the travelling fans having been booed at Stamford Bridge during Chelsea’s final pre-season friendly earlier this month.



The current record fee spent by a British club stands at £125m, paid by Liverpool to Newcastle last summer for striker Alexander Isak.

Sports.title: Differential options for Gameweek 2: Featuring Mamadou Sangare and Ben White
Sports.content:
THIS season we will suggest a handful of differential options for Dream Team managers to consider prior to each Gameweek deadline.

By differentials, we mean players who feature in very few teams and therefore have the potential to make a significant impact.

Mamadou Sangare (£3m)

Brentford’s new midfield general provided three assists in Gameweek 1.



He registered two during the Bees’ dismantling of Tottenham and then came off the bench on Tuesday night to set up one of Nathan Collins’s (£3m) goals against Birmingham in the Carabao Cup.



It’s early days but it appears Sangare will be a key player for Keith Andrews both in and out of possession.

Just 1.2% of gaffers took a punt on the ex-Lens midfielder for Gameweek 1 and they were rewarded with a 17-point haul.

Brentford are due to face Leeds at Elland Road this Sunday, a tricky fixture given the Whites’ home record under Daniel Farke, but the West Londoners could not have started better having scored nine goals in their first two outings.



Nathan Collins (£3m), Michael Kayode (£3m) and Vitaly Janelt (£2m) have also started in fine style.

Ben White (£4.5m)

It’s rare to find a viable differential in Arsenal’s ranks as the Premier League champions are generally well backed.

But their No4’s ownership of 3.9% looks low given he is likely to play all the minutes that matter at right-back while Jurrien Timber (£5m) is sidelined with injury.



Granted, Ezri Konsa’s (£4m) arrival may shake up the pecking order but the England regular is a centre-back first and foremost — he’s more likely to take minutes from Cristhian Mosquera (£4.5m).

White is not an entirely risk-free punt but the appeal is obvious; he assisted the Gunners’ third goal against Coventry and matched Riccardo Calafiori’s (£4.5m) haul of 10 points — for comparison the Italian is the second-most popular defender in the game.

Mikel Arteta will be confident of another positive result on Monday night when his side will face Aston Villa at Villa Park given the Villains’ shambolic display at Brighton.

Maxim De Cuyper (£3.5m)

Speaking of the Seagulls, their Belgian full-back was deployed as a left winger against the Villains and justified Fabian Hurzeler’s decision within 18 minutes.



De Cuyper (1% ownership) forced Victor Lindelof (£3m) into an own goal and then popped up in the six-yard box to double Brighton’s lead as Unai Emery’s troops capitulated at the Amex.

And because he’s categorised as a defender, he also banked clean sheet points from the 4-0 win for a total return of 18 points.

De Cuyper’s Gameweek 2 fixture is far from favourable as Chelsea’s front thee looked strong at Fulham on Monday night but out-of-position gems make for powerful assets in the world of Dream Team.

Yoane Wissa (£3m)

Dream Team bosses keen to target a specific fixture should consider Newcastle’s No9.



The DR Congo international played behind William Osula (£3m) against Liverpool but his underlying numbers caught the eye.

Wissa generated 0.94 xG from four shots, made four tackles, won four free-kicks, and provide an assist for Joe Willock (£2.5m).

Up next is a trip to Spurs, who were flattered by a 3-0 defeat to Brentford in their opening game.

Roberto De Zerbi’s side conceded 26 shots worth a whopping 3.96 xG and Newcastle’s attackers will be licking their lips at the prospect of facing such a vulnerable defence — although Pedro Porro (£4m) and Micky van de Ven (£3.5m) are expected to return for the North Londoners.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Wissa features in 2.3% of teams at the time of writing.



The deadline for Gameweek 2 is 6:30pm this Friday.

Sports.title: Liverpool make approach for Palace forward Sarr
Sports.content:
Liverpool have approached Crystal Palace over potentially signing winger Ismaila Sarr.

Andoni Iraola's side are considering their options after talks stalled with Brighton over Yankuba Minteh.

Sarr is one of the players Liverpool are exploring as they look to reinforce out wide.

Palace have no intention of letting Sarr go at this stage and consider the 28-year-old to be not for sale. He has three years left on his contract.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Crystal Palace manager Pierre Sage provides a transfer update on Jean-Philippe Mateta and Ismaila Sarr and says he expects both of them to stay at the club

Sarr missed Palace's opening weekend defeat at Everton. Reports claimed he was refusing to train but it is understood that the winger is currently injured.

Asked about Sarr's future during his press conference on Wednesday, Palace boss Pierre Sage said: "I understand for everybody that to have this kind of contact is difficult because you hesitate a lot, but for the moment he is with us.

"He is under contract, he is injured, and maybe you can link his injury and the situation.

"But for me, he is honest, and I have no problem with that. I spoke with him this morning about that. Yesterday about that too, and we just want him on the pitch, and all the rest for the other people"

PSG's Bradley Barcola is Liverpool's main target but there is a possibility that Liverpool sign more than one winger.

Cody Gakpo is the subject of interest from Tottenham and Manchester City. Liverpool are not open to selling the Dutchman as things stand and would need two wingers to be signed if he did depart.

What's happened to the Minteh deal?

Image: Brighton have rejected a bid from Liverpool for Yankuba Minteh

Liverpool's talks with Brighton for Minteh are not progressing as things stand.

Brighton are holding out for £80m after rejecting two bids from Liverpool. The latest offer from Andoni Iraola's side was worth £60m.

Liverpool are currently unwilling to reach that figure for Minteh, who is injured and expected to be out until October.

Sports.title: Solheim Cup captain Nordqvist announces shock mid-season retirement
Sports.content:
Solheim Cup captain Anna Nordqvist has announced via social media that she will retire from playing professional golf after this week's FM Championship, live on Sky Sports.

The three-time major winner will captain Team Europe at Bernardus Golf from September 11-13, having featured in each of the previous nine Solheim Cups as a player and been part of five winning teams.

Nordqvist has been a playing vice-captain in the last two contests but quickly ruled herself out of juggling captaincy with playing against Team USA in the Netherlands, despite still regularly featuring on the LPGA Tour and impressing in the majors.

Nordqvist won her maiden major in 2009 and last at the 2021 AIG Women's Open, among nine LPGA Tour titles during a career that saw her claim three additional Ladies European Tour victories and represent Sweden twice in the Olympics.

In a letter posted on social media, Nordqvist added: "Twenty years ago I came to the US with two suitcases, a golf bag and a dream of one day competing with the best golfers in the world.

Image: Nordqvist has been playing professionally since 2008

"While my dreams never quite took me this far, I am very proud of myself for how far I've come and grateful for the dream I've been able to live ever since. I can't say it has always been easy, especially being so far away from my family, but they have supported me every step of the way.

"I've fallen so many times, but I never gave up and I stood up every time I fell. I am forever thankful for everything this game has given me and the people I have met along the way.

"I don't know how to say goodbye to something that means so much to me, but this is going to be my last week walking inside the ropes competing on tour.

"I am not sure what the future has in store for me, but it is with a grateful heart I have decided to retire from playing professional golf to focus on my health and my family. Thank you to everyone who has supported me in this journey and been part of it along the way. It has meant the world to me."

Compatriot Annika Sorenstam - a 10-time major winner - replied to Nordqvist's post to pay tribute to a "great career", with Jessica Korda and Auston Kim among the others to send congratulations after her retirement announcement.

Sports.title: Chelsea considering late move for Villa's Martinez
Sports.content:
Chelsea are considering a late move for Aston Villa goalkeeper Emi Martinez.

The Argentina international's representatives have offered Martinez to Chelsea, whose current No 1 goalkeeper Robert Sanchez came under criticism after his error in Monday's win at Fulham.

Martinez needs to find a new club after Villa signed Zion Suzuki from Parma for nearly £30m.

Argentina's World Cup-winning goalkeeper was the subject of interest from Juventus but they chose to sign Guglielmo Vicario from Spurs.

Martinez has established himself as one of the top goalkeepers in the game during his time at Villa, who he has played 256 times for since joining from Arsenal in 2020.

At Villa, he won the Europa League in May of this year, whilst also helping the team into two Champions League campaigns under Unai Emery.

Martinez has been crucial for Argentina's recent success too, winning the World Cup in 2022 and finishing as runners-up in the 2026 edition. He also won two Copa America trophies in 2021 and 2024, as well as the Finalissima in 2022.

Merson: Martinez is one of the best goalkeepers in the world

Sky Sports' Paul Merson:

Martinez is available and he can be hard work sometimes. He comes across like that. But he's one of the best goalkeepers in the world.

And if Chelsea want to get back to being one of the best in the world, you've got to have a top goalkeeper.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jamie Carragher and Gary Neville believe Xabi Alonso should look into a last-minute signing of a goalkeeper after Robert Sanchez's shaky performance in Chelsea’s league opener against Fulham

Robert Sanchez is usually a good shot-stopper. This weekend, or against Arsenal at the Emirates in two weeks' time, he could be mind-blowing. He could make save after save after save and you'll sit there and go: 'Wow.' He could save Chelsea next week.

I don't like picking on goalkeepers because it's a hard job - and you make one mistake for every 50 mistakes the outfield players make with their passing.

But the match against Fulham was another game that he brought the other team back into the game.

Sports.title: Uefa poised to lift boycott threat after Fifa promises no World Cup sale repeat
Sports.content:
Uefa is poised to drop its threatened boycott of Fifa competitions after receiving concrete guarantees that the global governing body will never attempt a repeat of Gianni Infantino’s plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.

The Guardian understands European teams are likely to be cleared for participation in the upcoming Under-20 Women’s World Cup, along with subsequent tournaments, after Fifa provided the binding assurances that no equivalent of its president’s ill-fated scheme will be put on the table.

Uefa had threatened the boycott after Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal was revealed and doubled down after it was withdrawn, saying the condition that “such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again” had not been met.

Quick Guide How do I 

Despite exchanging barbs in public, Uefa and Fifa are understood to have been having private discussions over the terms of removing the boycott threat for several weeks with the European governing body finally getting the reassurances it required.

When Fifa confirmed its decision to abandon FFE four days after it became public it neglected to pledge that a similar privatisation plan would not be repeated, but it has now done so in private correspondence.

A decision to drop the boycott will allow England, who named their squad for the under-20 tournament last week, to travel to Poland in time for the opening game against Canada on 5 September.

View image in fullscreen England’s under-20s are in line to go to the World Cup in Poland. Photograph: Carlos Rodrigues/The FA/Getty Images

France and Spain had also listed their travelling party in anticipation that the boycott would be lifted. Portugal, Italy and the host nation are the other European countries due to compete.

While the boycott is yet to be publicly dropped, it is among the topics that may arise in a meeting of Uefa’s executive committee and federation chiefs in Monte Carlo on Thursday. The 55 heads of Uefa’s member associations will convene before the Champions League draw during what is traditionally a significant few days in the European football calendar.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Uefa’s position that Infantino must be replaced has not changed and further steps regarding its stance towards the Fifa leadership will also be discussed at the meeting. Italy’s football federation (FIGC) on Wednesday became the latest to publicly withdraw support for Infantino. “This decision is intended to clearly and transparently express the FIGC’s position ... regarding the recent initiatives promoted by the Fifa president concerning the governance and development of international competitions,” it said.

There will be relief in some quarters that younger players, in particular, will not become embroiled in the volatile battle for football’s future. But the fact that Fifa has been forced to mitigate for its president’s actions is another humiliation for a persistently scandal-hit organisation.

Sports.title: Ayyoub Bouaddi: maths student, chess fan and Manchester City’s new Rodri
Sports.content:
“He’s like a computer,” the former Lille head of academy recruitment Mathieu Frison says of the £85m Manchester City recruit Ayyoub Bouaddi. “You teach him something, he learns it and can do it immediately.” Bouaddi has the mountainous challenge at his new club of replacing the best central midfielder in the world. It would be difficult for any player but at 18 years old it feels monumental, although those who know the Morocco international best would not bet against him.

Bouaddi has known only Lille and Ligue 1 but is entering one of the biggest clubs in the world where a season without a trophy is deemed a failure. For someone so young, however, he has plenty of experience. He made his European debut three days after his 16th birthday and has played three full seasons in the first team, culminating in a place at the World Cup this summer.

At 13, Lille beat off competition from France’s elite to sign Bouaddi, after showing his parents the pathway he could follow to the first team. There was never lengthy discussion over money, just what would be best for a boy who wanted to reach the highest level. Lille’s track record is impressive, the club bringing through Bouaddi’s soon-to-be rivals Carlos Baleba and Leny Yoro, among others, in recent times.

Frison visited the Bouaddi family in Creil, an hour north of Paris, to explain why a move to Lille would be beneficial after scouts spotted Bouaddi playing for his home town team in a tournament. “He was not here at the beginning of the meeting with his parents, and he came in the house with the ball on a string,” Frison recalls. “He did a very good trick; he always had this ball in his hand and he always played in his house, so he was already very talented technically.”

City have faith in him, although plenty of the expenditure is on promise rather than a completed article. He is not someone who creates highlight reels but he does the dirty work and plays for the team. Others would seek someone with more miles in their legs but Enzo Maresca is rebuilding a midfield for the long term after Rodri’s departure for Barcelona and with a £52m deal agreed for Nico González to join Newcastle. The 23-year-old Elliot Anderson arrived from Nottingham Forest as the first cog in the wheel, and Enzo Fernández is wanted by his former Chelsea manager.

View image in fullscreen Ayyoub Bouaddi and his family chose Lille because of the pathway to the first team. Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty Images

Bouaddi, the only boy in four siblings, passed all his exams a year early, is studying for a mathematics degree remotely and is capable of speaking English. He is a deep thinker, someone able to cut out the distractions at home and on the pitch. “On the bus, while everyone is watching YouTube videos or listening to music, he will play chess for one or two hours,” Frison says. “In the evening when all the players played Fifa or were on their phones, he studied mathematics, physics, science. His parents didn’t need to push him to do this – he wanted to learn.”

Bouaddi represented the country of his birth, France, from under-16 to under-21 and is regarded as a huge loss for Les Bleus. “Bouaddi, for me, is one of the smartest players I’ve known in my coaching career,” says the former France under-18 coach Landry Chauvin, who had Bouaddi in his squad for the Lafarge tournament in Limoges in 2024. “He reminds me a lot of Yoann Gourcuff, who I saw in Rennes a few years ago. As soon as the tournament was over, I told Les Espoirs [France’s under-21s] that he should have nothing more to do with me, that he had to continue to progress and go above and beyond.”

View image in fullscreen Ayyoub Bouaddi plays for Morocco after representing France, the country of his birth, up to under-21 level. Photograph: Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty Images

Rodri has won everything worth winning over the past decade, while Bouaddi was growing up. Emulating the Spaniard will not be straightforward for a player who has plenty of developing to do. “When Maresca asks him to do something tactically, he knows that 100% Ayyoub will take the best position for the team,” Frison says.

“He will respect the game model with intensity, even when he is tired; he will respect the process. Everyone wants a player who can make the difference individually because they can help you to win the game but you need reliable players who you can trust 100% during 60 games of the season. And Ayyoub, he’s this kind of player.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Bouaddi has consistently mixed with – and surpassed – older players, quickly improving as he rapidly went through each step to the top. He was 16 when he featured under Chauvin’s France under-18s and on his 17th birthday he faced Real Madrid in the Champions League, playing 90 minutes against Jude Bellingham et al as his side won 1-0.

View image in fullscreen Ayyoub Bouaddi celebrates Lille’s Champions League victory over Real Madrid on his 17th birthday. Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters

“A very intelligent boy who adapts quickly, capable of playing in every position in the middle, capable of evolving in a changing environment, permanently working hard, but also always with his head held high,” Chauvin says. “He has the ability to scan the actions very quickly, to take the information before the others. Very comfortable technically, he always has the right position on the field. And on top of that, he’s a boy who’s charming in everyday life; very respectful, very well educated, who knows all the rules.

“The man who hides behind the footballer is simply a very beautiful person. Every time I went to Lille, I would send him a little text, and immediately he came to greet me, even though he was already a pro. Many in his place would have snubbed the under-18 coach but not Ayyoub.”

Sports.title: Chelsea in talks with Emiliano Martínez’s camp after being offered goalkeeper
Sports.content:
Chelsea have been offered Emiliano Martínez and are considering making an offer for the goalkeeper. Martínez has told Aston Villa he wants to leave but a move to Juventus collapsed last week after Villa had signed his replacement, Zion Suzuki, from Parma for £30m.

Goalkeeper has been a problematic position for Chelsea in recent seasons, with Robert Sánchez mainly the No 1 but prone to mistakes. Mike Penders, 21, is being lined up to become the first-choice keeper, but the new Chelsea manager, Xabi Alonso, selected Sánchez for Monday’s win against Fulham and two Sánchez errors led to goals.

The availability and offer of Martínez has intrigued Chelsea and they are mulling whether it is too good an opportunity to turn down. The 33-year-old is a vastly experienced serial trophy winner. He won the World Cup with Argentina in 2022 and reached the 2026 final. He also lifted the Europa League with Villa last season and the FA Cup with Arsenal in 2020.

Martínez was not in the squad for Villa’s heavy opening weekend defeat at Brighton. Marco Bizot started in goal, with Suzuki on the bench. Chelsea are in talks with Martínez’s camp about the terms of a deal that would solve both clubs’ problems.

Chelsea have failed to keep a Premier League clean sheet in 17 games – their longest run since August 1991 – and pundits have questioned whether Sánchez is the right goalkeeper to challenge for titles.

Sports.title: Martin O’Neill puts Champions League collapse among most painful Celtic nights
Sports.content:
Martin O’Neill has admitted that Celtic’s Champions League qualifying collapse from 4-0 up ranks as one of his most painful nights as the club’s manager.

Celtic held a four-goal aggregate lead against Lask on Tuesday when Callum McGregor scored in the 21st minute in Austria, building on a 3-0 first-leg victory, and appeared to be cruising into the league stage. But they lost 5-1 on the night after extra time to go out in extraordinary fashion.

Defeat sends Celtic into the Europa League and delivers a damaging financial blow that will cost the club at least £20m. O’Neill, who has overseen more than 300 games as the club’s manager, said the loss on Tuesday was one of the most painful.

“I would say absolutely, yes,” the 74-year-old said. “I’d put it down before the disappointment of losing the Uefa Cup final in 2003, but it’s so, so disappointing.

“We should have been out of sight by half-time. We scored a goal, which was great, we missed two great, great opportunities. And then we give them a lifeline just before half-time and then one just after it. And they come roaring back. And obviously we conceded, from our viewpoint, not good goals at all. But that’s my team and that’s my responsibility.”

Asked whether his squad was strong enough, O’Neill said: “These are tough games. And it might only be a Champions League qualifying game, but it felt like a Champions League game. I thought they were a fine side. But that doesn’t matter. We should have been able to have seen it through. And we didn’t do. Talking about the squad, that’s for another day.”

McGregor, the captain, accepted there were no excuses. “We got what we deserved,” he told Amazon Prime. “I thought we were so passive. All night. We actually looked scared to go and win the game, and when you are 3-0 up it’s psychological.

“To be honest I didn’t think we were that good in the first leg, either. We scored at good times and kind of got away with it. You go 3-0 and you think you’ve got a real chance but when you play like that you can’t have any excuse whatsoever.

“We have to suck it up, apologise to the supporters and the club because there is no way that we should lose that game … Now you’ll see what kind of characters are in there.”

Sports.title: Bristol City ready to ‘supercharge growth’ and prove women’s clubs can fly solo
Sports.content:
As radiant, August sunshine glistens around a peacefully silent Ashton Gate before Bristol City Women’s pre-season media day, Hannah Buckley takes a seat, pitch side, with a gleam in her eye, surveying the scene. The sight of a top-class venue makes her beam in a way that perhaps only somebody whose CV includes job titles such as regional facilities manager and head of infrastructure, safety and sustainability can. Nice stadiums, particular ones used by women’s sports teams, give her a kick.

But after more than 20 years in football, the past eight at the WSL, Buckley is working on building something rather different: a club capable of thriving independently from the auspices of a men’s club. She was appointed as the Women’s Super League 2 side’s chief executive in May, starting her role in June, at a fascinating time in the team’s history, after they were taken over by the investment group Mercury13 last year to break away from the Bristol Sport group that oversees Bristol City’s men’s team and the city’s rugby union and basketball sides.

That breakaway has ensured it has been a relentlessly busy summer and Buckley, in her first sit-down interview, explains some of their changes: “Our headcount in staff has doubled. We’re having to put in place all the back-house services, which historically would have been carried by Bristol Sport. We’ve made improvements at the training ground, we have upgraded our training pitch, and I think I’d describe it as: ‘We’re in the marginal gain phase,’ reviewing what we have to do [to] supercharge our growth and success.”

Buckley, a board member at Somerset County Cricket Club, remembers the anguish she felt when told girls could not play football at her school when she was 11. She revived her playing days at university but creating opportunities for young girls is partly why she says it was a “no-brainer to apply” for the CEO role at Bristol City. There is a vast catchment area for youngsters across the south-west and she says: “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. It’s a true ‘build’ project.”

View image in fullscreen Hannah Buckley, Bristol City Women’s chief executive, says: ‘We are technically nine months old as a business.’ Photograph: BCWFC

Mercury13, which has investment from familiar names such as the former Manchester United midfielder Juan Mata, owns three women’s clubs: FC Como Women in Italy, FC Badalona Women in Spain and Bristol City Women. Their standalone focus on women’s football, without ties to a men’s team, excites Buckley, who recently led the WSL’s design guidelines for building or upgrading venues specifically for women’s teams. She says: “Independent clubs don’t carry some of the risks that you potentially see where the men’s club may get relegated or [have a] change in ownership and so the independent nature of the club for me was a real opportunity.

“What’s really interesting for me with being part of a multi-club ownership group dedicated solely to women’s football is the opportunities for research, the opportunities for cross-collaboration with different sporting competitions, and actually demonstrating that you can make it work as a standalone women’s entity.”

The owners’ passion specifically for women’s football has also invigorated City’s head coach, Charlotte Healy, who took over in June 2025 after coaching at clubs including Manchester United, Manchester City, Liverpool, Chesterfield and Derby. Healy says: “This football club, I really feel like it cares about its women’s team.

“We had to evolve the workforce – when I came in, I think there was probably [only] seven or eight staff – but we’re already starting to see that the people we’ve brought in the building are good people and we’re really starting to see the benefit of their expertise.

“[For example] we’ve brought a performance wellbeing manager in, which I think was really important – helping the players, because being a professional footballer is not easy, to come in and play under pressure environments and have to win. We brought in a head of performance services in January, who [has] great WSL experience – because we can talk about ‘being WSL ready’, but if we’ve got staff who don’t know what WSL ready looks like, how are we going to get there?”

Buckley adds to that list of hires by saying: “We now have a commercial director and a head of finance, we now have a full-time marketing manager, a club secretary.” And then there have been the most important recruits: players.

They include the 20-year-old Australia defender Alexia Apostolakis, who signed from Melbourne City in July and says part of the reason she moved from the other side of the world was “how ambitious Charlotte and the staff were to get promoted”. Healy says of the summer recruitment: “We felt we needed more squad depth, and I think we’ve made some really good signings. We’ve again looked at younger players. Alexia is one of the best young players in Australia.”

View image in fullscreen The defender Alexia Apostolakis, a summer signing, is described as ‘one of the best young players in Australia’. Photograph: Ali Painter/WSL/Getty Images

The Finland forward Lotta Lindström, who signed from London City Lionesses, says Healy’s team having been the top scorers in WSL2 last term was part of the attraction. The 21-year-old has for two years running been in squads that have won the division, with London City in 2023-24, then on loan at Birmingham City last season, and she says: “I hope I can bring up that winning mentality and [help by] doing those little things right, those little things that actually make the difference between being good and being the best.”

Healy is not shy about stating their goal, as they try to improve on last season’s fourth place. Last term, the top two were promoted, with the third-place team going up after a playoff against the WSL’s bottom side. This time, there will be one automatic spot and the sides in second and third will battle for a place in a playoff against the second-bottom WSL side. Healy believes defensive improvements can help them take the next step: “We want this club to be in the WSL. We understand the challenges that come with that – every team wants to be in the WSL. We need to be a little bit more consistent. We scored the most goals in the league last year and finished fourth, so it is really clear that we needed to be better out of possession. Our biggest evolution needs to be without the ball and making sure that we concede fewer goals – if we can do that, we’ll be right up at the top.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Buckley, who was part of the Football Association facilities team that developed St George’s Park into the national football centre and therefore is perhaps accustomed to a patient approach, says rather more cautiously: “I would say it [WSL2] is the hardest league to get promoted from – you only have to slip up once or twice and the opportunity goes. You saw how tight the margins were last year.

“There are so many facets to success – building the right culture here, first and foremost, is the important thing, professionalising our environment and setting ourselves up for success. I’d hope that we achieve top three. I think that would be a fantastic outcome. But I also have to be really measured; we are technically nine months old as a business.”

She points to their opening fixtures – away to Sunderland, another side taken over by a multi-club women’s-focused ownership group, the Bay Collective, then at Ashton Gate against promotion-chasing Newcastle – as a good “barometer check”, before concluding: “Ask me again at Christmas!”

Robins tend to thrive at Christmas. Whatever their final position, this could be an intriguing case study to observe how well women’s teams can fly solo.
