World.title: INTERVIEW: Why I joined Rangers and what I want to achieve this season – Ifeanyi Okechukwu
World.content:
New Rangers International midfielder Ifeanyi Okechukwu says he is determined to make a statement at the reigning NPFL champions after completing his move to the Enugu club on a deal that will keep him at the Flying Antelopes until 2028.

The 21-year-old midfielder joins Rangers after gaining valuable experience with Niger Tornadoes, Enyimba and Nasarawa United, and he believes his journey through different NPFL environments has prepared him for the demands that come with representing one of the biggest clubs in Nigerian football.

In this interview with PREMIUM TIMES, Okechukwu explains why he chose Rangers despite interest from several other NPFL clubs, discusses his ambitions under coach Fidelis Ilechukwu, his expected role in midfield, Rangers’ title defence and continental ambitions, and the personal journey that has fuelled his dream of eventually playing in Europe.

Excerpts…

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

PT: You have now joined the NPFL champions, Rangers, on a deal that takes you to 2028. What was the conversation like when the opportunity to join the Flying Antelopes first came, and what ultimately convinced you that Rangers was the right next step for your career?

Okechukwu: When I got the call during the past season, I told them to wait until the season came to an end because I had other clubs interested in me, including Rivers United, Katsina United and my former club, Niger Tornadoes.

I told everyone to wait because I was hoping that an opportunity to move to Europe might come. But while waiting, I also knew I needed to make a decision here once the season ended.

So, I asked God to lead me, and my heart chose Rangers. It is one of the clubs I love. I have always wanted to wear the white-and-red jersey, so I could not say no.

It is not just because they are champions. The manager is also a great coach who can make me better every day. That was another major reason why I chose Rangers.

PT: You have experienced different environments at Niger Tornadoes, Enyimba, and Nasarawa United. What have those clubs taught you about the NPFL, and how have those experiences prepared you for the demands of playing for a championship-winning side like Rangers?

Okechukwu: One thing I know about NPFL clubs is that every club has its own experience.

When I signed for Enyimba, for instance, I felt the most pressure because Enyimba is a very big club, not only in Nigeria but in Africa as well. The experience there was very different from what I had at Tornadoes and Nasarawa United.

I feel the same thing here at Rangers. Rangers is a very big club with that same mentality, so you have to raise your level regardless of how the pressure comes.

That is something every big player faces when they move to a big club. I am ready whenever I am called upon to put on the white-and-red jersey.

PT: Rangers are not just another NPFL club. They are the reigning champions and will carry enormous expectations into the 2026/27 season. How do you intend to handle the pressure of joining a team where winning is now the minimum expectation?

Okechukwu: Laughs. One thing I always have in my head is winning. That mentality is already inside me, so the pressure is not going to bring me down.

Rather, it will improve my game every day because when you come to a big club as a big player, you also need to show that mentality.

As I said earlier, I am ready for the challenge. It is about winning, winning and winning for the biggest club in the country right now.

PT: What have you made of Rangers’ midfield options, and where do you see yourself fitting into Fidelis Ilechukwu’s plans? Are you coming to compete for a starting position immediately, or are you prepared to fight your way into the team?

Okechukwu: In football, one thing I know is that nobody comes to a club as the automatic number one starter in his position. I don’t think so. Everybody has to fight for his spot.

I am not the only big player who has been signed on. Rangers have brought in a lot of very good and quality players, just like me.

So, I am ready to fight for my position because there are also established players in the team who played very well in the same position last season.

It is going to be a tug-of-war and a very big task, but that is normal in football. Everybody has to work hard to earn a spot.

Our TA [technical adviser] is a very tactical coach. He can fit you anywhere he chooses. But I think I am going to be playing in the number 10 position for him this season.

PT: At just 21, you are making an important move at a crucial stage of your development. What specific areas of your game are you hoping to improve at Rangers, and what kind of midfielder should supporters expect to see this season?

Okechukwu: When you are young, that is the time you have to fight your way up. My dream has always been very big.

The fans should expect a very good player because I am a very mobile midfielder, and I am sure they will love that.

Our fans will see good football, assists and goals, by the grace of God. I believe that.

PT: Rangers will have domestic and continental responsibilities this season. Does the opportunity to play on the African stage have any influence on your decision to join the club, and what would it mean to test yourself against some of Africa’s best clubs?

Okechukwu: Yes, the decision to join Rangers is also because I want to play against the top clubs on the continent. That is something I have at the back of my mind.

But it is not just about playing against them. It is about defeating them and showing that we are ready for that level.

I have a lot of confidence in this team, and they have confidence in me as well. I know that when we come together, we can defeat any club, whether in Europe or Africa.

So, we are ready to fight on the big stage.

PT: The NPFL is becoming increasingly competitive, with clubs investing heavily in their squads. Do you believe Rangers have enough quality to defend their title, and what do you think will be the biggest challenge in trying to retain the championship?

Okechukwu: Laughs. Yes. Everybody is recruiting quality and experienced players because the NPFL, as it stands now, is one of the best leagues in Africa.

Many clubs do not want to be left behind, so it is no longer just a game; it is about the badge. Rangers have the best squad right now, and the number of quality players they have signed shows that they are ready to lift the trophy again.

We all know it will not be easy. As I said, we are going to fight in every game, taking it one step at a time.

We pray that, in the end, we will become champions again.

PT: You have moved between several NPFL clubs at a relatively young age. Looking back, what has been the biggest challenge in your journey so far, and was there ever a moment when you questioned whether you would reach this level?

Okechukwu: Laughs. Yes, I have really questioned myself before.

I remember when I was still playing in the NNL with Sokoto United. We qualified for the Super Eight in Enugu, and I invited my senior brother to come and watch me play.

At the time, an NPFL match was also taking place. It was a very big game that we had the opportunity to watch while we were still playing in the Super Eight.

It was Enugu Rangers against Enyimba, and they were competing for the league title. I was sitting with my senior brother, and as the match was going on, the crowd was something else to see.

My elder brother called my attention and said, “Ifeanyi, how I wish you were the one playing this match. I would have been happier than anybody.”

I told him, “Big bro, you see these two clubs? You will remember this. I will play for the two.” He laughed and asked, “How possible is it?” I looked at him and said, “Okay.”

But today, it has happened. I told him, “Bro, I have played for Enyimba and now Rangers.” He clapped for me and said, *“You will go far. Your heart is too big.”

But, I told him that I am not the one, that I have a big God and that I have faith. According to him, the journey is not yet over. I also told him that I would play in Europe, and now he believes me.

So, I did not question myself. I only worked and prayed. That is my weapon.

PT: Finally, what is the one promise you want to make to the Rangers supporters ahead of the new season? And when we look back at the 2026/27 campaign, what do you want Ifeanyi Okechukwu to have achieved that will make this move a defining moment in your career?

Okechukwu: I want to make a statement with the club. I am very focused on achieving this. I also seek their support and belief in me. I will always give my all to represent them every time I am called upon, and I promise not to fail them.

World.title: Enyimba supporters demand continental ticket in new NPFL season
World.content:
Supporters of Enyimba International Football Club of Aba have urged the club’s management to ensure that its ongoing recruitment exercise produces a team capable of securing a continental ticket in the forthcoming Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL) season.

The supporters made the call in separate interviews with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Aba on Tuesday.

NAN reports that Enyimba finished the 2025/2026 NPFL season in 11th position with 49 points from 38 matches.

The supporters expressed disappointment with the club’s performance last season, saying they expected better results from the former continental champions.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

One of the supporters, Obinna Ohacha, said he expected the club to return to continental football in the new season.

“Enyimba is a household name and has become a continental club after winning two CAF trophies; so we are not demanding too much from the club,” Ohacha said.

Another supporter, Ekenedirichukwu Odunze, said he was disappointed that the club battled against relegation for much of the season before escaping on the final match day.

“Now we are going into the new season, and I hope the management and recruitment team have done their job well to avoid unwanted excuses,” he said.

Also speaking, Ifeoma Egbelu said Enyimba occupied a special place in the hearts of Aba residents, who expected the club to excel every season.

“Unfortunately, Enyimba will not be playing continental football this coming season, but the club should know that the Aba people need continental football.

“Aba people need good and quality football to justify the money and time they spend at the stadium, because many of them are business people,” she said.

The supporters urged the club’s management to strengthen the squad with quality players and ensure effective preparation ahead of the new season.

They also called for greater commitment from the players and technical crew to restore Enyimba’s status as one of Nigeria’s leading clubs.

World.title: Appraising the security challenges in the North-West, By Samuel Aruwan
World.content:
Last week, yours sincerely was in Gusau, Zamfara State, as one of the panelists and resource persons at the North-West Security Summit, themed “Appraising the Security Challenges in the North-West,” at the instance of the Inspector General of Police, Olatunji Disu.

It was a week of thorough deliberations and deep reflections. It also afforded one the opportunity to sneak out to frontline areas for an assessment and to visit the Theatre Command Headquarters of the Joint Task Force, Operation Fansan Yamma (OPFY), under the command of Major General WB Idris.

Some of us arrived on Monday and Tuesday ahead of the full commencement of the event. On the opening day, the Governor of Zamfara State, Dauda Lawal, was on hand with his entourage. The Emir of Zamfara and Chairman of the Zamfara State Council of Emirs, Alhaji Attahiru Muhammad Ahmad, stood in for the Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III, and led the other monarchs. AVM Bashir Saidu Gamagira (rtd), the Wakilin Soron Zazzau, represented the Emir of Zazzau, Ambassador Ahmad Nuhu Bamali. Also present were Commissioners of Police, military commanders and a pool of resource persons.

The Inspector General of Police, IGP Disu, started the day with a thought-provoking remark: “The security of the North-West is a collective responsibility and we are prepared to confront its challenges collectively. The North-West remains a region of enormous human, economic and cultural importance to Nigeria. It is home to millions of Nigerians, a region of rich traditions, vast agricultural potential, important commercial corridors and some of our most revered traditional institutions.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Disu further said: “Yet, the region continues to confront serious security challenges, particularly banditry, kidnapping, arms proliferation, communal and ethnic conflicts, farmer-herder tensions, violent criminality and other forms of insecurity which threaten lives, livelihoods, economic activity and social cohesion. These challenges are serious. But they are not insurmountable.”

On what should be done, the IGP asserted: “What is required is not simply a multiplication of security operations. What is required is a coherent, sustained and intelligence-driven regional response, supported by political will, strong institutions, community participation and genuine collaboration among all stakeholders. This is the essence of this summit.

“Distinguished guests, our experience has taught us one fundamental lesson: no single security agency can secure the North-West alone. The police cannot do it alone. The military cannot do it alone. The intelligence agencies cannot do it alone. State governments cannot do it alone. Traditional institutions cannot do it alone. And, importantly, the communities themselves cannot be excluded from the security architecture.”

Before returning the microphone to Governor Lawal, the IGP bemoaned ethnic profiling and labelling, which he described as a setback to the campaign against banditry. He argued: “We must also be very careful about how we define the problem before us. Criminality has no ethnicity and terrorism has no religion. We must resist the temptation to collectively label communities or ethnic groups because of the criminal conduct of individuals. Such profiling does not help security operations; rather, it creates mistrust, deepens divisions and can ultimately provide criminals with the environment they need to thrive.”

Governor Lawal, in his remarks, said: “The security crisis confronting the North-West has evolved beyond isolated incidents of criminality. Banditry, kidnapping for ransom, cattle rustling and other organised criminal activities have developed networks that operate across state boundaries, exploit difficult terrain, and threaten rural livelihoods, food security, education, investment and social cohesion. The summit document also rightly identifies emerging urban threats, including local thuggery, substance abuse and the infiltration of radical groups.”

One quite agreed with the governor’s position, considering the use of improvised explosive devices buried by bandits along routes used by security forces.

He went on to reiterate the position of the Zamfara State Government: “There must be verifiable cessation of violence, disarmament, renunciation of criminality, appropriate accountability mechanisms, rehabilitation and reintegration, alongside adequate safeguards for affected communities. It cannot mean rewarding criminality or placing perpetrators above their victims. Effective security pressure can create the conditions under which genuine cessation becomes possible. Those who sincerely choose peace should have a structured pathway out of violence; those who reject peace and continue to terrorise innocent citizens must face the full consequences of the law.”

During the technical sessions, the following topics were presented and critically examined by the panelists: “Cross-Border Arms Proliferation and Intelligence-Sharing Dynamics”; “Insecurity in the North-West: Causes, Impacts, Challenges and Prospects”; “Insecurity and the Criminal Justice System in the North-West”; and “Strengthening Security Governance in the North-West through Multi-Agency Collaboration and Community Policing.”

Former Inspector General of Police Usman Alkali Baba, whose paper centered on security governance, argued: “Security governance encourages the adoption of a multi-agency collaboration approach, which is the integration of a whole-of-government approach to the security management architecture and optimal engagement with the security ecosystem. It is founded on the principle of inter-security agency synergy for the purpose of evolving a uniform understanding of the threat amongst state security services, developing mutual inter-agency trust and pulling professional assets together to present a common front against state adversaries and complement each other rather than work at cross purposes.”

The former police boss further stated: “Multi-agency collaboration remains a topical issue in the discourse on security governance. While it is undoubtedly critical in internal security management, my experience as Inspector General of Police indicates that the national security agencies, as currently constituted, are, in practice, more competitive than complementary in their relationships. Each agency operates largely in isolation rather than in synergy.”

He advocated the institutionalisation of a protocol, stating: “To compound these challenges, there is, as of today, no National Inter-Agency Coordination Protocol to clearly delineate roles, address the identified challenges and set out clear procedures to govern the synergy question amongst national security agencies within the national security space.”

In his presentation, CP Ahmed Bello, the Commissioner of Police in Zamfara State, described insecurity in the North-West as a complex crisis affecting Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto and Zamfara States. He noted that the region covers about 216,065 square kilometres, has an estimated population of 60 million and remains one of Nigeria’s major agricultural centres. Its international borders, forests and remote rural communities make effective security control difficult.

Bello traced the crisis from local disagreements over land, water and cattle to organised banditry, kidnapping, terrorism, cattle rustling, extortion and territorial control. He identified porous borders, the proliferation of small arms and light weapons, vast ungoverned spaces, climate change, farmer-herder conflict, poverty, youth unemployment, illegal mining and ideological infiltration as some of its major causes.

He said weak border monitoring allows criminals, weapons and contraband to move through the region, while limited government presence and inadequate public services leave rural communities exposed. Environmental degradation, desertification and shrinking water resources have increased competition between farmers and pastoralists. Poverty and unemployment make some young people vulnerable to recruitment, while illegal mining provides money and logistical support for armed groups.

Bello cited figures showing the severity of the crisis. According to his presentation, 2,266 people were killed between January and June 2025, while more than 580,000 people had been forcibly displaced by February 2025. He also drew attention to the effects of insecurity on farming. In some areas, farmers are required to pay illegal protection levies before gaining access to their farms. This reduces food production and contributes to shortages and inflation beyond the region.

He identified difficult terrain, weak rural telecommunications, overstretched security agencies, inadequate equipment and training, fragile amnesty programmes, vigilante-related conflicts and poor regional border cooperation as challenges to ongoing operations. In his view, military and police action alone cannot produce lasting security without the restoration of governance and public services in affected communities.

CP Muhammad Rabiu, the Commissioner of Police in Kaduna State, described the North-West crisis as an adaptive security and governance emergency rather than a conflict involving a single group. According to him, banditry, kidnapping, extremist infiltration and illegal economic activities reinforce one another. What began as cattle rustling, rural crime and local disputes has developed into organised cross-border violence financed by ransom, extortion, stolen livestock and illegal mining.

Rabiu reported a 29 per cent increase in violence in the North-West in 2024, more than 900 fatalities in Sokoto between 2024 and 2025, and nearly 620,000 displaced persons across the region by 2026. His figures covered different periods from those cited by Bello, but both accounts brought attention to the human and economic cost of the crisis.

Rabiu noted that joint operations, including Operation Fansan Yamma, had dismantled camps and increased pressure on armed groups. However, some of the gangs had fragmented into smaller units, making them more difficult to identify and track. Intelligence gaps, community mistrust, weak inter-agency coordination, criminal financing, cross-border mobility and inconsistent government policies continue to limit progress.

He proposed a regional intelligence mechanism that would combine human intelligence, geospatial intelligence, financial intelligence and shared operational records. He also recommended providing security agencies with drones, reliable communication equipment, mobile units, forensic facilities and rapid-response capacity, particularly in rural and forested areas.

Rabiu called for the tracing of ransom and extortion payments, proper regulation of legal mining, the dismantling of mining sites controlled by armed groups, and closer monitoring of livestock and arms markets. He stressed the need for stronger border patrols and intelligence cooperation with Niger Republic and other neighbouring countries. Traditional rulers, religious leaders, women, young people and civil society organisations should also be included in protected early warning and local dispute-resolution arrangements.

AIG MS Dalijan (rtd), Commander-General of the Zamfara State Community Protection Guards, focused mainly on the origins, development and management of banditry in Zamfara State. He traced the early crisis to demographic pressure and growing competition over land. As farming expanded into grazing reserves and cattle routes, incidents of livestock damaging crops increased, leading to disputes over compensation and resentment between farmers and herders.

Dalijan said declining confidence in the formal court system encouraged both communities to adopt self-help measures. Farmers recruited local vigilantes known as ‘yansakai’, while some herders formed armed groups in forest areas. Cattle rustling and kidnapping for ransom later developed into an organised criminal economy supported by informants, arms suppliers and other collaborators.

He identified several alleged sources of weapons available to bandits, including armed groups in Chad and Libya, traffickers operating through Niger, attacks on Nigerian security personnel, foreign herders, Boko Haram, Ansaru and sponsors of illegal mining. He particularly mentioned the alleged activities of the “Arlit Boys,” whom he described as trafficking networks that exchange gold for weapons and move them from the Niger-Libya border into Zamfara.

Dalijan also said that cooperation between bandits and terrorist organisations had made the conflict more complicated, including the sharing of knowledge and materials for the production of improvised explosive devices.

On the security response, he identified the military, police, Department of State Services, Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, Community Protection Guards, vigilantes and hunters as participants in coordinated operations in Zamfara. He noted that the Zamfara State Government had established the Askarawan Zamfara Community Protection Guards and provided drones, armoured personnel carriers and patrol vehicles.

He said these measures had reduced attacks along major roads and enabled many farmers to return to their farms. However, informants within communities, difficult terrain, inadequate air support, the need to avoid civilian casualties and growing cooperation between bandits and terrorist groups remain serious challenges.

Dalijan also examined weaknesses in the criminal justice system. He credited the monthly security coordination meetings convened by the Zamfara State Governor with helping to speed up investigations and court proceedings. However, he expressed concern about prolonged pretrial detention, the use of holding charges before sufficient evidence had been obtained, and the failure to separate minor offenders from hardened criminals.

He warned that keeping minor offenders with hardened criminals could weaken rehabilitation and expose low-level offenders to more serious criminal influences. He recommended the proper classification and separation of prisoners, the restoration of vocational programmes in correctional centres, and compensation and psychological support for victims of banditry.

Security consultant Dr Sani Abdullahi Shinkafi examined the legal framework governing criminal justice in the North-West. He explained that the system operates under the Penal Code, the Criminal Procedure Code or state Administration of Criminal Justice Laws, and Sharia criminal legislation in applicable states.

Shinkafi identified corruption, political interference, executive control of judicial funding and poor access to legal aid as obstacles to the administration of justice. He argued that political pressure and control over judicial funding could compromise the independence of the judiciary. He also noted that many courts lack digital recording equipment, adequate facilities and reliable electricity, while correctional centres suffer from congestion, poor sanitation, inadequate healthcare and limited vocational and psychological support programmes.

He recommended electronic surveillance and biometric monitoring along vulnerable border routes, with the involvement of the Nigeria Customs Service and the Nigeria Immigration Service. He also called for properly regulated vigilante and hunter groups, secure reporting and protection arrangements for witnesses and informants, and the use of the North-West Development Commission to support infrastructure, agriculture, education and employment in vulnerable rural communities.

In my own presentation as a panelist, my central argument was that insecurity in the North-West cannot be addressed through security operations alone. Arrests, rescues and battlefield successes will not produce lasting peace unless they are converted into proper investigations, credible prosecutions, fair trials and correctional outcomes that protect society.

Banditry is not limited to gunmen operating in the forests. It depends on wider networks of informants, arms suppliers, financiers, ransom handlers, illegal miners and receivers of stolen livestock. Our criminal justice response must therefore dismantle the entire criminal ecosystem rather than concentrate only on the armed men.

Police investigations must begin early, preserve physical and digital evidence, trace financial transactions and reduce dependence on confessional statements. Security and justice agencies across the North-West must share intelligence and coordinate investigations because criminal groups operate across state boundaries.

Prosecutors should work with investigators from the beginning so that charges are based on evidence that can be proved in court. Courts must also manage security cases firmly and promptly while protecting fair-hearing rights, witnesses and victims.

Correctional institutions must regularly review awaiting-trial cases, separate high-risk offenders and support rehabilitation, deradicalisation and reintegration. Communities must be treated as partners through confidential reporting channels, witness protection, timely feedback and properly supervised local security groups.

I recommended the establishment of a North-West criminal intelligence and justice coordination mechanism, mobile forensic teams, joint investigation and prosecution teams, and clear procedures for transferring suspects and evidence obtained during military operations to the police and prosecuting authorities.

Other recommendations included financial investigations into banditry networks, electronic tracking of cases, protection for witnesses and informants, and regular reviews of awaiting-trial detainees.

Implementation must go beyond creating committees. Every institution should have defined responsibilities, deadlines and measurable outcomes. These must be supported by transport, communication equipment, forensic capacity, trained personnel and adequate funding.

Success should not be measured only by arrests or the number of criminals killed. We should also measure the criminal networks dismantled, financiers and suppliers prosecuted, lawful convictions secured, victims rescued and protected, and communities safely returning to their farms, schools, markets and highways.

The conferees generally agreed that the security crisis in the North-West had gone beyond isolated incidents of criminality. Banditry, kidnapping for ransom, cattle rustling and other organised criminal activities have developed into networks that operate across state boundaries, exploit difficult terrain, and threaten rural livelihoods, food security, education, investment and social cohesion. Emerging urban threats, including local thuggery, substance abuse and the infiltration of radical groups, were also identified.

It was agreed that states must move beyond fragmented responses. Criminal networks do not recognise state boundaries, and the security architecture cannot afford to operate in silos. Intelligence gathered in Zamfara may prevent an attack elsewhere in the North-West, just as operations in neighbouring states may disrupt criminal networks threatening communities across the region.

There was also a consensus that the North-West needs stronger arrangements for real-time intelligence sharing, coordinated operations, interstate surveillance, community policing and the sustained disruption of the financial, logistical and supply networks that support organised crime.

At the end of the week-long event, the resolutions from the sessions were contained in a communiqué read by the Commissioner of Police in Zamfara State, CP Ahmed Bello. The communiqué called for coordinated security operations to be carried out simultaneously across the North-West, with the police taking the lead and receiving support from the military.

State governors were expected to take ownership of the operations, while traditional and religious institutions were to be involved. The communiqué also recommended functional emergency telephone lines, prompt responses to distress calls, handshake patrols and direct action against bandits in their enclaves. The supervising DIG for the North-West and the Commissioners of Police in the seven states were also expected to participate in the North-West Governors’ Forum.

On law enforcement and justice, the communiqué called for proper investigation and prosecution of persons involved in banditry and related offences. It proposed criminalising ransom payments, giving Area Courts criminal jurisdiction for the speedy administration of justice and establishing special courts for banditry-related cases.

It also recommended the creation of a Victim Trust Fund to compensate victims, as well as the reformation, rehabilitation and empowerment of convicted persons.

Other points included disarmament and reconciliation, the replacement of traditional cattle-rearing practices with ranching, and the blocking of identifiable cattle routes to restrict cattle movement. The communiqué also proposed laws prohibiting the Almajiri system because of the vulnerability of the children involved. An implementation committee was to be established immediately to ensure that the resolutions were carried out.

The discussions in Gusau brought out the different sides of the security crisis confronting the North-West. Security operations remain necessary, but force alone cannot provide a lasting solution. The region also needs functional institutions, credible justice, accountable leadership, economic opportunities, community trust and sustained cooperation among the affected states.

Samuel Aruwan is a postgraduate student at Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria. Email: [email protected]

World.title: Why women’s voice should be heard, By Sam Akpe
World.content:
It started with visible empty seats. Then, suddenly, the rotunda of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs — designed for elite class activities — got thronged with quality audience. It was a well-planned, well-attended, and brilliantly executed event, with a theme that spoke to the moment.

The audience comprised ambassadors, top government representatives, technocrats, seasoned policy makers, tested security experts, confirmed women leaders, development specialists, civil society groups, young leaders, partners, and representatives of everyone connected to the issues that formed the centre of discourse.

Coordinating the events, with her trademark diplomatic finesse, was the ever-elegant veteran broadcast journalist, author, mentor, and event compere extraordinaire, Mrs Eugenia Abu. She did what only Eugenia can do — from the introduction of guests to a full grasp of the issues that summoned them.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Noisy, active politicians seemed to have been deliberately excluded. A select few who were invited conveniently sent representatives. This created rooms for exclusive focus on key security and development issues, instead of politics disguised as patriotism.

Hosted by a non-governmental organisation: I Teach Africa, the summit was themed: Empowering Her for Governance: Advancing Women’s Leadership for Inclusive Governance and Security.

It aimed at discussing the importance of inclusive governance and women’s meaningful participation in leadership, peace, security, and national development.

With well-applauded keynote addresses, panel discussions, leadership conversations, stakeholder engagement, and strategic perspectives on strengthening inclusive governance and building more resilient and secure communities, it drew some conclusions on vital issues concerning security.

Host of the conference, Mrs Ebi Elezieanya drew impressive applause in her opening remarks. She said armed conflicts anywhere affect women and girls differently, stressing the imperativeness of participation of women in security decision-making, and their inclusion in conflict prevention strategies.

Citing certain international agreements, she observed that women inclusion in security policy-making is not simply a gender issue, but an absolute incontrovertible necessity, because while security protects a nation, inclusion gives every citizen a reason to defend the nation.

Two heart-wrenching documentaries on how terror activities affect women and children were shown. Tears rolled down several cheeks as the visuals and sounds of the well-scripted and beautifully delivered audio wrapped the hall in total silence, with the caption: The Woman’s Voice Must Be Heard.

In an explosive speech, Dr Otive Igbuzor informed the audience that the issue of national security is fully connected to sustainable stability which on its own cannot be achieved without inclusive governance, which would also remain a mirage without transformational leadership.

His view was that national security cannot be guaranteed where a large section of the population, especially women, young persons, the disabled, the poor and the marginalised, are excluded from the political and economic decision-making process.

In all, he noted that inclusion is a development imperative, because it determines whose voice is heard, adding that security embodies inclusion, good governance, development, credible elections, and strong institutions.

The highly cerebral retired national security expert whose life-time involvement in ensuring a conflict-free Niger Delta and Nigeria at large has been archived, His Majesty, Dr Ferdinand Ikwang — the Mkpisong Ekid Afid — was a part of the panel discussion.

Ikwang said, in response to a question, that the starting point for any national security discourse is the community where everybody grew up, and that avoidable negligence of institutional memory has been the reason for failures in security architecture in Nigeria.

In a presentation entitled, “Inclusion as Security: the Niger Delta Model and the Imperative of Empowering the Nigerian Women,” Chief Ndutime Alaibe told the audience that his experience in the Niger Delta has taught him one belief: People are more likely to protect a system in which they have meaningful stakes.

He revealed that over the years, Nigeria has seen and treated the Niger Delta substantially as a security problem, but a better understanding has revealed that beneath the security drawbacks were questions of development, justice; and a profound crisis of belonging.

His conclusion, arising from this realisation, was that inclusion is not merely a social policy, but a national security policy. He explained that for too long, Nigeria’s understanding of security has been dominated by the instruments of safety such as soldiers, police officers, intelligence agencies, weapons, checkpoints, and surveillance.

‘Timi confirmed that while these remain necessary because any responsible state must possess the capacity to enforce its laws, defend its territory and protect its citizens, sustainable security goes beyond absence of violence to include the presence of conditions that make violence less attractive, less legitimate and less sustainable.

He said this boils down to: Justice — where citizens believe in fair treatment; then opportunity — which connotes that gains such as jobs, businesses, education, and hope, are derived from stability; and belonging — which implies that citizens see themselves as participants and not spectators outside the national project.

‘Timi was categorical that where these variables are absent, security institutions would be repeatedly asked to manage the consequences, but where they are present, citizens themselves would become stakeholders in stability.

As someone who has repeatedly been involved in the management of security issues in the Niger Delta, ‘Timi recalled that for decades, communities have watched enormous wealth leave their environment while many remained without adequate roads, electricity, clean water, employment opportunities and environmental remediation.

He said young people have seen sophisticated industrial infrastructure criss-cross their ancestral lands while struggling to see any meaningful pathway for themselves in the prosperity which their land represents, and that the widening gap between what they see and what they can access most times ignited violence based on frustration.

Whenever this happened, he said the Nigerian state always responded with security operations. However, could that be the solution? This is what ‘Timi thinks: “force can contain violence. It cannot, by itself, resolve the grievance that produces violence.”

This implies, in his words, that a checkpoint cannot create employment, a gunboat cannot create political belonging, a military operation cannot substitute development, and intelligence gathering cannot permanently compensate a community that has lost confidence in the system.

Accordingly, “the lesson was not that security operations were unnecessary. The lesson was that security without political, developmental and economic inclusion could never be sufficient.”

As he spoke, certain initiatives introduced to control this awkward situation came to mind. They included the framework called the Niger Delta Regional Development Master Plan, dreamt to provide a comprehensive development charter for the region.

Then, the Presidential Amnesty Programme which introduced disarmament, demobilisation, rehabilitation and reintegration as an alternative to endless military confrontation; and the Nigerian Content framework which significantly opened more space for Nigerian businesses, professionals and workers within the oil and gas value chain.

Also, in the inclusion package has been the Petroleum Industry Act which created Host Communities Development Trusts, in formal recognition of the fact that communities hosting petroleum operations must have an institutional stake in development.

The community-embedded pipeline surveillance, working alongside soldiers, intelligence agencies, regulators and operators, is another initiative that has demonstrated the value of local knowledge and community participation in protecting critical national assets.

‘Timi noted that though these initiatives were different and imperfect, a common principle runs through them: “Move people from the margins of the economy into the architecture of the economy. That is stake-holding.”

He continued: “When communities participate in protecting national assets, local knowledge becomes national intelligence; employment becomes a security instrument; and infrastructure protection becomes a shared interest.

“This is what I mean by inclusion as security. Not the abandonment of the state. Not the privatisation of national security. But the intelligent integration of communities into the security and economic architecture of the state.”

Then he moved from the general inclusion to the specific. ‘Timi said one of the clearest weaknesses of the Niger Delta peace architecture was the insufficient inclusion of women — the same women who have been the most victimised gender whenever there was environmental crisis or security conflict.

The technocrat reminded the audience that women have variously suffered from environmental degradation, lost livelihoods, lost husbands, sons and family members, sustained households during periods of instability, and participated in community advocacy and grassroots peacebuilding.

He said, “Yet when formal structures of negotiation, disarmament and reintegration emerged, women were overwhelmingly on the margins. Now, we must acknowledge an obvious fact: Niger Delta women were not generally the ones who took up arms against the state, so one would naturally expect fewer women in a disarmament programme. But that is precisely the point.

“We defined peace too narrowly around those who carried weapons, rather than around all those who carried the consequences of the conflict — and all those who could help sustain the peace.

“That is a lesson we must not forget. And the problem extends far beyond the Niger Delta. Women constitute approximately half of Nigeria’s population, yet they occupy only about four per cent of the seats in our National Assembly. Nigeria is yet to elect a woman as Governor of any of its 36 States.

“This is not simply a women’s issue. It is a national capacity issue. It is a democratic legitimacy issue, and yes, it is a national security issue, because no country can sustainably secure itself while systematically underutilising the intelligence, experience, economic capacity and leadership potential of approximately half its population.”

Suddenly, ‘Timi waxed spiritual. He cited the Holy Book. First, he cited Galatians 3:28 which says “there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Then Acts 2:17 where we are reminded that “your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.” The hall erupted in applause.

Then the preacher declared: “The message is profound: talent, capacity, calling and responsibility are not the exclusive preserve of one gender. So, we must change the language. Women must not appear in our national security framework merely as victims to be protected.

“They must be recognised as agents of security — as intelligence professionals, police officers, military officers, mediators, community leaders, entrepreneurs, legislators, policymakers, negotiators and peacebuilders.”

He went ahead to dwell on women economic inclusion, political inclusion, security-sector inclusion, and inclusion in the community peace architecture, adding that women-led organisations, traditional institutions, youth organisations and community networks should be integrated into early-warning systems, mediation structures and local security dialogue.

His thinking is that the woman in a rural community who detects the early signs of radicalisation may be contributing as much to national security as the analyst sitting before multiple screens in a command centre, and that Nigeria’s security architecture must learn to connect the two.

His conclusion pulled the hall to its feet in approval. He said every constituency represented at the summit had a lever to pull. Government must, “make gender-responsive budgeting measurable. Let appropriations demonstrate our priorities more loudly than communiqués.”

To the National Assembly, he advised, “history has again placed the question of women’s representation before you. Let this generation be remembered for opening the door” while the security agencies should, “move beyond recruitment numbers. Build deliberate pathways into command and strategic leadership.”

He told the industry operators to “apply the discipline of Nigerian Content to women’s participation — in procurement, contracting, employment, technical training and executive leadership,” while development partners and civil society must “help us measure what works,” because inclusion without measurement and economic power is mere rhetoric and tokenism.

The take home from the summit as captured by ‘Timi was that when citizens are given justice, they build faith in the system. When given opportunity, they acquire a stake in the system. If given a sense of belonging, they acquire a reason to defend the system.

Ultimately, the most secured Nigeria will not simply be the Nigeria with the strongest security forces. It will be the Nigeria in which the greatest number of its citizens believe that the country belongs to them—and that they belong to the country.

The concern of participants at the summit was mainly whether government would listen, consider, and implement the ground-breaking suggestions put forward by experts on the burning issues of development, national security, and inclusion.

Sam Akpe writes from www.wordsworthglobal.com

World.title: How Adeleke thwarted APC’s bid to reclaim Osun
World.content:
The defeat of the All Progressives Congress (APC) in Osun State’s 15 August governorship election was more than another change in the state’s political map. It marked the failure of the party’s attempt to return to the Government House four years after its candidate, Gboyega Oyetola, lost the seat to Ademola Adeleke in the 2022 election.

For Mr Adeleke, the victory was the culmination of a political journey that began less than a decade ago and was shaped by a powerful family name, an upset senatorial victory, a bitterly contested governorship election, a year of litigation over credibility of the 2018 election and, eventually, two successful bids for the state’s highest political office.

In the 15 August governorship election, Mr Adeleke, the Accord Party candidate, defeated his closest challenger, Bola Oyebamiji of the APC, to secure another four-year term. Mr Adeleke polled 511,067 votes against Mr Oyebamiji’s 444,815, according to the results declared by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

The governor was presented a certificate of return on Wednesday in Osogbo by INEC National Commissioner representing the South-west, Kunle Ajayi. At the event, Mr Adeleke announced plans to establish a N500 million endowment fund for victims of election-related violence.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, the victory has taken Mr Adeleke from a politician whose emergence was initially closely associated with the influential Adeleke family to an incumbent governor whom Osun voters have chosen to retain.

But that victory also fits into a broader pattern in Osun politics, where incumbency and party structures have repeatedly failed to guarantee political survival.

From family influence to political contender

Mr Adeleke did not enter Osun politics from an ordinary political background. He is the younger brother of Isiaka Adeleke, Osun’s first civilian governor and later a senator representing Osun West. Their father, the late patriarch of the Adeleke family, Ayoola Adeleke, served as a Nigerian senator during the Second Republic (1979–1983), representing the old Oyo State Senatorial District. The Adeleke family has since remained influential in the state’s political and social landscape.

Mr Adeleke’s political breakthrough came in 2017, following the death of his brother, which created a vacancy in the Osun West senatorial district.

To join the contest, he had initially sought the APC ticket but defected to the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) after failing to secure the ruling party’s nomination. He subsequently contested the July 2017 senatorial by-election on the PDP platform.

The election outcome immediately established him as a political force to reckon with. He polled 97,480 votes to defeat APC candidate Mudashiru Hussein, who secured 66,116 votes, winning nine of the 10 local government areas in the senatorial district.

The victory was particularly significant because the APC controlled the state government under Governor Rauf Aregbesola at the time. It showed that the Adeleke name could still translate into electoral support decades after the family first left its footprints on the political landscape of the state.

Mr Adeleke soon turned that momentum towards the big prize: the Osun governorship.

Osun voters and the want of changing governments

Mr Adeleke’s rise cannot be fully understood without examining Osun’s electoral history.

Since the return to democratic rule in 1999, the state has moved between political parties and administrations, producing one of the most competitive electoral landscapes in the South-west.

Bisi Akande of the Alliance for Democracy governed the state from 1999 to 2003 before Olagunsoye Oyinlola of the PDP defeated him in the 2003 governorship election. Mr Oyinlola subsequently secured a second term in 2007.

But Mr Oyinlola’s second term was cut short by a prolonged legal battle. Rauf Aregbesola of the Action Congress of Nigeria (ACN) – one of the legacy parties of today’s APC – who had lost the 2007 election, challenged the result in court. The Court of Appeal in 2010 declared him the rightful winner, overturning the earlier result.

The 2010 ruling fundamentally altered Osun’s electoral calendar, making it one of the Nigerian states where governorship elections are held off-cycle. During Mr Aregbesola’s first term, PDP was the ruling political party at the federal level under former president Goodluck Jonathan.

Mr Aregbesola subsequently won a fresh mandate for a second term in 2014 after his party, ACN, merged with other political parties in 2013 to form the APC, and governed the state until 2018, when his party’s candidate, Gboyega Oyetola, succeeded him after defeating his closest challenger Mr Adeleke of the PDP by a razor-thin margin.

Before Mr Oyetola was declared winner, the September 2018 governorship election was first pronounced “inconclusive” after the 353-vote margin separating Mr Adeleke and Mr Oyetola was lower than the 3,498 votes cancelled across seven polling units. Mr Adeleke had polled 254,698 votes, narrowly ahead of Mr Oyetola of the APC, who scored 254,345.

The supplementary rerun election held on 27 September, 2018, however, swung the contest in Mr Oyetola’s favour, leading to his declaration as winner. Mr Adeleke and the PDP challenged the result through the courts, but after a prolonged legal battle, the Supreme Court delivered the final verdict and affirmed Mr Oyetola’s victory.

Mr Oyetola’s tenure, however, lasted only one term after voters returned power to the PDP and elected Mr Adeleke in 2022. He defeated Mr Oyetola, then the incumbent, in a rematch that marked a decisive shift in the state’s political direction.

The pattern is significant: Osun voters have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to change political control of the state. Sometimes that change has happened at the ballot box; in Aregbesola’s case, it followed a successful legal challenge to an election result and then by a ballot for his second term.

The next test for Adeleke

Once again, Mr Adeleke’s re-election has truncated the APC’s immediate attempt to reclaim Osun, but it has also created a new political obligation for the governor.

His first term was defined by visible infrastructure projects, interventions in workers’ welfare, debt reduction and increased revenue mobilisation, but also by unresolved questions over education spending, healthcare sustainability, local government administration and the completion and quality of some major projects.

There were concerns raised about lopsidedness of projects favouring his Ede axis of the state and proclivity to award government appointments to relatives.

The second term will therefore be judged less by campaign promises and more by whether the administration can convert its first-term interventions into lasting improvements and be fairer in its distribution of projects and appointments.

‘Osun election was a demonstration of people’s power’

Prince Gutap, an election expert at Yiaga Africa and its consultant on democracy, said the outcome of the Osun election should also be understood as the willingness of voters to assert their choice at the ballot box.

He said the people’s active participation was one of the clearest lessons from the election, particularly their determination to ensure that their votes counted.

Although Mr Gutap cautioned against using Osun’s experience as a direct template for the entire country, noting that voter participation differs across Nigeria’s regions. But he said the state offers an important example of how an engaged electorate can shape political outcomes.

“The willingness of voters to participate actively in the election was to ensure that their choice at the poll determines who governs them. And that is an important element of democratic development,” he said.

He pointed to an incident during the election in which citizens alerted the police after allegedly identifying a man they suspected was attempting to buy votes. According to him, police responded and arrested the individual.

“That’s the level of trust we want to have in our security agencies, that when we see a problem or when we see an issue, we can be able to walk to them and tell them, ‘There’s a problem here,’ and then they will quickly respond to it,” Mr Gutap said.

He noted that Osun State’s political history shows that voters can reward incumbents, but they can also withdraw that support when they decide to change direction.

“We have seen how voters have voted out incumbent governors at some points and, at other times, re-elected governors. What that tells us is that voters respond to leaders who address their problems and improve their welfare,” Mr Gutap added.

Also, public affairs journalist and analyst, Dayo Akintobi, expressed that the outcome of the recently concluded Osun’s governorship election demonstrated the growing power of Osun voters to determine electoral outcomes.

READ ALSO: Osun constitutes committee to disburse N500m fund to election violence victims

Speaking on Channels Television, Mr Akintobi said the outcome reflected the will of voters who remained engaged throughout the electoral process, despite concerns over violence, intimidation and alleged vote-buying ahead of the election.

According to him, voters’ determination to protect their ballots made it difficult for any political or institutional force to subvert their choice.

“What happened in Osun was what we call people power. People’s power showed its capabilities, and nobody rested on their laurels and allowed themselves to be trampled over by juggernauts, by political opposition, by even federal might,” he said.

The analyst also pointed to the reported prevalence of vote-buying during the election, arguing that if voters collected money but still voted according to their conscience, politicians could eventually begin to question the value of spending huge sums to influence voters.
