Participants engage with reading materials and exercises intended not simply to determine whether they can pronounce words, but whether they can understand, explain, question and apply what they have read.

TRFLI considers reading and comprehension essential to civic reform, arguing that access to information alone is not enough. Citizens must also be able to understand information, evaluate it critically and make informed decisions.

TRFLI in action: Participants engage in reading and comprehension exercises during the official launch of the initiative on August 22, 2026, at Kids and Us Preparatory Elementary School in Jackson Hill, Rehab Community, Paynesville.

“A citizen who can read, understand and think is a citizen who can build, lead and transform.”

The Reformpreneur Magazine Set for September Launch

TRFLI’s third flagship platform, The Reformpreneur Magazine, is scheduled to launch in September 2026.

The digital publication will expand the organization’s educational mission through articles, research, interviews, commentary and positive stories centered on Liberia and its people.

The magazine will cover issues including reform, entrepreneurship, education, agriculture and food security, leadership, civic responsibility, business, community development and the stories of Liberians working to create positive change.

TRFLI also expects the publication to contribute to a stronger culture of reading while connecting Liberians at home with the diaspora and friends of Liberia.

Three Programs, One Civic Mission

The three initiatives are designed to complement one another.

TRFL Radio Prime gives citizens a platform to listen, learn and engage.

The Reading & Comprehension Initiative provides an opportunity to read, understand, question and develop critical-thinking skills.

The Reformpreneur Magazine will provide a platform to read, learn, document ideas and share positive Liberian stories.

The organization describes the rollout as:

August 1: A voice for civic education.

A voice for civic education. August 22: Education in the community.

Education in the community. September: A platform for ideas, research and positive stories.

Why the Reform Front Liberia Was Established

TRFLI says Liberia’s future will depend not only on its political leadership but also on the quality of its citizens, institutions, businesses, educators, professionals, communities and civic organizations.

The organization was established around the conviction that national development requires responsibility at every level of society.

“Government has responsibilities. Institutions have responsibilities. Businesses have responsibilities. Community leaders have responsibilities. And citizens have responsibilities,” the organization says.

TRFLI seeks to encourage a culture in which Liberians become better informed, accept greater personal and civic responsibility, demand accountability appropriately, value education and reading, participate constructively in their communities and contribute solutions rather than merely identifying problems.

Nonpartisan, Civic and Educational

The Reform Front Liberia, Inc. emphasizes that it is not a political party or political campaign organization.

Its mission is civic and focuses on citizens, education, responsibility, accountability, entrepreneurship, community development and Liberia’s long-term progress.

The organization believes Liberians with different political views, backgrounds and experiences can find common ground around education, responsible citizenship, stronger institutions and national development.

Message From the Founder and Executive Director: Doug Zack Miller

Miller says Liberia’s transformation will require more than the efforts of any single individual, organization or government.

“Liberia’s transformation will not come from one person, one organization or one government. It will require citizens who are informed, responsible, educated and willing to participate in building their communities and their country.”

According to Miller, TRFLI was established because reform must move beyond conversation.

“We must educate, organize, build programs and demonstrate through action what responsible citizenship can accomplish.”

He said the organization’s three flagship programs are intended to provide different avenues for civic engagement.

“Radio Prime gives us a voice. Our Reading & Comprehension Initiative takes education directly into the community. The Reformpreneur Magazine will give us another platform to document ideas, entrepreneurship and positive Liberian stories.”

“We are starting deliberately and building step by step,” Miller added. “Our objective is not simply to talk about a better Liberia. We want to participate constructively in building one.”

What Comes Next

TRFLI says it intends to continue developing its programs carefully and sustainably, with an immediate focus on strengthening the three flagship initiatives already underway or scheduled for launch.

Radio Prime will continue its weekly civic education broadcasts, while the Reading & Comprehension Initiative will continue its community-based educational activities.

The first edition of The Reformpreneur Magazine is scheduled for September 2026.

As its organizational capacity grows, TRFLI says it will explore additional educational and community-impact programs consistent with its civic mission, with emphasis on sustainable initiatives with clear and achievable objectives.

An Invitation to Liberia and the Diaspora

The Reform Front Liberia is inviting citizens, educators, professionals, businesses, community organizations, young people, volunteers, Liberians in the diaspora and friends of Liberia to participate in its civic efforts.

Opportunities include volunteering, contributing professional expertise, partnering with programs, sponsoring initiatives and supporting the organization’s educational and community-impact activities.

TRFLI particularly welcomes businesses and institutions that view investment in education, informed citizenship and community development as an investment in Liberia’s future.

World.title: Chief Chimese seeks early inputs
World.content:
Chief Chimese of the Ushi people in Mansa District has urged the Food Reserve Agency (FRA) and the Ministry of Agriculture to commence the distribution of farming inputs under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) before the onset of the rains.

In an interview with the media, Chief Chimese noted that by September and October, farmers will begin land preparation ahead of the rainy season.

He emphasised that in order for farmers to maintain the positive trajectory of maize production seen in the 2025/2026 farming season, farming inputs must be distributed on time to ensure timely planting.

“I am grateful to the government for the way the Food Reserve Agency is working. Our farmers are being paid on time, and this time around we are appreciating the electronic system of paying farmers via mobile money services. This is why even when it comes to inputs, they should be given on time,” said Chief Chimese.

The traditional leader further observed that the government needs to start empowering farmers with irrigation systems so that the country can produce maize all year round.

“We are doing well in production, and just as President Hakainde Hichilema has been talking about increasing maize output, we now need to seriously consider irrigation so that crop production continues throughout the year,” he said.

Meanwhile, a farmer at Mano Satellite Depot in Mansa District, Aaron Chanda, commended the Food Reserve Agency for paying farmers through mobile money services.

“Previously, we used to line up at banks for days before receiving our money. Now, farmers are paid via mobile money within three days,” he said.

Mr Chanda added that the initiative is commendable and urged that payment services be further improved to make the cost of doing business easier for farmers.

World.title: PIDACC boosts Mwinilunga mechanisation
World.content:
Government through the Program for Integrated Development and Adaptation to Climate Change (PIDACC) with support from the African Development Bank (AfDB) has over the last one year handed over an assortment of agriculture mechanisation equipment to three wards in Mwinilunga District of North-western Province.

The equipment which include three tractors, three rippers with calter and crumbler, three maize shellers, three Boom sprayers, three multicrop planters and three trailers have been procured at the cost of overK5.1 million.

District Agricultural Coordinator Lewis Chiwele said the agricultural equipment has been distributed to Chibwika, Ntambu and Kakoma wards to support farmers and build resilience against the effects of climate change.

Mr Chiwele explained that the equipment has brought about agricultural efficiency as farmers are now able to prepare their fields, harvest and shell their crop within a short period of time while implements such as trailers are being used to transport their farm produce to markets and satellite depots.

“This program has proven that this support can improve the efficiency of our farming operations, most of our farmers have had challenges to prepare their land, to harvest, to shell, now with this support our farmers are able to save time” he said.

He said the program is equally critical in contributing to the government’s target of 10 million metric tonnes of annual maize production by 2031 adding that farmers in the three wards are eager to utilize the equipment to increase their agriculture productivity.

Boaz Mukanzu a farmer in Kamfumbu area of Chibwika ward thanked the government for implementing the PIDACC project stating that it has afforded him efficiency and reduced production cost.

Mr Mukanzu said using the machinery, he was able to cultivate over three hectares within a day and shell his maize on time which previously took him months to do.

“We thank the government because this project has significantly reduced our manual labour and we now can shell maize or cultivate as much as three hectares in a day,” he said.

The PIDACC project targets to build resilience in farmers that are vulnerable to effects of climate change through mechanisation in communities along the Zambezi river basin.

World.title: Opposition Alliance Asks African Union To Halt Hichilema’s Inauguration
World.content:
Lusaka — The Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance has asked the African Union to urgently intervene in Zambia’s post-election crisis, arguing that the closure of the country’s courts during the constitutional petition window and the planned September 1 inauguration of President-elect Hakainde Hichilema together threaten to place the disputed election beyond judicial scrutiny.

Former Zambian Ambassador to Ethiopia and Permanent Representative to the African Union, Emmanuel Mwamba, made the appeal in a letter dated August 25 addressed to African Union Commission chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf on behalf of the opposition alliance.

“The gravest of these breaches can still be arrested, but only before the inauguration scheduled for 1 September 2026 renders judicial scrutiny of the election moot,” Mwamba wrote.

He said Zambia was facing a situation in which the constitutional and judicial mechanisms designed to allow an election result to be challenged were themselves being disabled. Mwamba specifically cited the sealing of court premises across the country on August 24, including the Lusaka High Court complex and the building housing the Constitutional Court, by armed military and police personnel. He said lawyers had been instructed to leave the premises, and that an unsigned memorandum had been issued to Judiciary staff communicating the closure, with no formal public explanation offered of its legal basis, scope or duration.

Mwamba argued the timing made the closure especially serious, since it fell on the final day of the seven-day constitutional period for challenging the declaration of the President-elect before the Constitutional Court. He noted the Judiciary had itself recorded that the Constitutional Court Registry was required to remain open from 08:30 to 18:00 hours specifically for the purpose of receiving a presidential election petition.

“A State cannot demand that election disputes proceed through exclusively legal channels while physically sealing those channels, and it cannot rely on an impossibility of its own creation,” Mwamba stated.

He said the closures had already directly affected a petition involving former Law Association of Zambia president Linda Kasonde, activist Brebner Changala and the LCK Freedom Foundation, which names the Electoral Commission of Zambia, the Attorney General and Hichilema as respondents. According to Mwamba, that petition was transmitted electronically to the Chief Justice after physical access to the courts had been prevented, and the Judiciary had acknowledged receiving it before the Chief Justice referred the documents to the Constitutional Court to determine whether the filing was valid.

Mwamba contrasted that acknowledgment with a statement from Secretary to the Cabinet Patrick Kangwa that the Judiciary had not received any petition, arguing the two positions were irreconcilable. He also challenged the planned September 1 inauguration itself, saying it risked pre-empting the constitutional mechanism for resolving the dispute if it proceeded before the Constitutional Court had ruled on whether the petition was properly filed.

The letter further raised concerns over the reported deployment of the armed forces at polling stations, tallying centres and the National Results Centre, as well as the August 14 security operation at the residence of Tonse-Pamodzi presidential candidate Brian Mundubile. Mwamba said former Cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was killed during that operation, and that 11 people, including senior opposition figures, were reportedly arrested. He noted the operation occurred shortly after Mundubile had met the African Union Election Observation Mission, arguing this raised questions under the African Charter concerning security guarantees and cooperation with election observers.

Mwamba also questioned the conduct of the Electoral Commission of Zambia, citing its suspension of vote tallying and results announcement on August 14 and the subsequent declaration of results in the early hours of August 18. He said the Commission had declined to publish polling-station-level results in an analysable format or release Records of Proceedings at Tallying Centres and GEN20 forms.

He cited an analysis by Professor Nic Cheeseman of the University of Birmingham and Dr Nicole Beardsworth of the University of the Witwatersrand, which he said identified significant differences between presidential and parliamentary turnout figures in several constituencies, differences the analysis estimated could account for between 350,000 and 550,000 votes concentrated in ruling-party strongholds. Mwamba said the discrepancies warranted examination by the Constitutional Court rather than being treated as conclusive evidence of wrongdoing on their own.

The letter asks the African Union Commission to bring the matter before the Peace and Security Council under Article 24 of the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance, and to remain seized of the situation through the petition period and the planned inauguration. It further asks the AU to urgently engage the Zambian government to restore full access to the courts and to refrain from proceeding with the September 1 inauguration while the Constitutional Court considers the petition filing issue.

Mwamba called for the preservation of all electoral materials and audit-trail documents, including polling-station results, Records of Proceedings at Tallying Centres and GEN20 forms, alongside an independent investigation into both the closure of the Judiciary and the August 14 operation in which Kafwaya was killed. The alliance also wants the AU to call for the rights of those detained in connection with the election to be respected, including access to lawyers and the courts, and to consider further measures should the alleged breaches continue.

Mwamba said the African Charter should not be treated as merely aspirational, arguing that Zambia’s own institutions, churches and civil society organisations were themselves calling for regional intervention over what he described as a threat to judicial independence and the rule of law.

World.title: Zesco face Malawi’s Strikers in COSAFA semis
World.content:
Zambian champions Zesco Ndola Girls will face Malawi’s Silver Stars in the semifinals of the ongoing CAF Women’s Champions League | COSAFA Qualifier Botswana 2026.

Zesco and Strikers will clash in the first semifinal on Thursday afternoon.

Strikers booked a date against Zesco after defeating Nsingizini Hotspurs 5-1 on Tuesday evening to make it two wins from three in Group B.

Carolyne Mathyola netted a hat-trick, while there were further strikes from Grace Kakangula and Gladys Banda.

The match between Zesco and Strikers is expected to be another battle between old foes Zambia and Malawi on the COSAFA platform.

Zesco were beaten finalists last year and have more experience, but Strikers have shown enough in this tournament to suggest they can be a match for anyone.

The Ndola-based Zambian champions booked their semi-final spot in style, securing top spot in Group A with a 2-0 victory over hosts Gaborone United at the Gaborone United Stadium on Monday evening.

Zesco finished Group A with maximum 9 points from 3 games: following victories over Lesotho Defence Force (1-0) and Zimbabwe’s Herentals Queens (5-2).

Zesco coach Florence Mwila says her side is ready for the semi-finals.

“We are prepared. This is a tournament so you meet any opponent and you must be prepared,” she told journalists in Gaborone.

Meanwhile, Sundowns confirmed top spot in Group B with a 4-1 win over Costa do Sol in their final pool encounter at the Gaborone United Stadium on Tuesday.

It was another comfortable outing for The Brazilians as goals from Asanda Hadebe, Wendy Shongwe, Ronnel Donnelly and Melinda Kgadiete sealed victory.

Lucia Moçambique scored directly from a corner for Costa do Sol to take her tally in the tournament to four goals and move into the outright lead in the Golden Boot race.

Sundowns collected a full haul of nine points from their three group games, though they conceded for the first time in the tournament.

World.title: Let love lead: Zambia’s digital conscience after the ballot
World.content:
For generations, Zambia has worn the identity of a peaceful nation, a country where people of different tribes, faiths and political loyalties have lived side by side, recognising one another first as fellow citizens. It is worth asking, honestly, whether that identity is beginning to slip.

It has become disturbingly common to see a person’s death met not with condolence but with mockery, insult or a political score being settled in real time on social media. Behind every death sits a family in mourning. Death is not a contest, and it is certainly not licence to humiliate the departed or gloat over their pain.

Before posting anything online, a simple test still applies: is it true, is it necessary, is it kind? Words now move faster than judgment. A careless post can circle the country within minutes; a cruel meme can land in front of a grieving child and remain there indefinitely.

Freedom of expression carries a corresponding duty. The right to hold an opinion does not confer the right to strip a grieving family of dignity, or to desecrate the memory of the dead. Zambia’s stated values of human dignity, unity and non-discrimination cannot live only in the Constitution or in ceremonial speeches. They must show up in how citizens actually speak to one another, especially when political feeling is running hottest.

The greater danger is not today’s cruelty but its normalisation. Children are watching, absorbing the words their elders choose and the behaviour their communities reward online. No nation builds lasting peace while quietly teaching its youngest citizens that laughter is an acceptable response to another person’s death, simply because that person voted differently.

The Zambia worth protecting is one where political opponents can still greet each other, where neighbours mourn together regardless of ballot choices, and where death is answered with dignity rather than derision. Before sharing an unkind word about someone’s passing, one question is usually enough to give pause: what if this were my own father, my mother, my sister, my child?

Before political affiliation, Zambians are Zambians. Before tribe, they are human beings. It is time to disagree with dignity, contest ideas rather than insults, and mourn with compassion instead of celebrating with hatred. Politics must never be allowed to strip that humanity away.

By Osmond Kalaba

Source: Zambia Daily Mail (“Call for Zambia to embrace love, humanity”)

World.title: Petition Or No Petition, Zambia’s Courts Hold The Real Verdict
World.content:
Zambia’s transition of power now rests on an unresolved legal question with a fixed deadline attached: does the Constitutional Court have a valid petition in front of it, and can it rule before Hakainde Hichilema is sworn in on September 1. The Constitution gives the court 14 days from a properly filed petition to decide. Nobody, not the Judiciary, not State House, not the lawyers involved, agrees on whether that clock has even started.

The stakes go beyond procedure. A government bond auction closed this week with demand exceeding its K6.3 billion target by 37 percent, a sign investors are pricing in political continuity after the election. That confidence assumes the transition holds. An unresolved petition, or a Constitutional Court ruling that reopens the result, would test it directly.

The Judiciary’s official account is simple. Chief administrator Nalishebo Imataa told Secretary to Cabinet Patrick Kangwa that no petition had reached the Constitutional Court Registry by 18:00 hours on August 24, the seventh and final day allowed under Article 103 of the Constitution. Kangwa announced the September 1 swearing-in on that basis. Lawyer Linda Kasonde disputes the premise entirely. She says she attempted to file electronically through the Registry before the deadline and the submission bounced, so she forwarded the documents instead to Chief Justice Mumba Malila’s private email address. Malila has confirmed receiving them, called the method “highly irregular,” and referred them to the Constitutional Court regardless of the irregularity, meaning the question of whether the filing counts sits with the court itself rather than settled by administrative rejection.

Neither side has produced a timestamped record resolving the dispute. The Judiciary has not released logs showing the Registry submission failed or when. Kasonde has not published proof of the attempted filing time. That gap is the actual story: not who is lying, but that nobody has yet shown their work.

What sharpens the doubt is what was happening at the courts during the window Kasonde says she was trying to use. The Law Association of Zambia has confirmed court premises in Lusaka and Ndola were sealed off with tape marked “Crime Scene,” with no public explanation released at the time. LAZ president Lloyd Kaluba says the association still has no formal word on the legal basis for the closure, its scope or its duration, and has demanded both reopening and clarification.

State House rejects any link to the petition. Chief communications specialist Clayson Hamasaka says the August 24 measures covered the Ministry of Justice, the National Prosecution Authority and the Attorney General’s Chambers as well as the Judiciary, calling them intelligence-led precautions rather than action against a single litigant. His position is that the filing window opened on August 18, when the Electoral Commission declared the result, and that courts operated normally on the working days before the closure, with no petition lodged in that stretch. He has challenged anyone claiming a prepared petition was blocked to produce evidence of when and how they tried to lodge it. The Judicial Workers Union offers a third, unrelated explanation, with president Peter Mwale saying the closure followed the arrest of a Judiciary security officer over a detected threat and had nothing to do with any petition.

Constitutional lawyers are split on what happens if the Court finds the filing came late. Mehluli Batakathi says the seven-day window is absolute and no avenue remains once it closes. Tresford Chali argues the Court can extend the deadline where circumstances beyond a petitioner’s control, court closures among them, justify it, and that the Constitution should not be read so rigidly that the facts on the ground are ignored. Which interpretation prevails will likely determine whether the Court even reaches the merits of the case.

A second, separate legal challenge adds further pressure regardless of how the filing dispute resolves. Activist Brebner Changala and Kasonde have petitioned the Constitutional Court citing Christian Churches Monitoring Group data placing Hichilema’s vote share at 56 percent against the Electoral Commission’s declared 60.5 percent, and alleging vote figures were altered between polling stations and constituency tally centres.

The petitioners also cite the killing of former Lunte Member of Parliament Mutotwe Kafwaya and the deployment of the Zambia Defence Force to polling stations as evidence the election environment fell short of constitutional standards. Kafwaya’s death has kept NRPUP’s presidential candidate, Brian Mundubile, and running mate Makebi Zulu, out of public view; both say they remain in a secure location over safety concerns, a decision that has split their own party. NRPUP’s registered president, Ezra Tembo, has broken with his party’s candidates to congratulate Hichilema and accept the result.

The Drug Enforcement Commission’s parallel case has not slowed the legal standoff but has added to the week’s uncertainty. The agency says 79 people of nine nationalities, arrested at Evana Estates in New Kasama, ran a digital laboratory targeting government systems linked to the Electoral Commission, with computers, hard drives and foreign currency seized. Spokesperson Allan Tamba says all suspects will be processed under normal constitutional protections.

What happens next has a clock on it. If the Constitutional Court accepts either petition as validly filed, Article 103(2) gives it 14 days to rule, a window that would run past the scheduled September 1 inauguration. Whether the ceremony proceeds as planned, is delayed, or goes ahead under legal challenge is now the single fact markets, diplomats and Zambians themselves are waiting on the Court, not the politicians, to settle.

World.title: When Words Become Weapons
World.content:
The Book of James offers an old warning for a modern crisis: the tongue is small, but it can set a forest ablaze. After a contested election, Zambia is discovering just how quickly loose words can outrun public patience.

Abigail Kabandula, a scholar who has spent more than a decade studying conflict in Somalia and South Sudan, watched Zambia’s 2026 election unfold with mounting unease, not chiefly because of the political contest itself, but because of how casually some quarters flirted with violent language, against a backdrop of reported firearms and machetes seized from individuals allegedly preparing for confrontation.

Zambia has been fortunate. It has absorbed political tension, disputed results and sporadic violence without ever tipping into the full-scale civil wars that have scarred its neighbours. That record breeds a dangerous illusion that war happens elsewhere, to other people. Kabandula’s own experience argues otherwise. At the University of Zambia she befriended a Burundian who had walked, largely on foot, across the continent to escape ethnic slaughter in 1993, unsure if any of his family had survived and unable to go home. Years later, at Meheba Refugee Settlement, she found Hutu and Tutsi refugees still housed apart more than a decade after Rwanda’s genocide the mistrust too deep, even then, for them to live side by side. War, she learned, does not end when the shooting stops. Buildings can be rebuilt. Trust between neighbours is far harder to restore.

That is the lesson James’s counsel offers today: truth must still be spoken, but it must be disciplined and evidenced, never weaponised. A supporter declaring readiness “to die and to kill” is no less combustible than an opponent accusing the state of wanting to “kill people with military weapons” before any claim has faced a courtroom. Both freeze public opinion into camps before the facts have had their say.

Government has alleged armed insurrection and militia activity; opposition figures have called the security response fabricated and political. Contradictory public explanations on both sides including a violent statement first dismissed as artificial intelligence before later being acknowledged as genuine have only corroded trust at the moment the country needs it most.

History is not subtle about where this road leads. Rwanda’s genocide did not begin with machetes; it began with language that stripped neighbours of their humanity long before killing followed. The former Yugoslavia told its communities that coexistence was weakness until checkpoints and killing fields replaced daily life. Kenya’s 2007 election crisis showed how quickly disputed results, ethnic suspicion and inflammatory broadcasting can combine to cost more than a thousand lives.

Maturity now requires government to separate criticism from treason and dissent from conspiracy unless proof says otherwise and it requires opposition figures to separate resistance from recklessness. Courts exist to determine guilt; accusation is not conviction, and evidence must always travel further than a slogan. No grievance, however real, is worth the country in which it is aired. Zambians who can disagree politically while still sharing a meal, marrying across tribal lines and sending their children to the same schools have built something rare and it survives only as long as the tongue that built it does not turn against it.

By Dr Lawrence Mwelwa and Abigail Kabandula

Source: The Mast (“A nation can bleed from the tongue before the sword,” Weekly Reflections) and Zambia Daily Mail (“Flirting with war: A cautionary tale”)

World.title: Mazembe trample Nkana in test match
World.content:
In a closed-door pre-season friendly, Nkana FC on Tuesday welcomed continental heavyweights TP Mazembe of DR Congo as they suffered a 3-1 defeat at home in Wusakile.

Yet for Coach Elijah Tana and the 13-time Zambian champions, the scoreline at Nkana Stadium told only half the story.

According to Tana, the friendly match was not about winning. This was about measuring.

Mazembe are no ordinary opponents. Five-time CAF Champions League winners.

The standard-bearers of Central African football. For a Nkana side rebuilding ahead of the 2026 MTN Super League Transition Season, this was exactly the kind of test Tana asked for.

“We wanted high-level opposition,” a member of the technical bench told this magazine after the game. “You learn more in 90 minutes against Mazembe than in three games against local sides.”

Kalampa came out with purpose. The frontline pressed high, and early on Lazarous Kambole beat the offside trap and forced Mazembe’s defence into a scramble inside the box. For 43 minutes, Nkana looked the more energetic side.

In the 44th minute, just before halftime, Dante Joël Molindo Mbala found space and broke the deadlock. 1-0 to Mazembe at the break.

If the first goal was a warning, the next two were a masterclass.

4Barely a minute after restart, Bingi Belo struck to make it 2-0 before Gideon Mwanza added a third with a composed finish. 3-0.

With 21 minutes left, Kalampa got a lifeline when Charles Zulu stepped up and converted from the penalty spot.

With Nkana pushing, Kambole, tireless as ever, almost pulled a second in the 78th minute but was denied by a superb save from Mazembe keeper Aliou Faty.

Meanwhile, Nkana’s defeat comes as Zambian football prepares for a unique 2026 Transition Season – a bridge campaign designed to realign the league calendar.

World.title: Zambia: 'I Became Protective' - A Cancer Survivor's Fight to Fix Zambia's Health System
World.content:
"Once you go through something as traumatic as a cancer diagnosis, you automatically become protective of the next person," said Karen Nakawala, a Zambian broadcaster and cervical cancer survivor.

Nakawala knows that trauma firsthand. In 2019, her life changed when she was diagnosed with cervical cancer.

The diagnosis forced Nakawala to confront the disease she would later dedicate much of her life to talking about publicly. After treatment, she converted her experience into advocacy, determined to help other women recognize the importance of early screening and seeking care.

During her own treatment, she said she saw gaps throughout the healthcare system, with many women falling through the cracks, a realization that pushed her from patient to advocate. "I believe that cancer healthcare solutions should be culturally grounded given our diverse culture and should be rooted in those who live it," she said.

Through her journey, she created Teal Sisters Foundation, an organization that has become a platform for women to access information, share their experiences, and seek support without judgment. Her private Facebook community, initially created as a safe space where women could speak openly about their health without being judged, has grown to more than 137,000 members. The women-only Facebook community aims to boost access to cervical cancer screening, prevention and treatment in Zambia.

Cancer is an increasing burden in Zambia.

The International Agency for Research on Cancer indicates that cervical cancer is still the most prevalent form of cancer in the country, with 4,730 estimated new cases in 2024. It was also the most prevalent form of cancer causing death and accounted for 2,769 cancer-related deaths in the same year. Breast cancer was the second most prevalent form of cancer among women, with 1,555 estimated new cases and 730 deaths.

Zambia has the third-highest burden of cervical cancer in the WHO African Region after Eswatini and Malawi

There is also a huge shortage of specialists in the country. Ministry of Health data shows that Zambia has just six oncologists serving a population of about 20 million people. To help close this gap, Zambia has, since 2006, invested in training nurses to play a greater role in cervical cancer prevention and care, including screening, treatment and vaccination.

Against this backdrop, the reopening of the radiotherapy and imaging unit at Lusaka's Cancer Diseases Hospital takes on particular significance.

For years, patients needing radiotherapy faced a major gap in the country's cancer-care system. Lusaka's Cancer Diseases Hospital was shut down in 2020 for a major upgrade. Its closure left patients with fewer treatment options and forced them, in some cases, to seek care outside the country. Nearly 1,000 patients were left waiting for radiotherapy during the interruption, with about 600 referred to India for treatment, according to health authorities.

Nakawala described the six-year gap as "the worst period in Zambia's cancer healthcare space."

She said the country lost many women to breast and, in particular, cervical cancer, some diagnosed at early stages that could have been treated with good outcomes had radiotherapy been available. Those who could afford it traveled outside the country for treatment, she said, at "an astronomical out-of-pocket spend for families." That gap, she said, has left a large backlog of patients now waiting for treatment, placing pressure on the newly reopened unit.

Zambian Cancer Society/LinkedIn The opening of the refurbished radiotherapy and imaging section of the Cancer Diseases Hospital, Lusaka

Zambia's reopening of the radiotherapy and imaging cancer treatment facility at Lusaka's Cancer Diseases Hospital pushed for better women's cancer care in Africa. The facility was upgraded and commissioned by President Hakainde Hichilema in August, 2026. It can now treat up to 60 patients a day.

For patients, the restoration of the service means that specialised cancer treatment can once again be accessed closer to home, reducing the delays, travel and financial pressure associated with seeking care abroad. The hospital's upgraded radiotherapy services include external beam radiotherapy, treatment planning and brachytherapy, supported by advanced imaging equipment.

"The first thing that comes to mind is the relief that patients and their caregivers feel," said Nakawala. "It is always better to receive treatment close to home where you are surrounded by loved ones."

Cancer treatment can be isolating, she said, and travelling abroad can deepen that isolation when patients cannot afford to take a caregiver with them. The reopening of the radiation unit therefore brings hope while potentially shortening treatment delays and reducing cancer mortality in the country.

Still, she cautioned that 60 patients a day "is not enough, but it is a positive step forward," and that treatment capacity should grow once the unit is fully operational. However, the government must ensure that there is a solid plan for servicing and reinvesting so that we get uninterrupted optimal operation and services, which will be much to the benefit of both government and patients, she added.

Hichilema said that the installation of advanced cancer treatment equipment at the Cancer Diseases Hospital in Lusaka is a major step towards positioning Zambia as a regional centre for cancer diagnosis and treatment. He said Zambia is now the third country in Africa, after South Africa and Egypt, to have the equipment, which will allow patients to access specialised cancer treatment locally rather than travelling abroad, including to India.

The reopening comes at a critical time for Zambia, where the burden of cancer continues to place pressure on an already stretched health system. The burdens of breast cancer, cervical cancer, and HIV are overlapping among women in low- and middle-income countries.

Nakawala said the six-year closure exposed how centralized cancer treatment has been in Zambia. Even when cancer was caught early, she said, most deaths during that period were driven by lack of access and delayed treatment, worsened whenever machines broke down, and treatment was interrupted - sometimes never resuming. She pointed to several consequences of the resulting gaps in services: late-stage diagnosis, as patients often wait to seek care until pain and side effects become advanced; higher mortality tied to delayed or absent treatment; and a heavier financial burden on the country, since sending patients abroad for treatment costs more than treating them at home.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women in sub-Saharan Africa, with an estimated 129 000 new cases in 2020.

Yet survival remains far lower than in high-income countries, with five-year survival estimated at around or below 50% in the region. The burden is expected to grow sharply, with the number of women diagnosed each year projected to nearly double by 2040. The African Breast Cancer – Disparities in Outcomes (ABC-DO) study found that 50% to 90% of women in different African countries are diagnosed when the cancer has already reached an advanced stage, when treatment is more difficult, and the chances of cure are lower.

According to the study, inadequate treatment access and late diagnosis are responsible for the poor outcomes. Many women recognise changes in their breasts and seek medical help, but face long waits before receiving a diagnosis and starting treatment.

WHO Africa Zambia steps up cervical cancer screening with HPV testing

In the study, half of women in Zambia and Namibia and three-quarters in Uganda reported having breast symptoms for more than six months. Survival at three years was just 46% among women in Zambia and Uganda, compared with 58% among Black women in Namibia and South Africa and 36% in Nigeria. The study estimates that more than one-third of breast cancer deaths in sub-Saharan Africa could be prevented through earlier diagnosis and timely access to high-quality treatment.

Nakawala attributed the same regional shortfall in equipment behind those numbers. "38% of countries in sub-Saharan Africa have no radiotherapy equipment at all," she said, "and 60-70% of women are diagnosed at a late stage."

She said five in ten women diagnosed with breast cancer in sub-Saharan Africa will not survive five years, compared with nine in ten who survive in high-income countries. She listed stigma, lack of awareness and information, financial constraints, distance, and limited access to screening and timely treatment as the biggest barriers keeping women from care.

"In Zambia, cervical cancer is the number one killer of women, yet it is highly preventable. It is followed by breast cancer, which, if caught early, can be treated with good outcomes," said Nakawala.

Breast cancer can also be treated with good outcomes when detected early.

Breast cancer, she said, is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women in Africa, with cases expected to double by 2040.

Zambia's ambition to become a regional centre of excellence in cancer care will therefore require more than a single upgraded facility. She said decentralization is essential so the burden doesn't fall entirely on the newly upgraded Lusaka unit. She added that two additional centres are under construction in Ndola to serve the northern region and in Livingstone to serve the south.

Beyond radiotherapy, Nakawala said government needs to work more closely with civil society organizations to raise awareness and share information with women, particularly given the gap created by years without radiation treatment. She called for greater investment in women's health and more equitable access to care. She said that Zambia should align more closely with the World Health Organization's Global Cancer Initiative to speed up early detection and diagnosis and improve survival.

She also pointed to the role of groups like the Africa Breast Cancer Council, of which she is a member, in helping governments strengthen advocacy, stakeholder engagement, and community efforts to reduce stigma by sharing best practices across member countries.

Nakawala argued that geography should not determine whether a woman survives cancer.

"No one single person should be disadvantaged because of their geographical location. We are all entitled to good healthcare services regardless of geography," she said.

She said that when the world talks about universal healthcare, it must reach beyond urban areas to everyone, which is why decentralizing cancer care matters so much. For Zambia and the wider region, that means bringing cancer services closer to the people who need them through greater investment, training and decentralisation.

"Let us all be intentional when it comes to cancer," Nakawala said. "Governments and international communities should support advocacy programmes which are centred on prevention and early diagnosis."

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 26, 2026
World.content:
Ramaphosa Vows Arrests Over Anti-Migrant Violence

President Cyril Ramaphosa has pledged that perpetrators of violence against foreign nationals will be arrested and prosecuted once police have gathered sufficient evidence. He rejected claims that the government tolerates xenophobia. Ramaphosa also denied that South Africa had been isolated by other African leaders over the recent violence. He said the country remained a respected pan-African actor. He said the government had engaged African leaders on migration and that regional cooperation was needed to address the underlying causes of migration, including insecurity and poor governance.

Nigeria Launches Manhunt After Mass Abductions

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has ordered a manhunt for armed kidnappers who attacked four villages in Niger State. The attackers killed more than 40 people and abducted an unverified number of residents. Local officials said that as many as 500 people may have been taken. A video released by the kidnappers appeared to show some of the captives alive in a forest. Survivors have fled to neighbouring states and Benin. Others are receiving treatment for injuries. The attacks, which also involved improvised explosive devices, come amid growing insecurity in the region and concerns over the spread of jihadist groups along Nigeria's north-western border areas.

Anger Mounts After Deadly Guinea Landfill Collapse

Two days after a deadly landfill collapse in Guinea, rescuers are using giant excavators to search for victims. Anger is growing among residents who said that they had repeatedly warned authorities about the landfill's dangerous condition and urged its closure. At least 31 people have died, and more than 20 were injured after a landfill collapsed in Conakry's Dar es Salam neighbourhood following heavy rain. Hundreds of displaced residents are sheltering at a school, and dozens of households remain at risk. The site has been linked to previous deadly collapses and severe pollution. The government plans to replace it with a new landfill, which has been underway since 2022.

ICC Clears Libya Case for First Trial

The International Criminal Court has confirmed 17 charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity against former Libyan security official Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri. This paves the way for the first Libya-related case to reach trial since the ICC opened its investigation 15 years ago. El Hishri is accused of torture, rape, murder, enslavement and other abuses against Libyan and migrant detainees at Tripoli's Mitiga prison. Survivors and rights groups said that the case could expose the wider system of migrant detention and exploitation in Libya, including alleged links to European migration-control policies. They called for further investigations into the responsibility of European officials.

Close 

Interpol Arrests 58 in Global Cybercrime Operation

Interpol said 58 people linked to organised West African cybercrime networks have been arrested in a global operation targeting romance and investment scams across 22 countries and six continents. Operation Jackal IV, conducted between November 2025 and June 2026 and identified 263 suspects. It uncovered fraud involving cryptocurrency, email compromise, money laundering and sextortion, including the targeting of minors. In South Africa, police arrested 39 people, raided seven sites, and seized $2.67 million. They also blocked 257 bank accounts linked to a syndicate. Interpol said the operation highlights the growing global reach of networks such as Black Axe and the importance of international cooperation in disrupting their finances. Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network with trafficking, prostitution and killing operations around the world.

World.title: South Africa: Mogotsi Escape Plot Report Due in Court - South African News Briefs - August 26, 2026
World.content:
Mogotsi Escape Plot Report Due in Court

Self-proclaimed political fixer Brown Mogotsi’s alleged escape plot is set to return to court on 1 September, reports EWN. The case was postponed after the State could not produce a report from Correctional Services to prove his alleged attempt to break free. Mogotsi allegedly planned to disguise himself in a Correctional Services uniform and walk out of the Johannesburg Magistrates Court cells. He was removed from a police van before being taken to court and placed in leg irons, with security also tightened. Mogotsi has been in custody since May after failing to secure bail over allegations that he provided false addresses.

Gauteng Health Probes Bribery Allegations



The Gauteng Department of Health is investigating allegations that officials may be accepting bribes from patients in exchange for appointments, access to medical files and the collection of medication outside normal procedures, reports SABC News. Department spokesperson Steve Mabona condemned bribery, corruption and preferential treatment in public healthcare. He said that the allegations are serious enough to warrant an investigation into whether officials are soliciting or accepting payments from patients.

Biko Family Seeks Testimony From Apartheid Spy

The reopened inquest into the 1977 death of anti-apartheid activist Steve Biko could examine the role of former apartheid spy Craig Williamson, reports EWN. Biko’s family is seeking to have him subpoenaed. The family says Williamson’s previous evidence that Biko was under surveillance could help answer questions about what security forces knew before his death. Biko’s widow, Nontsikelelo, is also expected to testify about the surveillance operation. The family has requested more time to prepare her and review evidence from the original inquest and Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The court is expected to rule on the postponement request.
