We cannot do what we do without your support. All registry offices in Poland can now recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other European Union countries, after a government regulation issued in May went into force. The decision came in response to a ruling by the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) requiring Poland to recognise such unions. Deputy prime minister Krzysztof Gawkowski expressed his “great joy, because finally in Poland we have a law that gives the right to dignity”. The government’s plenipotentiary for equality, Katarzyna Kotula, warned local authorities that they will be breaking the law if they refuse to comply with the new rules. However, the mayor of one town in a conservative region has already declared that his administration will not recognise such marriages. He argues that doing so would violate Poland’s constitution, which mentions marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Od jutra polskie państwo będzie lepiej chronić godność i prawa swoich obywateli. Nowe wzory aktów małżeństwa umożliwią transkrypcję zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych z pełnym szacunkiem dla par. To koniec administracyjnej fikcji i niepewności, z którą przez lata… pic.twitter.com/mRZYkEg9W4 — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) August 22, 2026 Polish domestic law still does not allow any form of same-sex unions to be formed. However, last year, the CJEU ordered that the country recognise same-sex marriages conducted in other EU member states. That was followed by a similar ruling from Poland’s own Supreme Administrative Court (NSA). One obstacle to implementing those decisions was that, previously, Poland’s civil registry only allowed male-female marriages to be entered. But, under a regulation issued by the government in May, the system now allows either mixed-sex or same-sex marriages. Even before that went into force on Sunday, some Polish cities, starting with Warsaw and Wrocław, had already begun transcribing same-sex marriages conducted abroad into their registries. They simply listed one spouse in the “man” section and the other as a “woman”, even though that was not accurate for one of them. But some local authorities have refused to do so, pointing to article 18 of Poland’s constitution, which states that: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” Such doubts were cited by the mayor of Zakopane, a town in southern Poland, last week when he announced that his administration did not intend to begin recognising foreign same-sex marriages after the regulation came into force. “We will not be issuing such transcriptions in Zakopane,” said Łukasz Filipowski, quoted by local news service Nasze Miasto. He argued that doing so would “not be in accordance with the constitution”, adding that, while Zakopane is “tolerant”, it “promotes the traditional family model…[as] our foundation”. Filipowski pointed to a ruling in July by the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), which found that the government’s regulation conflicts with the constitution’s definition of marriage. However, the government considers the TK to be improperly constituted and therefore regards its rulings as invalid. Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has ruled that a new regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage certificates to be registered in Poland is unconstitutional. The government says it will not implement the rulinghttps://t.co/xDAzLjcJQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2026 In response to Filipowski’s remarks, Kotula told broadcaster TVN that officials who refuse to recognise foreign same-sex marriages “will be breaking the law”. She said that the personal views of officials cannot “translate into what [legal] actions they take” and that the government would be monitoring the situation. Gawkowski – who, like Kotula, is a leading figure in The Left (Lewica), a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition – also warned municipalities against issuing refusals. He noted that, as well as the CJEU ruling, Polish courts have also issued orders to recognise foreign same-sex marriages. “In the end, these local authorities will lose [a court battle], so why embarrass themselves? Let’s not look for legal tricks. Let’s just implement something that has been done in other, normal countries for years,” Gawkowski told Polsat News. However, even once same-sex marriages are transcribed into Polish civil registries, there remains uncertainty about what legal consequences that will have in practice, especially given that Poland’s domestic law does not allow for any legally recognised form of same-sex union. Legal experts say that it may take years – and potentially many more legal challenges by same-sex couples – for the situation to be clarified. Separately, parliament earlier this year approved a bill, proposed by the ruling coalition, that would have granted same-sex couples in Poland certain rights normally granted to married couples. However, the law was vetoed by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Ukraine to establish new national pantheon as Poland warns against honouring massacre figures
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. President Volodymyr Zelensky has signed a law establishing a new national pantheon to commemorate Ukrainian historical heroes. While it is not yet known which figures will be honoured there, Poland has expressed concern that they will include nationalist leaders associated with massacres of Poles in World War Two. On Sunday, a Polish deputy foreign minister warned that Kyiv “will have a huge problem” integrating with the European Union if it celebrates such individuals. But Zelensky reiterated that “only Ukrainians will decide who is a hero to us”. The establishment of the pantheon has taken place against the backdrop of a diplomatic crisis triggered in May by Zelensky’s decision to name a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. Parts of the UPA were responsible for the so-called Volhynia massacres during World War Two, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. Poland regards the episode as a genocide, though Ukraine strongly rejects that label. Many Ukrainians hold the UPA in high regard for the role that it played in fighting for independence from Moscow-backed Soviet rule. Poland condemned Zelensky’s decision and stripped him of the country’s highest honour, the Order of the White Eagle. In response, the Ukrainian president announced in late June that he would seek to create a new national pantheon, because “no one will dictate which heroes we should honour”. A bill creating the pantheon was subsequently approved by the Ukrainian parliament in July, and, on Saturday, Zelensky signed it into law, just ahead of today’s celebrations of Ukrainian independence day. “A Ukrainian pantheon will definitely be established, and only Ukrainians will decide for themselves who our heroes are,” declared Zelensky at a meeting with military veterans on Saturday. “All our true heroes…who fought for Ukraine, for our independence…deserve due honour.” However, the introduction of the law only now begins the process of building the pantheon itself – where the remains of those chosen as national heroes will be reburied – and the establishment of an advisory body that will decide which figures should receive such an honour. It therefore remains unknown for now who will be included in the pantheon. However, on Sunday, Polish deputy foreign minister Marcin Bosacki warned against honouring figures associated with the Volhynia massacres. “Every nation and its government has the right to choose the heroes they deem appropriate,” emphasised Bosacki in an interview with broadcaster TVP. “However, if individuals responsible for mass crimes against civilians, such as [Stepan] Bandera or [Roman] Shukhevych, are included in Ukraine’s national pantheon, it would significantly worsen Ukraine’s relations not only with Poland but with Europe in general,” he added. Bandera was the leader of a faction of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN-B), which in turn founded the UPA. Shukhevych was a military leader of the UPA. Both figures continue to be honoured in Ukraine, often prompting protests from Poland. 🇵🇱 Polskie MSZ ostrzegło Ukrainę przed „ogromnymi problemami” z Europą z powodu Bandery i Szuchewycza „Ukraina wie, że z tymi, którzy zabijali nie tylko Polaków, ale także Ukraińców, Czechów, Żydów i Romów, na swoich sztandarach będzie miała ogromne problemy z integracją… pic.twitter.com/hyujMppbEw — NEXTA Polska (@nexta_polska) August 24, 2026 “Ukraine knows that, with those who murdered not only Poles, but also some Ukrainians, Czechs, Jews and Roma, on its banners, it will have a huge problem integrating with Europe,” added Bosacki. However, the deputy minister also emphasised that, “strategiaclly, the interests of Poland and Ukraine remain very close” and that Poland must continuing “supporting Ukraine in defeating the aggressive Russia”. “We do not differ much with the Ukrainians, only with certain parts of the Ukrainian authorities after their absolutely erroneious decision to name a unit after the ‘heroes of the UPA’.” The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Polish government figures have previously made it clear that, if Ukraine honours figures associated with historical massacres, that will make it harder for the country to achieve its ambitions of joining the EU. In June, deputy prime minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz warned that “you can’t build a pantheon to those who destroy European cooperation”, and that countries seeking EU membership should “not build national identity…on events, people or systems that in some way raise objections or pain among EU partners”. Kosiniak-Kamysz declared that, just as Zelensky said no one will tell Ukraine who they can honour, “no one will tell us how to vote on the entry of any state into the European Union”. That was an allusion to the fact that Poland, like all other EU member states, can veto Ukraine’s accession to the bloc. Polish and Ukrainian media have widely quoted Poland's deputy PM as saying: “With Bandera, Ukraine will not enter the EU.” However, he did not actually speak those words. We explain what @KosiniakKamysz actually said and how it came to be misinterpreted https://t.co/S3bozRIJTA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2026 ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Rising US sprint star Sam Blaskowski seeks to switch allegiance to Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A rising US track star has declared his intention to represent Poland, the country of his ancestors. Sam Blaskowski’s personal-best 100 metres sprint time of 9.89 seconds is more than a tenth of a second faster than the current Polish national record. “I plan to make Poland the finest sprinting nation in the world. I want to win medals for Poland,” the 23-year-old told Polish broadcaster TVP Sport. Sam Blaskowski przed naszymi kamerami mówi o tym, dlaczego chciałby reprezentować Polskę! 🇵🇱 Więcej o tej sprawie 👉 https://t.co/oC8MJ4moV6 pic.twitter.com/Nw1i7YqrIp — TVP SPORT (@sport_tvppl) August 23, 2026 Blaskowski says that two of his ancestors, Franciszek and Julian, left Poland in 1905, at a time when the country was still partitioned between Germany, Austria and Russia. “My last name is Polish. But for a long time, I didn’t understand that these were my roots. Everything changed recently, because my parents and I talked a lot about our roots,” he explained to TVP Sport. He was contacted by Piotr Maruszewski, coach of the Polish sprint team, after clocking a time of 9.89 seconds in May, which is the joint-ninth-best run by anyone in the world this year. The Polish 100m record is still held by Marian Woronin, who ran 10.00 in 1984. View this post on Instagram A post shared by D3 Glory Days | D3 Running Podcast & News (@d3glorydays) Maruszewski has since been persuading and helping Blaskowski to apply for citizenship, including hiring lawyers to obtain documents proving the sprinter’s heritage. Under Polish law, people who have a Polish parent, grandparent or great-grandparent who was born in or lived in Poland after January 1920 are themselves regarded as holding Polish citizenship. That means Blaskowski’s ancestry may not be enough to qualify. However, it could be enough to convince Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, who has discretion to grant citizenship to anyone he wishes. Last year, Nawrocki granted citizenship to Vladimir Semirunniy, a speed skater who fled from Russia to Poland. Semirunniy now represents the Polish national team, including at this year’s Winter Olympics, where he won a silver medal. Given that Blaskowski last represented the United States as a junior over four years ago, he is not subject to World Athletics’ mandatory waiting period for athletes transferring national allegiance. At yesterday’s Silesia Diamond League meeting in Chorzów, Poland’s biggest annual athletics event, Blaskowski told Citius Mag that he expects to be able to represent Poland at next year’s World Championships in Beijing. “I want to inspire the next generation… to make an impact on people around me, and I think the best way to do that is to go and represent Poland,” he told TVP Sport at the same event. “Not only do I have heritage there, but people [in Poland] are very aware of your talent and they give so much appreciation for our sport, and I think it’s a great place.” He added that he and his parents plan to visit their ancestors’ hometown of Sompolno in central Poland on Monday before he again competes in Szczecin on Wednesday. In Chorzów, Blaskowski came fifth in his semi-final against some of the world’s sprinters, just ahead of European champion Romell Glave. Poland’s current top male sprinter, Dominik Kopeć, finished ninth and last in 10.32. The final was won by Jamaica’s Oblique Seville in 9.83 seconds, ahead of another American with a Polish surname, Kenneth Bednarek, who was adopted as a child by a woman with Polish heritage. “The love and support I received from Poland today were truly incredible,” Bednarek wrote on social media after competing at the same event two years ago. “I’m thrilled to have run here for the first time and can’t wait to return with my mom, who has Polish roots.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by Kung Fu Kenny (@kenny_bednarek) Blaskowski would not be the first sprinter to switch allegiance to Poland. Belarusian runner Krystsina Tsimanouskaya received Polish citizenship in 2022, having been granted a humanitarian visa the previous year after the Tokyo Olympics. This month, high jumper Maria Żodzik, another Belarusian who was granted Polish citizenship in 2024, won silver at the European Championships, adding to another silver at last year’s World Championships. At the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris, Poland’s athletes disappointed, finishing with just one bronze medal in track and field events and one gold and ten medals overall, the country’s worst result since 1956. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: How will the Law and Justice split affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak The biggest-ever split within Poland’s main right-wing opposition party is a serious self-inflicted wound, signalling a more fragmented conservative landscape and complicating the right’s path back to power. While it provides a tactical boost for the Tusk government, there is still every chance of a conservative comeback if the right-wing parties cooperate effectively. Radical-right challengers At the end of last month, the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, saw the biggest split in its 25-year history. The rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open and bitter factional conflict over the party’s future direction. PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right. However, it lost power following the October 2023 parliamentary election, which led to the formation of a coalition headed up by Donald Tusk, leader of the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party. Since last autumn, PiS has seen its polling numbers decline to the party’s lowest level of support for 15 years. At the same time, it has been challenged by two radical right competitors: the free-market Confederation (Konfederacja) and the ultra-nationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), which together began to match, or even exceed, PiS’s level of support. Responding to declining support At the heart of this conflict was a bitter clash between longtime party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and Mateusz Morawiecki, who served as PiS prime minister from 2017 to 2023 but grew increasingly impatient with the former’s dominance. Two main factions emerged centred on a bitter dispute on how the party should respond to declining support and political competition on its right flank. The hardline traditionalist-conservative faction, often referred to as the “butter-makers” (maślarze), was more Eurosceptic and advocated a clearer right-wing agenda that included pushing ahead with radical state reconstruction and promoting a conservative vision of national identity and traditional values. In their reading, PiS lost support to its right-wing competitors because it was not radical enough and the solution was to sharpen its ideological profile and double down on hardline rhetoric. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 This group gained influence in party structures and when, in March, Kaczyński designated one of its key figures, former education minister Przemysław Czarnek, as the party’s prime ministerial candidate in the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, this was widely seen as a clear signal favouring the traditionalist-conservative faction. Morawiecki and his allies in the modernising-technocratic faction, often called the “scouts” (harcerze), also had strong conservative values and at times were very critical of Poland’s post-1989 establishment. However, they advocated a strategy of stressing economic competence, pragmatic governance and boosting Polish prosperity over hardline rhetoric on moral-cultural issues as a more effective way of appealing to voters less influenced by traditional institutions such as the Catholic church. Although they were also critical of Brussels overreach, Morawiecki’s faction preferred to avoid escalating conflict with the EU and argued that PiS had to broaden its appeal to younger, urban, more centrist-conservative Poles who found radical cultural rhetoric off-putting. Programmatic differences and personal ambitions The conflict became so destabilising because, although rooted in genuine programmatic and strategic disagreements, personalities and individual ambitions also played a major role. While Kaczyński maintained formal control of the party, his advancing age escalated debates over PiS’s direction and leadership, and these tensions intensified after the party failed to translate its presidential candidate Karol Nawrocki’s surprise summer 2025 election victory into broader momentum. For his part, Morawiecki grew increasingly impatient and frustrated as hardliners sidelined him, while his supporters were afraid that they would be excluded from PiS candidate lists at the next election. These long-simmering tensions came to a head in April, when Morawiecki announced the formation of Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), a think tank-like platform focused on economic development The association was widely interpreted by Kaczyński and PiS hardliners as a direct challenge to party unity and the leader’s authority. The leadership ruled that Development Plus violated the PiS statute, which explicitly prohibits members from joining political organisations that conflict with the party’s goals. While Morawiecki insisted that it was simply a modest intra-party policy forum, by registering an organisation with dozens of parliamentarians, he gave his faction a formal institutional shell that could potentially act as a launchpad for his own rival breakaway party. Initially, Kaczyński and Morawiecki came to a compromise agreement whereby Development Plus would work within an official party expert group. However, in July the situation escalated when the PiS leadership issued an ultimatum banning members from participating in internal political factions (clearly targeting Development Plus) and instructing parliamentarians to sign loyalty declarations confirming that they were not involved in any such groupings. Most complied, but 40 parliamentarians affiliated with Development Plus refused to do so, accusing the leadership of political blackmail. Ultimately, Kaczyński announced that, by refusing to sign, Morawiecki and his allies had effectively left the party, while Development Plus framed it as expulsion over policy differences caused by “plotters” surrounding the party leader. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 An even more fragmented right The loss of 40 deputies means that PiS is no longer the largest parliamentary caucus, thus losing procedural advantages, committee control and visibility. The departing group includes many experienced and talented politicians, particularly in the economic and foreign policy fields. The split also reduces PiS’s funding, staffing, and in some regions local organisation, as well as creating the risk of demoralisation and further defections. Even if the Polish right secures a parliamentary majority at the next election, PiS’s relative influence could be greatly reduced. Although Kaczyński’s formal party leadership remains unquestioned, the split signals to the broader right that his authority is waning and undermines his claim to be the undisputed hegemon and central broker on the right; he is increasingly now one leader among several. It also further erodes the model that Kaczyński has built over many years as the main ideologue and ultimate arbiter of internal PiS factions. In earlier crises, this personal authority and control gave him leverage to keep everyone on board so that disagreements were managed internally, and even disillusioned figures usually stayed in, or returned to, the party. Indeed, by adding a fourth distinctive player, the PiS split further compounds the divisions on the Polish right that have deepened since the last election, transforming what was once a relatively consolidated “big tent” bloc into a multi-polar competitive field. For sure, polls conducted after the split show the combined right-wing vote as competitive overall, but even if this level of support remains stable, or even increases slightly, it is now divided across more options. This is significant because Poland’s proportional electoral system uses the d’Hondt counting system that favours larger groupings. It also creates the risk that smaller right-wing parties such as Morawiecki’s new grouping could fall below the 5% parliamentary representation threshold, so their votes are excluded from seat allocation. All of this makes it harder for the right to translate raw voter support into political power. Moreover, even if the right-wing parties win a combined parliamentary majority, post-election coordination becomes much more complex with four (or more) actors whose leaders’ rivalries, different priorities and historical animosities complicate forming a stable coalition government. Nawrocki’s role will be crucial In the light of this, Nawrocki has emerged as a critical unifier with crossover appeal across the fractured Polish right. His presidential election victory showed that he could attract support well beyond traditional PiS loyalists and consolidate a broad right-wing coalition, including the vast majority of voters from both Confederations. As president, he operates outside direct party control and has cultivated an image as an authoritative unifying figure on the right, which gives him much greater moral and symbolic stature than a partisan leader immersed in day-to-day machinations. Nawrocki has also used his constitutional powers and standing, including a legislative veto that the government lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority to overturn, to position himself assertively as a powerful counterweight to the Tusk administration, and is currently Poland’s most popular politician. Nonetheless, Nawrocki’s potential to act as a possible right-wing unifier and broker is limited. For sure, he can use the presidency to set a broad conservative agenda and mediate negotiations among the various right-wing groupings to secure pre- and post-election agreements. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland's largest opposition party, PiS, has called on President @NawrockiKn to help unify the country’s various right-wing opposition forces ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections https://t.co/Q3BFSOSfTG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 10, 2026 However, Nawrocki has no formal unifying mandate and his success ultimately depends on whether the various actors are willing to be led. Without broader cooperation, even his efforts will only mitigate, not eliminate, the damage from a divided right, and personal and ideological rivalries currently run deep and cannot be easily overridden. Moreover, not only is the president expected to remain formally above the fray and not engage too openly in day-to-day politics, he also lacks the control over party organisational machinery needed to micro-manage and enforce messy backroom deals. Pivotal but not transformative? Initial polling conducted since the split suggests that Morawiecki’s new grouping would likely clear the 5% threshold and enter parliament with a small-to-medium-sized fraction; according to Politico Europe, it is currently averaging around 6% support. Although this could make it a pivotal player in coalition talks, it does not suggest that the grouping can dramatically reshape the country’s political landscape. Moreover, its support appears to be drawn mainly from PiS’s traditional electoral base, so it is simply further fragmenting the existing right-wing vote rather than drawing in a significant number of new voters who hitherto supported the governing coalition parties. For sure, Morawiecki‘s project has advantages that many newcomers lack, notably its leader’s very high name recognition and a sizeable bloc of high-profile, political heavyweight allies, much larger than any previous PiS breakaway faction. His grouping immediately became the third largest parliamentary fraction, giving it visibility, funding, and organisational backbone. However, although there are some rare exceptions that usually involve major figures with significant resources breaking from established parties, it is a familiar pattern in post-1989 Polish politics for a brand new “startup” party to show an early bounce, benefiting from initial media coverage, only to fade or disappear as voters drift back to more established groupings or abstain at the next election. Sustaining momentum requires local organisational infrastructure, reliable funding, rapid professionalisation, and a clear identity, which new parties often lack. Indeed, to be successful a new startup should really attract at least 10% support initially simply because of its “newness”. Over the years, PiS breakaway politicians have established new parties that either quickly disappeared from the political scene or were eventually reintegrated into the grouping. Temporary relief for Tusk From a short-term tactical perspective, the PiS split is a welcome political gift for the Tusk government, shifting the media focus away from criticisms of its record and recent scandals and controversies. It has for example, blunted the opposition’s ability to maintain a sustained assault over a scandal involving high earnings for, and mismanagement by, a KO-connected doctor, alleged VIP access and potential patient harm at the Warsaw South Hospital, which had previously dominated the summer news headlines. The ruling coalition is likely to survive until next year's election, but its prospects are hampered by a weak domestic record, writes @AleksSzczerbiak The government has therefore made security key to its reelection narrative, but that also carries risks https://t.co/w2UeNaTwAO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 1, 2026 However, the PiS split has not resolved the deeper image and performance problems that have dragged down the Tusk government’s approval ratings. The administration struggles with perceptions of slow delivery on promises while facing a hostile president, and if these problems persist, or new controversies reignite strongly once the PiS drama cools, the government will very quickly find itself back on the defensive. The PiS split only provides temporary relief; to win the next election, the ruling coalition needs to improve its own standing, not rely on opposition mistakes. World.title: Not Ready for Summer to End? 3 Places to Take the Kids Before August Ends
World.content:
The end of the summer holidays is in sight. While school supplies, pencil cases and sports shoes are already making their way onto shopping lists, there are still a few days of summer left to enjoy.

Before the September school routine kicks in, here are three ways to make the most of the final days of August with the family.



Letni Letna

When: 12–31 August

Where: Prague, Letenské sady

Letenské sady is taking on a new look until 31 August, transforming into a colourful festival village. The Letní Letná Festival isn’t just about evening acrobatics for adults. It also offers a programme for younger visitors called Letní Letná for Children.

From morning until late afternoon, the huge children’s tent comes alive with fairy-tale performances and other activities. Kids can take part in creative and juggling workshops, explore an interactive play area made from recycled materials or take a ride on the iconic hand-carved wooden carousel.

Most of the children’s activities take place under the festival tents, so an unexpected rain shower won’t disrupt the day.

The festival also offers a “Night Watch” childcare service for children aged four and up. Parents can enjoy the evening programme while experienced entertainers look after their children.

When: 24–29 August

Where: Liberec and the surrounding area

Fancy a trip beyond Prague at the end of August? Head north to Liberec from 24 to 29 August, when the city hosts Crystal Valley Week, a celebration of Czech glassmaking and jewellery.

This year’s theme focuses on the interconnection of cultures, with the Czech glass bead at the centre of the programme. Children can also enjoy a free ride aboard the special Crystal Tram, which has been decorated this year to resemble a long-distance train.

There are plenty of opportunities to make your own jewellery from glass beads, with workshops and craft sessions taking place throughout Liberec for both children and adults.

When: Sunday, 30 August, 11:00–19:00

Where: Prague, Ladronka Park

On the last Sunday of the summer holidays, skip cooking lunch and head to the F.O.O.D. Picnic in Prague’s Ladronka Park. The popular event returns for its 16th edition this year.

Entry to the festival grounds is free, with 120 food and farm stalls to explore, including food trucks. There is also a large children’s zone with games and creative workshops, as well as a raffle for younger visitors.

It’s a family-friendly way to spend the final Sunday of the holidays, combining food, activities and a relaxed atmosphere before the new school year begins.

World.title: Airbnb Accounts for 1 Percent of Prague’s Housing Stock, Analysis Finds
World.content:
Prague’s short-term rental market has grown into a professional business but Airbnb accounts for only a small share of the city’s housing stock, according to a new analysis.

In June 2026, around 7,878 entire apartments and houses in Prague were actively listed on Airbnb. With roughly 720,000 apartments across the capital, that represents about 1.1 percent of the total housing stock.

The situation is very different in individual parts of the city. In Prague 1, Airbnb-listed properties account for around one-fifth of all apartments, according to the Prague Institute of Planning and Development (IPR). In Prague 2, the share is around 7 percent, while in some outer districts it is below 0.5 percent.



The concentration of short-term rentals has also changed the nature of the market. IPR data show that hosts managed an average of two apartments in 2019. By 2024, that figure had risen to three, while more than half of Prague’s Airbnb listings were operated by hosts with at least five properties.

This means short-term accommodation is increasingly being run as a business rather than as occasional home-sharing.

Prague’s housing shortage is much larger

Despite the impact Airbnb can have in central neighborhoods, the analysis points to a much bigger problem behind Prague’s housing crisis — a long-term shortage of new construction.

Since 2006, Prague has accumulated a housing deficit of more than 91,000 apartments, according to the analysis. That shortfall is about 11.5 times larger than the number of apartments currently listed on Airbnb.

Even if every Airbnb property in the city were suddenly returned to the long-term rental market, Prague would still be short more than 83,000 homes.

The accumulated construction deficit reportedly became larger than the number of active Airbnb apartments around 2009 or 2010. Since then, the gap has continued to grow.

This suggests that Prague’s housing crisis began well before short-term rentals reached their current scale.

Tourism brings other concerns

Housing availability is also not the only issue surrounding short-term rentals.

Residents in central Prague have complained about noise, disruption and visitors staying in residential buildings.

The city also collects accommodation fees from short-term stays, although payment is not automatic because apartment owners must register and pay the fees themselves.

The debate over Airbnb in Prague therefore extends beyond housing. While short-term rentals can change the character of central neighborhoods and create problems for residents, the latest figures suggest that the city’s wider housing shortage is primarily the result of years of insufficient construction.

World.title: ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival Returns to Prague for Its Fifth Edition
World.content:
The ASEAN Committee in Prague (ACP), representing the embassies of ASEAN member states, together with the embassies of China, Japan and the Republic of Korea, will host the fifth edition of the ASEAN Plus Three Film Festival (APTFF).

The festival will begin on Monday, September 7, 2026, at the Municipal Library of Prague.

Organised in cooperation with the Municipal Library of Prague, the festival will run until September 14 and feature seven full-length films, alongside a curated selection of short films from across the ASEAN Plus Three region.



Since its launch in 2022, the APTFF has introduced Czech audiences to the diverse cultures and cinematic voices of ASEAN and its Plus Three partners.

Previous editions have featured acclaimed films including Escape from Mogadishu (Republic of Korea), Father and Son (Viet Nam) and Yuni (Indonesia).

This year’s programme includes Solata: Friends Are the Family We Choose (Indonesia), Babah (Malaysia), The Beginning (Myanmar), I’m Perfect (the Philippines), 4 Tigers (Thailand), Song of the South (Viet Nam) and One and Only (China).

A selection of short films will also be screened during the opening night on September 7.

The programme includes Mbiyodo/Communal Work (Indonesia), Ninavau (Malaysia), Myanmar Be Enchanted (Myanmar), Lola Loleng/Grandma Loleng (the Philippines), Give to Getters (Thailand), Welcome to Viet Nam (Viet Nam), My Chinese Ecological Notes (China), Pukkulapottas and Hours in the Forest (Japan), and Persona (Republic of Korea).

Beyond its cultural programme, the festival is part of a broader effort by ASEAN and its Plus Three partners to introduce Czech audiences to the region, its societies and creative industries, as well as its shared identity as a community of more than 690 million people.

All screenings are open to the public and free of charge. Films will be shown in their original languages with English and Czech subtitles.

The full programme and schedule are available on the Municipal Library of Prague website.

World.title: GALLERY: Light Installation “Synapse” Coming to Florenc Metro Station
World.content:
Jan Poš light installation Synapse will go on display in the Florenc Line C metro passage at the end of September.

The artwork will track passengers’ movements and complement the existing Battle of Sokolovo mosaic. Prague city councillors approved around CZK 1.38 million in funding to complete and install the artwork.

“Synapse” is a light-based installation by visual artist Jan Poš (1996) and the winning entry in the “Light for the Metro” competition held in 2023.



The aim was to create a light artwork for the passage connecting the north and south concourses of Florenc metro station. A total of 23 artists and teams submitted proposals, with four advancing to the final stage, which was conducted as a competitive dialogue.

The five-member jury considered the artwork’s long-term maintenance and its ability to withstand demanding operating conditions.

According to Poš, the artwork, installed on the wall opposite the underpass’s main staircase, comes into view as metro passengers ascend or descend the stairs.

It becomes part of their daily journey while remaining elegantly set apart, creating a space where it can stand on its own and offer a moment of respite from the hustle and bustle.

Poš says the work’s format and style enliven and build on the Battle of Sokolovo mosaic, creating a bridge between the past and present of the city.

The artwork was originally due to be installed alongside the completion of the reconstruction of the station’s ceiling slab. Prague’s public transport operator, DPP, has been repairing the structure since 2022 due to corrosion.

World.title: Partial Lunar Eclipse to Be Visible From Prague at Dawn on August 28
World.content:
Prague residents willing to get up early on Friday, August 28, will have a chance to witness a partial lunar eclipse, with almost the entire Moon passing into Earth’s shadow shortly before it sets.

The eclipse will reach its maximum at 6:12 a.m. CEST. By then, only a narrow section along the Moon’s northern edge will remain illuminated.

In Prague, the Moon is expected to set at approximately 6:17 a.m., leaving only a few minutes to observe the eclipse at its peak.



The partial phase will begin at 4:33 a.m. As the event progresses, Earth’s shadow will gradually cover the lunar surface, reducing the bright portion of the Moon until only a thin illuminated crescent remains visible.

Astronomers at the Silesian University in Opava say observers will need an unobstructed view towards the southwest, as the Moon will be low above the horizon throughout the most important part of the event.

The eclipse follows another major astronomical event visible from the Czech Republic earlier this month, giving skywatchers a second opportunity to observe a rare celestial phenomenon within a short period.

Unlike a solar eclipse, observing the Moon does not require protective eyewear. The eclipse can be seen with the naked eye, while binoculars or a camera may provide a closer view.

For the best chance of seeing the maximum phase, observers should choose a location with a clear southwestern horizon and arrive before dawn. Weather conditions will also play a decisive role in whether the eclipse is visible.

World.title: September 19: Prague Hosts Indian Festival of Music, Food, and Community
World.content:
Prague will host its annual celebration of Indian culture, Ganeshotsav, on Saturday, September 19, at Kulturní dům Ládví.

Ganeshotsav, the festival honoring Lord Ganesha, is more than a celebration of Indian culture—it’s a way to bring people together.

Since 2021, the festival has grown into a space where Indian and Czech communities can meet, connect, and enjoy shared traditions.

The event is organised by Maharashtra Mandal, Czech Republic, a registered non-profit dedicated to promoting friendship and understanding between Indian and Czech residents.

The festival features traditional Indian rituals, music, dance, and food, and welcomes everyone to join in the fun.

Like last year, this year, the festival adds a charitable aspect: part of the registration fees will go to support non-profits in the Czech Republic.

“With this initiative, we want to contribute to the development of communities both in our country of origin and in the country that is now our home,” says the organizers to Prague Morning.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Maharashtra Mandal Czech Republic (@maharashtramandalczechrepublic)

By partnering with like-minded organisations, the festival encourages intercultural dialogue, mutual respect, and connections between diverse communities living in the Czech Republic.

Like last year, organizers will support small entrepreneurs from the Indian community who will present the diversity of Indian cuisine.

The project is called “”Our Annapoorna -The Taste of Every Indian Household”, and will offer visitors a diverse selection of traditional dishes from different corners of India.

The cultural program, featuring music, dance, and traditional rituals, will run from 5:00 PM to 8:30 PM

World.title: A Multi-Brand K-Beauty Pop-Up Is Coming to Prague This September
World.content:
A Korean beauty pop-up will bring eight K-beauty brands and K-pop entertainment to Prague’s Vltava River this September.

The HARUNARU K-Beauty Pop-up will take place aboard KVASOUL, a self-brewing boat restaurant, from September 4 to 8.



An industry preview for beauty professionals and influencers will be held on September 3.

Visitors will be able to discover, test and buy products from eight Korean brands, including GASH, ranked No. 1 at Olive Young, South Korea’s leading beauty retailer, and ilso, known for its pore-care products.

The event will also feature K-pop performances, a Random Dance Challenge, an idol-style makeup show and a dedicated selection of K-pop albums and merchandise.

The pop-up is aimed at introducing emerging Korean beauty brands to consumers and industry professionals in the Czech Republic and across Central and Eastern Europe.

Entry is free, although visitors are encouraged to register online in advance.

The event is organized by Bramasole Prague s.r.o., which operates several Korean restaurant brands in Prague.

World.title: Dancing House Marks 30 Years With a Free Weekend of Dance in Prague
World.content:
Prague’s Dancing House will celebrate its 30th anniversary with a free two-day program of dance classes, performances and workshops on August 29 and 30.

Jiráskovo náměstí, next to the landmark on the Vltava embankment, will host a temporary stage and dance floor throughout the weekend.



The program will run from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can join professional instructors for classes in bachata, street dance and Latin American dance. There will also be sessions for children, dance demonstrations and opportunities to meet and talk with instructors.

The event is open to all levels, with participants able to watch performances or take part in the classes.

Weekend program

The schedule is the same on both days until the evening finale.

11:00 a.m. – Opening

11:05 a.m. – Children’s dance class

11:50 a.m. – Talk with the instructor

12:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

12:05 p.m. – Bachata class

12:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

1:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

1:05 p.m. – Street dance class

1:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

2:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

2:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

2:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

3:00 p.m. – Hat Jazz performance

3:05 p.m. – Children’s dance class

3:50 p.m. – Talk with the instructor

4:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

4:05 p.m. – Bachata class

4:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

5:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

5:05 p.m. – Street dance class

5:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

6:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

6:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

6:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

7:00 p.m. – Acrobatic performance

7:05 p.m. – Hula Hoops performance

The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Could Trump save Orbán’s international lobbying organisations from collapse?
World.content:
It had previously been suggested that former prime minister Viktor Orbán could, with Trump’s help, secure a deputy secretary-general’s post at the United Nations, granting him diplomatic immunity. Meanwhile, the MAGA movement associated with Trump could take over some of the international organisations established by Orbán’s governments and operate them as its own lobbying vehicles within the European Union – an economic and commercial rival.

A vast and costly international lobbying operation

Over 16 years, Viktor Orbán built not only a formidable, if politically unstable, power base in Hungary. In Brussels, too, he established an institutional network designed to support conservative and radical-right forces, influence policy debates and cultivate European alliances.

Following the electoral defeat, however, one of the system’s most important pillars – funding from the Hungarian state and its affiliated bodies – appears to be crumbling.

J. D. Vance in Budapest – the organiser is the MCC. Source: MCC

One of the network’s central players was the Brussels office of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium (MCC). Opened in 2022, the institution focused on issues favoured by the Orbán system and its wider alliance network, including migration, gender politics, climate change and the external funding of civil-society organisations in the European Union.

Its work was supported by an annual budget of more than €6 million – equivalent to between 1.8 billion and 2 billion forints – underpinned by assets worth roughly 500 billion forints provided by the Orbán government. This is what Péter Magyar’s government, backed by a two-thirds majority, effectively stripped from the MCC with a single stroke of the pen.

Alongside the MCC, the Danube Institute, The European Conservative magazine and the foundation behind CPAC Hungary were also part of the circle of organisations supported by the Orbán government with many billions of forints in public money.

The House of Hungary was another important element of the network. In 2021, the Hungarian state bought the Brussels building, dating from the 18th century, and opened it as an events venue ahead of Hungary’s EU presidency in 2024. The property is now standing empty, however, and no decision has been made on its future use.

Trump and Orbán in the White House last November. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

Trump could rescue some institutions

After the change of government, the new administration ended or reviewed state support for several of these institutions. The MCC found itself in a particularly difficult position. Frank Furedi, the head of its Brussels organisation, has said that the centre could eventually be forced to close without a new source of funding, although it might continue operating on a smaller budget.

Expert assessments suggest, however, that maintaining a network on the scale and with the intensity seen during the Orbán era is no longer realistic.

This is where Donald Trump and the American MAGA movement could enter the picture. According to a Bloomberg analysis cited by Portfolio, programmes have already emerged in the United States to support European conservative civil-society organisations working on sovereignty, migration, censorship and “lawfare”.

If you missed – Fundamental changes in Hungary’s foreign policy reflected in new UN guidelines

The institutions linked to Orbán could therefore find new American backers – particularly as Trump’s allies are themselves seeking to strengthen ties with Europe’s radical right in order to expand their influence over EU affairs.

The question, then, is not necessarily whether Orbán’s Brussels network will disappear, but who will take over its funding, in what form it might survive and whose interests it would serve.

Influence is valuable amid mounting conflict

As is well known, neither Trump nor his movement regards the European Union or the NATO member states as allies in the same way as previous American administrations did. The threat of a tariff and trade war is gathering over both sides of the Atlantic; the dispute over Greenland remains unresolved; and Washington and Brussels do not necessarily share the same view on how to bring Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to an end.

There are also disagreements over American intervention in Iran and the regulation of US technology giants in Europe.

For Trump, an effective lobbying organisation could therefore prove valuable on several fronts: in academia, among civil-society groups and in politics.

World.title: Renowned Hungarian author Péter Nádas dies
World.content:
World-renowned author Péter Nádas died on Wednesday morning in his home in Gombosszeg, in southwest Hungary, the author’s official Facebook page said.

Nádas was born in Budapest in 1942. He worked as a photographer and journalist at several outlets in the late 1950s and the ’60s. His first book, The Bible, was published in 1967. He published novels, dramas, essays continuously afterwards while continuing to work in journalism and the theatre. His seminal work, A book of memories, was published in 1986 in Hungarian and in 1997 in English. It was lauded as one of the outstanding achievements of post-war Hungarian writing, and one that had mapped out new ways of literary expression. His last book, Halott barataim (My dead friends), was published in 2025, MTI wrote.

Péter Nádas in 2025. Photo: Facebook/Nádas Péter

Throughout his career, Nádas was awarded the Kossuth and Jozsef Attila Prizes, the Szechenyi Prize, the Middle Cross of the Order of Merit of the Republic of Hungary, the Austrian State Prize for European Literature, and the Grand Cross of the Order of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Nádas has lived and worked in the remote village of Gombosszeg in southwest Hungary since 1984. The family has asked the public to respect their privacy until further communication.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar commented on Nadas’s passing on Facebook, saying: “Kossuth prize holder, world-renowned author Péter Nádas passed away this morning. Farewell, Maestro!”

How a classic Hungarian comic heroine became a global animation sensation – Jucika racks up 60 million views!

Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony said on Facebook: “This country, this city has a lot to thank to Péter Nádas. We will now forever regret not to be able to repay that debt.” Nádas, an honorary citizen of Budapest, “has shown to the wide world where this city is in Europe,” he added.

“Péter Nádas represents simultaneously the highest levels of world literature and the most beautiful, delicate, heart-warming Hungarian literature,” Karácsony said.

World’s third public statue of Freddie Mercury unveiled on Lake Balaton – but it bears a striking resemblance to a Hungarian poet

World.title: Cause of poisoning at Debrecen battery plant revealed — but there is good news too
World.content:
We have previously read reports about battery plants and several companies in the battery industry allegedly seeking to evade Hungarian regulations, doing so with political backing and, when all else failed, simply paying derisory fines. The action taken over the latest incident at CATL’s Debrecen battery plant, however, could be good news for the workers there and their colleagues elsewhere in the sector. That is so even if, judging by the available evidence, the company appears to have made a serious mistake over personal protective equipment — and that mistake appears to have caused the problem.

Serious poisoning at Debrecen battery plant — but the factory reported it itself

Work has been suspended in three production areas at CATL’s Debrecen battery plant after elevated nickel exposure was identified in a total of nine employees. An official inspection found that the company had failed to provide the required personal protective equipment properly and in full. Proceedings have also been launched with a view to imposing a fine. Enikő Tompa, the Tisza Party’s MP for the area, has been particularly active in the case.

The incident came to light after CATL Hungary Kft reported seven cases to the occupational safety authority on August 10, followed by a further two on 13 August. The company then began the necessary investigation. According to information obtained by Debreciner, elevated nickel levels were detected in several cases during mandatory biological exposure monitoring involving more than 400 employees.

The good news, at any rate, is that the company did not attempt to cover up the incident but followed the appropriate procedure. This could prove important for the remaining 391 employees, particularly in light of previous cases in which companies opted to pay a fine while continuing to expose Hungarian and guest workers to danger.

Telex: Samsung’s Göd plant may have poisoned its workers for years because the Orbán government helped it

The Mikepércs Mothers for the Environment Association previously reported that, according to information in its possession, a cathode-powder spill may have occurred at the plant, sending heavy metals into the air. The civic group claimed that nickel and cobalt levels in some workers may have reached several times the permitted limit, and said it had also received reports of exposure to chromium and lithium.

Te Debrecen battery plant of the Chinese CATL. Photo: Facebook/Tompa Enikő

These claims, however, have not been confirmed by the official information currently available. The authorities have formally reported only elevated nickel exposure among nine employees.

Work halted in three areas as substantial fine looms

The occupational safety authority inspected the plant on 11 and 12 August. It found that the employer had failed to provide personal protective equipment adequately. As a result, from 10.30 AM on 12 August until the breaches were rectified, work was prohibited in the cathode- and anode-foil laser-cutting, anode- and cathode-foil winding, and cell-drying areas of the cell-production building.

According to a follow-up inspection carried out by the authority on 17 August, CATL had not resumed the suspended activities. Proceedings to impose a fine are nevertheless under way over the breaches.

Enikő Tompa, the local MP, contacted the Ministry of Rural and Settlement Development to request information about the incident. She said that, if the violations were confirmed, CATL could face a substantial fine. She cited the case of SK On in Iváncsa, which was fined 100 million forints for breaches of occupational safety regulations.

Meanwhile, according to government information, the investor was granted an occupancy permit for the first phase of the project on 25 August after remedying the outstanding deficiencies. Permission for the second phase had previously been refused because the completed building had not been shown correctly on the site plan.

Debrecen’s municipal authorities said they had learnt of the incident from the press and had no jurisdiction over the matter. CATL did not respond to Debreciner’s request for comment.

World.title: Parliament’s Culture Committee rejects opposition candidates to public media authority
World.content:
Parliament’s culture committee has not backed the opposition parties’ candidates to the Independent Public Media Authority. Zoltán Moys, nominated by Our Homeland, Zoltán Márti of the Christian Democrats and Beatrix Siklósi, who was nominated by Fidesz, each received four votes in favour and seven against.

At their (separate) hearings ahead of the vote, the candidates highlighted the importance of credibility, professionalism and creating cultural values. They also stressed that public media must stand above party politics.

Committee head Alexandra Szentkirályi of Fidesz said after the meeting that the fact that none of the nine members of the body was elected by the deadline was “autocratic” and “cinema”.

Chairwoman Szentkirályi speaking at the session. Photo: MTI

Central bank probe is to start

An ad hoc parliamentary committee established to investigate the use of public monies by the National Bank of Hungary (NBH) for non-core activities aims to determine political responsibility, the committee’s chair said ahead of its inaugural meeting on Wednesday, MTI wrote.

Attila Csőszi, an MP of the governing Tisza Party, said the committee would not take over the role of the judiciary. He added that recommendations would be made to improve transparency and accountability when the probe finished. The committee will probe the management of assets in the NBH’s foundation and the renovation of the central bank headquarters.

Csőszi said the former Fidesz-KDNP government had tried to establish a regulatory environment that made it impossible to trace the public monies in the NBH foundation, paving the way for “institutionalised theft”. The committee will hear testimony of the people involved, he added.

Csőszi noted that the two committee members delegated by opposition Fidesz and KDNP had both voted for amendments to the central bank act allowing assets to be channelled to NBH foundations. Fielding questions, he said the committee would wind up its work with a report by December 31.

World.title: Fundamental changes in Hungary’s foreign policy reflected in new UN guidelines
World.content:
Hungary condemns Russia’s military aggression, fully supports Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity while urging negotiations towards sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees, according to the guidelines set for the Hungarian delegation participating in the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, published in Tuesday’s issue of the official gazette Magyar Közlöny.

According to the supplement to the resolution signed by Prime Minister Péter Magyar, the Hungarian delegation participating in the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly is tasked with acting in accordance with the government’s objectives and upholding Hungarian national interests.

Russia’s behaviour poses a threat to Hungary, Europe and the global order, and also places the Hungarian minority living in Transcarpathia in serious danger, the document said, adding that the government supports all efforts aimed at initiating negotiations toward sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees.

Péter Magyar and Volodimir Zelensky at the EU Summit on 18 June 2026. Photo: Facebook/Péter Magyar

War in Gaza, Iran, USA

On matters relating to the war in Gaza, the delegation is to present Hungary’s position that lasting peace can be achieved on the basis of resolutions adopted by the UN Security Council, by ensuring the protection of civilians, respecting Israel’s right to self-defence, disarming Hamas and improving the humanitarian situation in Gaza. It added that direct negotiations between the parties formed the basis for Israeli–Palestinian reconciliation.

The long-term settlement of the Israel–Hezbollah conflict likewise required the protection of civilians, recognition of Israel’s right to security, the restoration of Lebanon’s sovereignty and the disarmament of Hezbollah, it said.

The resolution stressed that the Government highly valued the efforts of the United States and regional mediators to bring conflicts in the Middle East to an end.

Under the resolution, the delegation is also required to represent Hungary’s position on the conflict involving Iran: rather than resorting to military escalation, the parties should resolve their disputes at the negotiating table while keeping diplomatic channels open. It stressed that Iran must not be allowed to acquire nuclear weapons under any circumstances.

It noted that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the disruption of maritime trade posed a global risk to energy security. Hungary therefore supported every effort aimed at restoring stability in the region.

EU, migration, water issues

The guidelines also state that Hungary – working closely with the International Energy Agency and the European Union – will constructively support all measures capable of safeguarding Europe’s and the world’s energy supplies, while easing the supply-security challenges caused by the conflict in the Middle East.

The delegation must pay particular attention to advancing the Hungarian Government’s position on migration within the framework of the United Nations. It must also make clear that border protection and the rules governing residence on their territory fall within the national competence of member states, while drawing attention to the immediate security risks posed by migration.

Péter Magyar reveals how long he plans to be prime minister as Viktor Orbán’s party falls apart

In another section, the delegation was instructed to continue paying close attention to international processes aimed at implementing goals and targets relating to water and sanitation, to help promote the institutional reforms required for their implementation and, accordingly, to reaffirm Hungary’s commitment to establishing a permanent UN water process. It must also monitor preparations for, and the proceedings of, the UN Water Conference to be held in December, and ensure that Hungary’s position is properly represented.

The guidelines further call on the delegation to support the work of the International Court of Justice and other generally recognised international dispute-resolution bodies, and to back the general recognition of the ICJ’s jurisdiction. It is also expected to oppose the politicisation of international legal and judicial forums in order to preserve their impartiality.

The delegation is tasked with reaffirming Hungary’s support for the UN Secretary-General’s proposals to reform the organisation’s governance. Hungary also intends to continue contributing to the renewal of the General Assembly’s role and to reforms of the UN’s development and environmental systems, the resolution said.

If you missed: Péter Magyar reveals how long he plans to be prime minister as Viktor Orbán’s party falls apart

Featured image: Facebook/Orbán Anita

World.title: Péter Magyar reveals how long he plans to be prime minister as Viktor Orbán’s party falls apart
World.content:
It appears that Péter Magyar and the Tisza Party he leads will continue to shape Hungarian public life for some time to come. Yet the country’s current prime minister is making remarkably modest claims in this regard, while his intended involvement in public affairs appears strikingly limited. Viktor Orbán has always planned for the long term; Péter Magyar’s ambitions extend much less far into the future.

Orbán and the longue durée

As prime minister, Viktor Orbán invariably set out lengthy time horizons for his tenure in office. Although, during the past four years, he regularly spoke of eventually having to hand over the baton to the next generation, the last person to seriously question his position as leader was perhaps János Lázár, before the 2018 election. That challenge ended with Lázár being sidelined. This April, Lázár suffered a major defeat alongside his former boss, having served as one of the faces of the campaign.

Orbán always planned at least as far ahead as 2030. In his telling, that was how long it would take to put the country right after the “social-liberal” rampage. Those deadlines, however, were repeatedly pushed back. During the latest campaign, for example, Lázár regularly described Hungary as a half-finished country, implying that much remained to be done before their work – whatever it might have been – could be completed.

Péter Magyar has adopted a far more modest outlook as prime minister, although he threw himself into even the first few months of his first term with extraordinary energy and a punishing workload. He says he sleeps little and values the time he spends with his family and children, but that there is no time for rest at present. “Perhaps there will be time for a little rest in seven years and eight months,” he wrote in a Facebook post yesterday. In the accompanying photograph, he can be seen leaping up two steps at a time while holding a national flag – suggesting, among other things, that slowing down is not currently an option.

Péter Magyar at Paks NPP during the energy and water crisis. Orbán did not even Photo: Facebook/Ruszin-Szendi Romulusz

Among the Tisza government’s first measures was a constitutional limit stipulating that a prime minister may serve no more than two terms – eight years in total – at the head of the Hungarian Government. The calculation above is therefore easy to understand. Although many questioned whether Péter Magyar genuinely intended to honour the restriction, he appears to be standing by his promise.

Living, working or doing business in Hungary?

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

That said, the new constitution that Tisza intends to draft by next autumn could establish a semi-presidential republic, with a directly elected president enjoying a strong mandate and correspondingly broader and more powerful powers. Nothing currently prevents someone from moving directly from the office of prime minister to that of president, although there has been no such example – in either direction – since the collapse of communism.

Could Hungarians directly elect a much stronger president next year? This is what one of Tisza’s strongmen now says

For now, at least, Tisza has the power to reshape Hungary’s constitutional order as it sees fit. It holds 141 seats in Parliament – comfortably more than the two-thirds majority required. More importantly, if an election were held today, it would receive an even stronger mandate, with roughly two-thirds of the vote.

Tisza has an overwhelming majority in the Hungarian Parliament. Photo: Facebook/Forsthoffer Ágnes

Meanwhile, Fidesz, the party led by Viktor Orbán and Hungary’s strongest opposition force, is showing signs of disintegration. Tibor Navracsics, a former European commissioner and minister, and Orsolya Ferencz have established an independent platform called the Civic Democrats. János Bóka, Fidesz’s parliamentary group leader, welcomed the move. Yet in Hungarian political history, the emergence of platforms within a party has invariably been the prelude to its collapse – as happened with the Hungarian Socialist Party and, more recently, Jobbik.

Orbán and János Bóka. Photo: MTI

Andrea Virág, strategic director of the Republikon Institute, also told Népszava that Viktor Orbán – despite enjoying the support of almost 100 per cent of his party – had remained virtually silent as party leader in recent months, while Hungary was facing an energy crisis, a water crisis and, in her view, a constitutional crisis.

According to Andrea Virág, this suggests that Viktor Orbán has voluntarily withdrawn from the political stage and is looking for someone to whom he can hand over the baton. She argues that he has abandoned his party, has no strategy for a return and that everything around him is now showing signs of collapse.

World.title: Hungarian firefighters and vehicles sent to Serbia to aid the battle against forest fires
World.content:
Hungary is sending 12 firefighters and four vehicles to Serbia to aid the battle against forest fires, Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai said on Facebook late on Tuesday.

The contingent left for Serbia on Tuesday, Pósfai said. He thanked the firefighters working to extinguish fires in Hungary nationwide. Hungary is committed to strengthening international relations and regional safety, Pósfai said, noting that Serbia was one of several European countries facing a “critical situation”.

“We hope that human and technical resources offered will help contain the Serbian wildfires as soon as possible,” Pósfai said. Other foreign units are also assisting in extinguishing the fires in Serbia under the EU Civil Protection Mechanism. Four firefighting helicopters have arrived in Serbia: two from the Czech Republic, one from Romania, and one from Slovakia. Additionally, German and Romanian ground firefighting units have joined the efforts.

Hungarian firefighters in North Macedonia before. Photo: National Disaster Management Authority

Nearly 4,000 hectares have burned in the Deliblato Sands, with over 3,100 hectares of forest affected. The most severe damage has impacted the wildlife and forest ecosystems of the protected area.

Fires continue to burn elsewhere in Serbia, with the most challenging situation in the Stolovi Mountains near Kraljevo, where difficult terrain, strong winds, and dense smoke hinder firefighting efforts. The Serbian Meteorological Service has warned that persistent heat, lack of rainfall, and occasionally strengthening winds continue to favour the outbreak and spread of wildfires.

World.title: Hungary’s ‘winged phallus’ memorial taken down as officials offer strange explanations – video, photos
World.content:
The wooden monument intended to commemorate the Battle of Mohács — but swiftly dubbed a “winged phallus” by the public — has been removed in the Hungarian town of Devecser, with both the mayor and the deputy mayor behind the initiative offering rather curious explanations.

Deputy mayor ‘did not see’ phallus

An unusual monument was unveiled in Devecser on August 20, Hungary’s national holiday marking the foundation of the state. It was intended to commemorate the Battle of Mohács, whose 500th anniversary falls on August 29 — this Saturday.

The deputy mayor claimed the statue had been completed at breakneck speed: officials were still debating the design on August 19, only for the unveiling to follow the next day, complete with a priestly blessing, children’s entertainment and all the usual trimmings.

Check out our previous article in the issue HERE.

This is how the original wooden memorial looked. The deputy mayor says she learned about the scandalous resemblance only from the social media conversation. Photo: Facebook/Nyárs Hajnalka

Speaking to RTL Híradó, Hajnalka Nyárs, the deputy mayor who conceived the project, said that the organisers had not “seen into it” what others immediately did. She accepted, however, that viewers were free to see whatever their individual imaginations suggested in a work of art.

In this case, much of the country saw a winged phallus in the wooden statue, which was supposedly meant to depict a helmeted Turul — the winged bird of Hungarian mythology. It was intended as a memorial to the Hungarian, Czech, Croatian, Serbian and other soldiers who died fighting bravely for their homeland on the Mohács plain.

A nation remembers Mohács

August 29 marks the 500th anniversary of Hungary’s defeat at the Battle of Mohács. On that day in 1526, Louis II, King of Hungary and Bohemia, was defeated by the Ottoman ruler Suleiman on the Mohács plain — and lost his life in the aftermath.

The defeat effectively marked the collapse of the medieval Hungarian state and the beginning of Ottoman occupation across large parts of the country for more than a century and a half. The occupation profoundly altered the ethnic balance of the region, shaping the course of later history. Mohács was therefore regarded by contemporaries — and remains regarded by modern historians — as a decisive historical watershed.

499 years ago: the Battle of Mohács Memorial – photos and video

It is little surprise, then, that Mohács has already been hosting a steady programme of commemorations and cultural events this week. The anniversary itself, on Saturday, will be marked by a major ceremony and a historically faithful re-enactment of the battle.
