World.title: Meta reaches $16.68 billion settlement over social media harms to children
World.content:
META. The logo of Meta at the Meta Lab in Los Angeles, California, US, on May 20, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) Meta will impose daily usage limits and restrict nighttime usage by children who use Facebook and Instagram, and enhance measures to prevent children from accessing age-restricted content

Meta Platforms agreed to pay a maximum $16.68 billion and make major changes to Facebook and Instagram to resolve claims by states across the US that the company designed those platforms to addict children, misled consumers about their safety and improperly collected children’s personal data.

The settlement resolves claims brought by 29 US states, and will end a federal trial that had been one of the highest-profile tests yet of allegations that social media companies harmed young users.

Meta will impose daily usage limits and restrict nighttime usage by children who use Facebook and Instagram, and enhance measures to prevent children from accessing age-restricted content.

The Menlo Park, California-based company denied wrongdoing in agreeing to settle.

Wednesday’s settlement also resolves lawsuits by California, Illinois, New Mexico and Washington, D.C., over privacy claims related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where the consulting firm collected personal data of millions of Facebook users. Those states will receive $459.3 million to resolve those lawsuits.

Shares of Meta rose 2.3% in early trading.

The claims were part of a broader wave of litigation brought by states, local governments, school districts and individuals alleging that Meta and other social media companies fueled a nationwide youth mental health crisis.

The trial in the Oakland, California, federal court covered claims from California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey that Meta violated their state laws protecting consumers.

It also covered claims from 29 states that Meta ⁠violated the federal Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting personal data from users it knew were children without parental notification or consent, and using the data to train machine learning and generative AI models.

Meta has long argued it could not have misled consumers about whether its services were addictive because “social media addiction” is not a recognized psychiatric condition.

Before the trial began on August 18, Meta said California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were seeking up to $1.4 trillion in penalties. The states suggested that the figure would be closer to $200 billion.

A mental health crisis

Meta, Snapchat and its parent Snap, YouTube and its parent Alphabet, and TikTok and its parent ByteDance still face thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts over claims they knowingly designed their platforms to have features that addict children and teenagers, fueling a mental health crisis. A trial in Nashville over claims brought by Tennessee against Meta began last month.

The federal cases were consolidated before US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in Oakland, and include lawsuits brought by individuals, school districts and state governments.

Earlier this year, Meta lost both phases of a landmark lawsuit brought by New Mexico. A jury in March ordered it to pay $375 million after finding it had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms. On August 6, a judge found Meta had created a public nuisance and ordered it to pay an additional $567 million and implement youth-safety measures.

Also in March, the first trial over an individual’s claims against Meta and Google ended with a verdict in the plaintiff’s favor. A Los Angeles jury found the companies liable for plaintiff Kaley G.M.’s depression and anxiety and ordered them to pay a combined $6 million in damages.

The companies have said they will appeal those verdicts. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sara Duterte trial: Prosecution navigates minefield after sub judice ruling
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – After the impeachment court laid out clearer sanctions against violators of the sub judice rule on Wednesday, August 26., the prosecution panel has been more careful than ever.

No public or private prosecutor faced House-organized press conferences, while some gave relatively few words during chance interviews.

“Personally, I will behave,” private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said.

The ruling read by presiding officer Chiz Escudero promised public reprimand for first-time offenders of Rule 18 of the impeachment rules handbook, and a fine of P30,000 for every succeeding offense. The said provision prohibits senator-judges, prosecutors, the respondent, and their defense team from commenting on the merits of the case outside the court.

While the penalties apply not only to the prosecution but also to the defense, it is not difficult to surmise that the House side is whom Escudero is referring to when he says one party has violated the sub judice rule more than the other.

When Escudero read remarks the court found problematic, most of the soundbites came from prosecutors, such as Jay Tolosa, Amando Virgil Ligutan, Mae Divinagracia, and Terry Ridon.

Wednesday’s ruling was triggered by defense lawyer Sheila Sison’s previous move to call out Ligutan for posting on Facebook that misleading questions are not allowed even during cross-examinations. The comment was an apparent reaction to the claim made by defense lawyer Kristine Ferrer before the court.

Before Escudero issued his ruling, Ligutan was given the opportunity to deliver his counter-manifestation, in which he insisted he did not violate the court’s sub judice rule.

“To the defense, the post is not about you. It is not personal. It is about the law that we all adhere to. It is about what we teach the public who are watching our trial. Correcting a mistake is never wrong. Doing it while a hearing is ongoing, online, does not make it not right,” Ligutan added.

Play Video

Press briefing sans prosecutors

As the impact of the ruling reverberates, the House opted not to let a member of the prosecution team face the media for its regular lunch break and post-trial press conferences on Wednesday.

Instead, the media relied on soundbites of prosecution spokesman Zia Alonto Adiong, and deputy speakers Paolo Ortega, Janette Garin, and Jay Khonghun. For Rappler’s special coverage, we were able to book Manila 6th District Representative Benny Abante, one of the endorsers of the impeachment complaint that became the basis of the impeachment articles transmitted to the Senate.

Play Video

“(The sub judice rule) should also extend to the respondent,” Adiong said. “Whatever she says should also be guided by the sub judice rule…(such as her statement on the impeachment process) ‘bending the law,'” Adiong said.

Duterte’s statement in early August — an apparent swipe at the House and the impeachment court — was notably absent from Escudero’s examples of remarks that violated the sub judice rule.

While Escudero was delivering his speech, Duterte in fact issued another statement calling out the prosecution for calling her a scam mastermind, and senator-judge Raffy Tulfo for describing her special disbursing officer Gina Acosta as “stupid.”

Lead prosecutor Jinky Luistro later informed the court about Duterte’s latest remarks. Escudero said the enforcement of new sanctions will apply prospectively, giving her the same clean slate as prosecutors who made the statements flagged by the court.

Absolute prohibition?

Prosecutors Kapunan, Ridon, and Tolosa said they respect the court’s decision, although the ruling creates a more complicated communications terrain.

The prosecution team, for one, has to discuss whether Tolosa stays on as its spokesperson. The defense team already said it is looking for a new talking head as defense lawyer Michael Poa seeks to relinquish the post.

Play Video

“Perhaps we need some clarification regarding the order, because it sounded like an absolute prohibition to talk about matters that may touch on the merits of the case. There’s an exemption to that sub judice ruling under jurisprudence which is the doctrine of true, fair, and accurate reporting. If you’re just quoting what has already been stated by the witness in an open court…that shall not be a violation of the sub judice rule,” Tolosa said.

“This is not a regular trial. It is a political, constitutional, and legal process. It is very different from the proceedings prescribed in regular courts,” Ridon added.

The new rules appear to constrain the defense less than the prosecution, which bears the burden of proof while also seeking to win the court of public opinion, as the sui generis trial — a proceeding that is a class of its own — unfolds.

“That’s a very eloquent way of issuing a gag order,” constitutional lawyer Lulu Reyes told Rappler.

Play Video

– Rappler.com

World.title: The Senate curbed remarks in Sara Duterte’s trial — on what legal grounds?
World.content:
The Senate highlights the sub judice or the rule that 'restricts comments and disclosures pertaining to judicial proceedings to avoid prejudging the issue, influencing the court, or obstructing the administration of justice'

Instead of reprimanding those who allegedly discussed the merits of Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment case, presiding officer Chiz Escudero reminded the parties about the limitations of what they can discuss on the floor.

Escudero set the possible penalties against violators: a public reprimand or admonition for the first offense, and then a P30,000-fine for each subsequent offense.

This rule applies to all parties in the ongoing impeachment.

“You know who you are, and based on the records, we know who you are,” said Escudero.

“[You are enjoined] from making public statements or otherwise discussing, sharing, or endorsing comments pertaining to the merits of this pending impeachment trial, and from engaging in trial by publicity, as they directly threaten the independence of the Court, degrade the dignity of the tribunal, and risk turning it into a circus, and weaponize the media to substitute public outrage for actual evidence,” he added.

So what are Escudero’s legal grounds for implementing this order?

Sub judice

The sub judice rule is the principle that bars parties from discussing the merits of the case to avoid undue pressure.

The Supreme Court defines this principle in Romero et al. v. Estrada as the rule that “restricts comments and disclosures pertaining to judicial proceedings to avoid prejudging the issue, influencing the court, or obstructing the administration of justice.”

This rule is not exclusive to court or legal proceedings. This is also found in the Senate’s impeachment rules.

Sub judice in the context of an impeachment trial not only applies to lawyers, but also to the senator-judges and to Duterte herself.

“The Presiding Officer and the Members of the Senate shall refrain from making any comments and disclosures in public pertaining to the merits of a pending impeachment trial. The same shall likewise apply to the prosecutors, to the person impeached, and to their respective counsel and witnesses,” says the procedures’ Rule 18.

Reminder to senator-judges

Escudero, in expounding on the sub judice rule, also mentioned the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (CJCA), or the code of conduct for judges. He cited Canon III, Section 10, which bars judges from making comments in and out of court that could affect the outcome of the case.

Escudero also mentioned CJCA’s Canon IV, Section 24: “A judge shall not engage or use any form of expression which tends to violate, or has the effect of, violating the sub judice principle, provoke or inflame divisive and contentious issues of public concern, or project an image not compatible with the dignity of their position.”

Apart from citing jurisprudence or past court decisions, the presiding officer also mentioned a portion of the oath taken by senator-judges before the trial: “To do impartial justice according to the Constitution and the laws of the Philippines.”

He also took note of the impeachment rules’ Rule III: “Senators shall observe political neutrality during the course of the impeachment trial. ‘Political neutrality’ shall be defined as exercise of public official’s duty without unfair discrimination and regardless of party affiliation or preference.”

Play Video

More penalties

Apart from contempt or the penalties mentioned by Escudero, counsels may also face separate punishments if their remarks or actions violate other rules like CPRA or the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, the code of conduct for lawyers.

“Where the same conduct appears to violate CPRA, the Chair may direct the clerk to transmit the certified copy of the pertinent order, transcript, and records to the Supreme Court or the Office of the Bar Confidant for whatever action the Supreme Court may deem proper. Such transmittal is a referral, not a finding or penalty of professional discipline. Disciplinary jurisdiction over…members of the bar still remain with the Supreme Court,” said Escudero.

Meanwhile, senator-judges who violate their impeachment oath may be slapped with an ethics complaint before the Senate committee on ethics and privileges.

“Under Rule 10, Section 13(2) of the rules of the Senate, the committee on ethics has jurisdiction over all matters relating to the conduct, rights, privileges, safety, dignity, integrity, and reputation of the Senate and its members,” said Escudero. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sub judice effect: Sara’s defense team considers replacing Poa as spokesperson
World.content:
'The option would be to look for another spokes. But in the meantime, since there's no new spokesperson yet, I will maintain my job as the spokesperson. But with the ruling now, I think I'll have to have a discussion with her (Duterte) again,' says Michael Poa

MANILA, Philippines – Apart from discouraging both House prosecutors and members of the defense team from giving media interviews, the Senate impeachment court’s sub judice ruling may also lead to the replacement of Michael Poa as defense spokesperson.

Speaking to reporters, Poa said he will discuss the latest ruling with Vice President Sara Duterte, adding that the defense team will comply with it.

The Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, August 26, reminded the parties of the sub judice rule or the principle that bars them from discussing the merits of the case. Presiding officer Chiz Escudero also told the parties about his earlier advice to designate different spokespersons who will not be restricted by the sub judice rule.

“So, sa atin, medyo risky na rin talaga kasi (So, for us, it’s really a bit risky already),” the defense spokesperson said.

“And there are times when your questions also would…put us in a corner to answer certain things that might delve into the merits. And it’s not your fault, right? But because of the ruling, I need to discuss the matter with the Vice President,” he added.

Rule 18 of the Senate impeachment rules bars the presiding officer and senator-judges “from making any comments and disclosures in public pertaining to the merits of a pending impeachment trial.” This also applies to the House prosecutors, private prosecutors, members of the defense team, and to Duterte herself.

Unlike the House prosecutors who have spokespersons who are not members of the prosecution team, the defense’s talking heads are concurrently serving as counsels. Poa is the spokesperson, while defense lawyer Justin Nicol Gular is his deputy.

Poa said he has no replacement yet, but noted that the defense is looking for a spokesperson who can explain and laymanize the impeachment process well.

“Someone who can really communicate well. And when we say communicate well, it means someone who can laymanize this very technical process,” he added.

Play Video

The defense spokesperson revealed he had laid out the options to Duterte the first time Escudero suggested picking spokespersons who are not members of the legal team. Poa told the Vice President he could remain as spokesperson, but he would have to leave the legal team, or remain as her lawyer and give up his spokesperson duties.

“And her immediate answer was that she wants me as her lawyer,” said Poa.

“The option would be to look for another [spokesperson]. But in the meantime, since there’s no new spokesperson yet, I will maintain my job as the spokesperson. But with the ruling now, I think I’ll have to have a discussion with her again,” he added in a mix of Filipino and English. – Rappler.com

World.title: First warning? Escudero reminds Sara Duterte, through lawyer, of sub judice rule
World.content:
Presiding officer Chiz Escudero gives the reminder after Vice President Sara Duterte made a social media post about the trial at about the same time he read his decision on the sub judice rule

MANILA, Philipines — Presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero on Wednesday, August 26, reminded Vice President Sara Duterte to abide by his sub judice ruling which he issued during that day’s impeachment trial.

Escudero gave the reminder to Duterte through her defense counsel, after lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro made a manifestation that the Vice President had just violated the rule through a social media post that morning, as the presiding officer read his ruling.

“We would like to respectfully manifest to the honorable impeachment court that almost simultaneously to the reading of the ruling of the honorable impeachment court on the issue of the sub judice rule, the respondent VP Sara Duterte, made a public statement,” Luistro said, before being told by Escudero that he was already aware of this.

Escudero responded: “Given that it was done while the ruling is being issued, prospectivity would still apply. However, the presiding officer would like to remind — through the lead counsel for the respondent — her client to kindly observe the ruling of the presiding officer as well as the rules of the impeachment court, specifically Rule 18 on the subject matter, in regard to making comments on the merits of the case.”

“Because henceforth the necessary actions will be taken against her not only by the court but also given she is a lawyer, via what the presiding officer earlier mentioned in relation to the CPRA and the Office of the Bar Confidant,” he said.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison took note of the reminder.

In his ruling, Escudero noted that under Rule 18 of the Senate Impeachment Rules, all parties in the trial are barred “from making public statements or otherwise discussing, sharing, or endorsing comments pertaining to the merits of this pending impeachment trial, and from engaging in trial by publicity, as they directly threaten the independence of the court, degrade the dignity of the tribunal, and risk turning it into a circus, and weaponize the media to substitute public outrage for actual evidence.”

In relation to erring members of the Bar who are parties in the trial, Escudero said that “the certified in-incident record will be transmitted and formal referral will be made to the Office of the Bar Confidant, the Integrated Bar of the Philippines and/or the Supreme Court for possible disciplinary sanction regarding the person’s license to practice.”

Escudero also a few select soundbites of unnamed personalities that violated the sub judice rule, one of them traced back to Duterte. Escudero said past violations would not be sanctioned but warned all parties concerned of the strict enforcement of his ruling moving forward.

‘First warning’

Impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol explained that said that Escudero took the position regarding Duterte’s post as at the time, he had not finished reading the entire ruling so technically, no violation was committed.

Tongol also said that Escudero’s reminder to Duterte could be considered as a “first warning,” and that further violations would be lead to sanctions.

“Kapag third strike, fourth strike na hindi na talaga natuto even with the fine, then the presiding officer will issue an order to refer the matter to the Supreme Court for the disciplinary action by the SC if the person…ay covered by the CPRA,” Tongol said.

(If it’s third and fourth strike then the presiding officer will issue an order to refer the matter to the SC for disciplinary action by the SC if the person is covered by CPRA.)

Tongol stressed that Escudero’s rulings are meant to protect the “constitutional integrity of the trial” and to shield the proceedings from “extrajudicial trial by publicity.”

What about the senator-judges?

Despite the ruling, a couple of senators noticeably used some terms flagged by the impeachment court in its decision.

In his interjection during the prosecutors’ presentation of Office of the Vice President (OVP) assistant chief of staff Lemuel Ortonio, Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson flagged what he described as “copy-paste” programs in the OVP’s regular budget and list of activities for the confidential funds.

Lacson did not mince words, calling it “stupid” to use virtually identical program descriptions and physical targets for its regular budget and confidential funds.

Senator Raffy Tulfo tried to cushion his approach by apologizing to Ortonio for how he was about to describe him — “nagtatanga-tangahan (pretending to be dumb),” in relation to how he scrutinized the confidential funds implementation of former OVP security chief Raymund Dante Lachica.

Play Video

Ortonio said that he took offense with Tulfo’s comment, as he just did his job. Later, Escudero, with the permission of Tulfo, asked that the term be replaced with “feigning ignorance” in the record.

Lachica as witness?

With Lachica pinpointed as the chief implementer of the OVP confidential funds, Senator Erwin Tulfo urged both prosecution and the defense to present him as a witness, while Lacson urged the court to issue a subpoena duces tecum to the documents related to Lachica’s confidential funds implementation.

The defense team earlier said they have no plans yet to tap Lachica as a witness, though the latter had said that he was willing to testify.

Play Video

Escudero said the court cannot compel the parties to call a particular person as a witness but it may call a witness and issue subpoenas for documents after the parties have presented their witnesses and pieces evidence.

Senator Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri, for his part, called on the Commission on Audit to issue its final findings on the notice of disallowance on the OVP’s confidential funds. — Rappler.com

World.title: Can Kazakhstan’s AI Strategy Deliver Both Growth and Smarter Governance?
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is moving toward a broader AI-driven transformation of the economy and public services under a government action plan that sets measurable digitalization targets through 2029, with artificial intelligence increasingly integrated into education, healthcare, transport, finance and industrial management.

Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov approved the action plan on Aug. 26 as part of implementing the national Digital Qazaqstan Strategy through 2029, approved by presidential decree. It brings together measures to transform services for citizens, support businesses and the economy, and modernize the public administration system.

Rather than focusing solely on introducing individual digital services, the plan seeks to establish digital systems across entire sectors, with AI and real-time data becoming part of how government agencies and businesses make decisions.

AI moves from pilot projects to mass adoption

Education is among the areas where the strategy sets one of its most ambitious targets. Through the expansion of the AI-Sana program, at least 80% of school, college and university graduates are expected to acquire basic AI skills by 2029.

At the same time, the government will expand advanced AI training for students and professional development for teachers. By 2028, at least 80% of universities and colleges are expected to integrate AI technologies into educational processes and update curricula to meet economic needs.

The approach reflects a broader shift in AI’s role in Kazakhstan’s digital policy. Instead of treating artificial intelligence primarily as a technology-sector issue, the government plans to incorporate it into education, healthcare, infrastructure, industry and public administration.

From digital services to predictive government

Healthcare digitalization will focus on creating a unified data management system and expanding services that can be accessed without visiting medical institutions.

By 2029, the government plans to increase the number of citizens using medical self-service platforms, connect more healthcare organizations to a common digital environment with real-time data exchange and expand the use of AI in clinical decision-making.

A similar principle will apply to public services and social support. The government plans to expand proactive services, automated processes and auto-signing mechanisms, with a target of reducing the time required to provide government services and social support measures by at least 50% by 2029.

The objective is to reduce the number of steps citizens must take and gradually shift from a system in which people apply for services to one in which government systems can identify and provide eligible services proactively.

Digital infrastructure becomes part of industrial policy

The strategy also treats digitalization as a tool to improve the productivity and resilience of major economic sectors. In the fuel and energy sector, at least 70% of assets are expected to be connected to digital monitoring systems by 2029. This would allow operators to track asset condition in real time and identify potential reliability risks earlier. Digital traceability of energy resources will also be expanded.

Construction is another sector where the government plans to establish a digital environment covering the full project lifecycle, from design to operation. By 2029, all new technically complex facilities are expected to be managed within a unified digital system.

These measures could make digital data increasingly important not only for administrative purposes, but also for managing physical infrastructure and anticipating operational risks.

Kazakhstan targets digital logistics

Transport and logistics are another major focus of the plan, with digitalization extending across the movement of goods from border crossing points to major transport corridors and multimodal hubs.

One priority is reducing the time freight vehicles need to pass through selected border crossings. The government plans to expand digital tools that collect and process shipment information in advance, reducing the number of procedures that require manual intervention.

Under the Smart Cargo initiative, priority shipments will receive digital passports and end-to-end tracking, allowing cargo to be monitored throughout its journey.

Meanwhile, intelligent transport analytics will be introduced across key transport corridors, border crossings and multimodal hubs. Such systems could allow authorities to assess infrastructure capacity in real time, manage traffic flows and respond more quickly to bottlenecks.

This is particularly significant for Kazakhstan as it seeks to strengthen its position as a transit and logistics hub between major markets. The effectiveness of the digitalization effort will therefore depend not only on the technology itself, but also on how effectively different transport systems and border authorities can exchange data.

Digitalization targets businesses and financial institutions

For small and medium-sized enterprises, the plan emphasizes reducing administrative burdens and providing more targeted digital tools. Businesses will be able to assess their level of digital maturity and receive individual digitalization roadmaps. Digital compliance and risk-based supervision are also expected to reduce physical inspections of low-risk SMEs.

Tax administration is similarly set to move toward a more automated model, with more processes carried out without additional action by taxpayers. The government describes this approach as “invisible” tax administration, aimed at reducing the share of the unobserved economy.

The financial sector will also undergo digital transformation. By 2028, at least 80% of second-tier banks are expected to be connected to a secure digital information exchange system. The same target applies to financial organizations that provide products to individuals and are connected to the Unified Digital Platform.

AI investment expected to generate measurable returns

The strategy places particular emphasis on ensuring that digitalization produces an economic rather than purely technological effect. In Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund portfolio companies, digital and AI initiatives are expected to contribute 5% annually to EBITDA growth.

For Baiterek National Management Holding, AI monitoring is planned to cover 100% of investment projects by 2029. The government also aims to strengthen Kazakhstan’s domestic IT industry and increase its presence in international markets. Exports of IT services and digital solutions are targeted to grow by at least 50% by 2029.

Regional robotics competence centers and support for domestic technology integrators implementing commercial projects are among the measures intended to support the development of a technology-driven economy.

Data centers and cybersecurity become strategic priorities

The planned Data Center Valley is intended to attract global technology and cloud providers, expand computing capacity and create infrastructure for large-scale AI adoption.

The project is expected to increase Kazakhstan’s ability to process and store data domestically while providing infrastructure for new AI services and the development of the local digital industry.

At the same time, expanding the use of data and AI increases the importance of cybersecurity and personal data protection. The action plan therefore includes measures to strengthen government information systems, improve cybersecurity awareness and develop digital safety culture.

Government digital systems will also be connected to the Personal Data Access Control service, which is designed to give citizens greater visibility and control over how their personal information is used.

Taken together, the measures suggest that Kazakhstan’s digitalization agenda is moving beyond digitizing individual government services toward a model in which data, AI and interconnected digital infrastructure become part of the country’s economic and administrative architecture.

World.title: 262 Foreign IT Specialists Receive Digital Nomad Status in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA – A total of 262 foreign IT specialists have received residency or visa statuses in Kazakhstan under the Digital Nomad Residency and Digital Nomad Visa programs, according to updated figures from Astana Hub.

As of August 2026, 250 foreign IT specialists have obtained permanent residence permits under the Digital Nomad Residency program, while another 12 have received Digital Nomad Visas after completing the required procedures.

The programs are designed to attract international technology professionals to Kazakhstan, strengthen links with the global technology community and facilitate the exchange of expertise with local IT companies and professionals.

Since the programs were launched, Astana Hub has received 1,517 applications from IT specialists representing 71 countries across the region, Europe, North America, Asia and the Middle East.

The number of applications does not correspond directly to the number of visas or residence permits issued, as applicants must complete several stages, including application review, obtaining an Astana Hub petition and subsequent procedures with government authorities. As of August, Astana Hub had issued 1,069 petitions following its review of applications – 1,030 under Digital Nomad Residency and 39 under Digital Nomad Visa.

Astana Hub stressed that a petition is neither a visa nor a residence permit and does not automatically guarantee that an applicant will receive the relevant status. The technology hub reviews applications and issues petitions when candidates meet the established requirements, while final decisions on visas and residence permits are made by authorized state bodies.

The 262 specialists who have received the relevant statuses account for nearly 17% of all applications submitted since the programmes were launched.

The programs target foreign IT professionals who meet established professional criteria and are considering Kazakhstan as a place to live and work. Eligible specialists include software developers, product managers, artificial intelligence professionals, data analysts, technology entrepreneurs and startup founders, as well as executives of international technology companies and other digital professionals, including those working remotely for foreign employers.

According to Astana Hub, the presence of international IT professionals could contribute to knowledge exchange with Kazakh teams, the development of technology entrepreneurship and the growth of the country’s professional IT community.

Foreign specialists living in Kazakhstan may also contribute to local economic activity through spending on goods and services. Over the longer term, some could launch projects in Kazakhstan, invest in local technology teams and create new jobs.

The programs therefore form part of Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to strengthen its technology ecosystem by combining international expertise with the development of domestic digital talent and businesses.

World.title: Central Asia Explores Islamic Finance as Path to Greater Financial Connectivity
World.content:
TASHKENT – Islamic finance is emerging as a potential new channel for connecting Central Asia with global capital, as Uzbekistan works to build regulatory and market infrastructure for Sharia-compliant investment. Speaking at the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum in Tashkent on Aug. 26, Central Bank of Uzbekistan Governor Timur Ishmetov outlined Uzbekistan’s efforts to develop Islamic microfinance, banking and capital markets as part of a broader strategy to diversify the financial system and attract international investment.

The initiative comes as Central Asian countries seek to strengthen financial connectivity with markets beyond the region and develop new investment channels. Uzbekistan is positioning Islamic finance as one component of this emerging financial architecture, alongside fintech, digital payments, cross-border finance and capital-market development.

Speaking at the forum, Ishmetov said Uzbekistan is developing its approach to Islamic finance in stages, covering microfinance, banking and capital markets.

From Islamic microfinance to banking

According to Ishmetov, Uzbekistan has already established the first layer of its Islamic finance infrastructure through Islamic microfinance.

Twelve microfinance organizations currently provide Islamic financial services based on contracts including Murabaha, Ijara, Salam, Mudaraba and Musharakah.

The second stage began with the adoption of a law on Islamic banking on June 29, which established a legal framework for Islamic banking activities in Uzbekistan. The legislation allows both fully fledged Islamic banks and Islamic banking windows within conventional banks to operate under dedicated Islamic banking licenses.

“Furthermore, the two-tier Islamic finance governance framework has been traditioned in accordance with the best industrial practices, including the establishment of a central bank Islamic finance board and Islamic finance boards within conventional banks,” Ishmetov said.

“One of the key challenges in the development of Islamic finance is ensuring neutrality in taxation of conventional and Islamic financial transactions,” he added.

He noted that the new legislation introduced a dedicated taxation regime designed to provide neutrality in areas including value-added and income taxes, alongside relevant exemptions from state duties.

Next step: Islamic capital markets

The third stage of Uzbekistan’s strategy is developing an Islamic capital market. According to Ishmetov, a draft capital markets law includes a dedicated chapter on Sukuk, or Islamic bonds, and had recently been approved by the Legislative Chamber of Parliament at first reading.

Ishmetov said Uzbekistan has also developed a 2026–2030 roadmap for the national Islamic finance industry in cooperation with the Islamic Financial Services Board. The Cabinet of Ministers approved the roadmap, which includes 39 measures across five thematic areas.

“Accordingly, over the coming years, our efforts will focus on further strengthening the legal and regulatory framework, developing human capital and enhancing public awareness, deepening international cooperation, facilitating the start of Islamic banking operations, building supporting infrastructure for Islamic finance and other priorities,” he said.

FinTech as an enabler

Ishmetov also linked the development of Islamic finance to the country’s broader digital transformation.

“We see FinTech as an important enabler of Islamic finance as an overall ecosystem and one of the key drivers for innovation, investment and productive economic activity,” he said.

Digital financial services, he added, can improve efficiency and transparency while enabling financial products to be delivered at greater scale.

“In this new era of digital economy, we believe that provision of financial services, including Islamic financial services, through digital channels will play an increasingly important role in creating new opportunities for innovation, investment and economic development,” Ishmetov said.

This intersection between Islamic finance and financial technology was one of the broader themes of the Tashkent forum, which also examined digital payments, artificial intelligence, tokenization, digital assets and cross-border financial infrastructure.

For Central Asia, the development of Islamic finance could provide an additional connection to capital markets in the Gulf, Türkiye and South and Southeast Asia. Uzbekistan’s emerging regulatory framework could therefore serve not only domestic borrowers and investors, but also support wider regional financial integration.

World.title: Experts: Kazakhstan’s Oil Export Strategy Faces Growing Need for Diversification
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s decision to cut its 2026 oil production target from 98 million tonnes to 96 million tonnes after disruptions affecting the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) has highlighted the country’s continued dependence on a major export route and the need to strengthen alternatives, experts say.

Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said at an Aug. 25 government briefing that attacks on CPC facilities in January and again in July had resulted in nearly 3.5 million tonnes of lost oil production.

“We planned to produce 98 million tonnes, but the adjusted plan is now 96 million tonnes. The losses in production from the attacks on CPC will amount to 3.5 million tonnes,” Akkenzhenov said.

The minister said Kazakhstan and oil producers had also adjusted maintenance schedules to preserve as much production as possible in 2026. Tengizchevroil shareholders decided to postpone major maintenance until next year, while maintenance work at fields operated by North Caspian Operating Company was also moved to 2027. Maintenance at the Karachaganak field, meanwhile, is expected to begin in mid-September and is projected to reduce production by nearly 400,000-450,000 tonnes.

The developments highlight a broader challenge for Kazakhstan: as a major oil exporter, the country’s production capacity is only one part of the equation. Maintaining reliable access to international markets through secure and diversified export routes is equally important.

CPC remains critical to Kazakhstan’s oil exports

Kazakhstan produces substantially more oil than it consumes domestically, making export infrastructure a critical component of the country’s economic security. The CPC remains the country’s principal export route for crude oil, connecting Kazakhstan’s major producing fields with the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk.

Repeated disruptions have therefore created a challenge that goes beyond temporary reductions in pipeline throughput. They have raised questions about how quickly Kazakhstan can redirect crude if its main export route becomes unavailable or operates below capacity.

Economist and independent oil and gas reserves evaluator Abzal Narymbetov highlights that Kazakhstan’s position as a major net oil exporter makes diversification particularly important.

“Kazakhstan produces approximately five times more oil than it consumes domestically. This makes Kazakhstan a distinctly oil-exporting country,” Narymbetov wrote in his Energy Analytics Telegram channel.

He also said the strategic issue is not simply increasing production.

“The main question for Kazakhstan is not only how much oil to produce, but how to maintain export volumes, develop supply routes and increase added value within the country,” Narymbetov wrote.

According to him, in the longer term Kazakhstan should also focus on processing more crude domestically and developing petrochemicals and other higher-value products. This suggests that the current disruption could be viewed not only as an infrastructure problem, but also as a broader question of how Kazakhstan manages its dependence on oil exports.

Baku-Supsa emerges as an alternative

Akkenzhenov has identified the Baku-Supsa route as one potential alternative to CPC. Asked whether Kazakhstan had discussed transporting more crude through Azerbaijan, the minister said direct negotiations had not yet taken place, although preliminary groundwork existed.

“For this, first of all, we need to determine our position domestically in Kazakhstan. There is some groundwork from previous negotiations, but direct negotiations have not yet taken place,” Akkenzhenov said.

“Just imagine: we lost 3.5 million tonnes because of the attacks on CPC, although we could have redirected these volumes through the port of Aktau and the Baku-Supsa pipeline. Its capacity, by the way, is 5 million tonnes,” the minister added.

The minister’s comments point to a key limitation, however. An alternative route can provide strategic value even if it cannot replace CPC in terms of capacity. Baku-Supsa’s reported capacity of 5 million tonnes is substantially smaller than the volumes Kazakhstan exports through CPC. Its importance therefore lies less in replacing the main route and more in providing additional resilience when the main system is disrupted.

Diversification does not mean abandoning CPC

The current situation does not necessarily imply that Kazakhstan can or should move away from CPC. Instead, it highlights the economic value of having several export options. Political science expert Gaziz Abishev said that CPC remains an essential part of Kazakhstan’s economic security because the country invested in the project specifically to create an efficient route for its oil exports.

“CPC is an indispensable element of Kazakhstan’s economic security,” Abishev wrote on his Telegram channel, stressing that the pipeline was developed as an economic project rather than as a geopolitical instrument.

“Receiving oil revenues, Kazakhstan either accumulates them in the National Fund or spends them on social needs – in the interests of its people,” he wrote, adding that the country has maintained a neutral position while calling on all sides to pursue peace.

A test of Kazakhstan’s energy resilience

The latest production target adjustment shows how an external disruption to a major export corridor can translate into a measurable impact on Kazakhstan’s domestic production plans.

The loss of nearly 3.5 million tonnes and the reduction of the annual target to 96 million tonnes do not fundamentally change Kazakhstan’s position as a major oil producer. But they demonstrate the economic consequences of concentrated export infrastructure.

Akkenzhenov’s description of Baku-Supsa as “vital” suggests that the government is increasingly viewing alternative routes not simply as commercial opportunities, but as part of national energy resilience. At the same time, CPC will remain the backbone of Kazakhstan’s oil export system because of its scale and established infrastructure.

The challenge is that alternative routes have different capacities, infrastructure requirements and costs. Moving additional volumes through the Caspian requires sufficient port capacity, tanker availability and infrastructure on the other side of the sea. That means diversification is not simply a matter of signing agreements. It requires sustained investment in the entire logistics chain.

World.title: AqylSu: Turning Kazakhstan’s Shanghai AI Vision Into Working Water Platform
World.content:
Kazakhstan boasts to have an AI diplomacy and a digital-government track record. What it is missing is a platform that turns both into water reaching the people who need it.

During President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to Shanghai this July, he addressed the World Artificial Intelligence Conference, describing AI as an industry now building out a “comprehensive infrastructure” that will shape the future of the global economy, trade and international connectivity. He cited the United Nations statistics showing that global investment in AI infrastructure is growing by an average of 47% a year, with the global AI market on track to approach $5 trillion by 2033. His main argument was about fairness: AI should become a driver of more equitable and inclusive development, and every country needs a chance to build its own human capital, digital infrastructure and institutions around it, not just the few states currently leading the field.

Kazakhstan did not just make the argument in Shanghai — it proposed and acted on it, co-founding the new World AI Cooperation Organization alongside 28 other states within months of the idea being proposed, with Tokayev offering the capital of Kazakhstan as host of its first meeting. The obvious next step is what Kazakhstan actually builds with that vision once the delegation flies home. A very powerful candidate sitting in the country’s own fields is water.

A crisis moving faster than the diplomacy meant to fix it

Kazakhstan is among the world’s 30 most water-stressed countries and has lost over 21% of its per capita water availability since the start of the 2000s. More than 45% of its water actually originates outside its borders. The Caspian Sea is now at its lowest level in over 400 years and shrinks at a fast accelerating rate. None of this is moving on a diplomatic timetable. Yet the country’s main global response is a proposed International Water Organization (IWO) championed by Tokayev under UN auspices since 2025, but discussions are still focused on how the organization should eventually take shape. A parallel regional process, Tajikistan’s Dushanbe Water Framework, remains an important initiative, yet it is not expected to be adopted until the 2028 UN Water Conference.

Both processes matter, and neither is wrong to exist — a UN-backed framework can build an institution that carries international legitimacy, but that takes time and lasting credibility. The problem is that water insecurity is moving much faster than the diplomacy designed to address it. With every year that passes, the gap between the crisis and the response grows a little wider. Kazakhstan has already showcased that it can act quickly when it sees a strategic opportunity. Its recent leadership on AI cooperation in Shanghai showed its capabilities of bringing countries together and building new institutions. Water diplomacy now requires the same sense of urgency.

The idea: an AI platform that matches specific needs to specific help

The proposal currently taking shape is called AqylSu — meaning “smart water” in Kazakh. The idea was inspired by Kazakhstan’s own eGov.kz system, the main aim of which is to bring the same efficiency to international water cooperation. Instead of relying on long, case-by-case negotiations, AqylSu would provide a single digital platform where countries could submit their requests, find suitable partners, and track progress. While Kazakhstan has gained international recognition worldwide for its digital governance, no similar system currently exists for cooperation on water between countries.

The idea is simple. A country that faces a specific water-related problem, such as a shortage of water filtration equipment, would submit a structured request through the platform. An AI-powered matching system would verify the country’s request using independent data, including images and water-stressed indicators, before comparing it with registered countries and technical organizations that have already declared available equipment or funding. This would allow countries with specific needs to be matched with those who are available to provide practical support for those in need.

Where financing is required, countries with the resources could contribute voluntarily. Further complex requests could be reviewed by a committee working with UN-Water and the International Water Organization, while every request and outcome would be recorded on a public dashboard to further ensure transparency and accountability.

Fast precedents: Saudi Arabia’s Global Water Organization and Tajikistan’s Dushanbe Process

Kazakhstan does not need to guess whether a fast, nationally driven water initiative would work — Saudi Arabia has already begun running the experiment. In September 2023, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman announced the creation of the Global Water Organization (GWO). By May 2025, eight founding states — Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Spain, Greece, Senegal, Pakistan and Mauritania — had signed its charter in Riyadh, with Saudi Arabia funding the organization’s operations for five years and hosting its headquarters. At Saudi Water Week in Jeddah in mid-2026, the GWO had approved its bylaws, governance model, and a four-year strategy, and is preparing for its first General Assembly. Tajikistan’s own Dushanbe Water Process has moved on a similar diplomatic timeline: in May 2026, at its fourth conference, Emomali Rahmon proposed a brand-new Dushanbe Water Framework, expected to be carried forward by the UN Water Conference in 2028, which Tajikistan will host. Both paths show that nationally driven water diplomacy can move fast — but both remain platforms for coordination and policy dialogue, not systems that match one country’s specific need to another’s specific offer. That is precisely the operational layer AqylSu is designed to add.

Two working models for how the mechanism would actually run

AqylSu draws its inspiration from a system the United Nations uses. The UN Volunteers program, which supports agencies such as UNICEF, maintains a global roster of registered professionals and matches them with specific requests from country offices based on their skills. AqylSu follows a similar approach. Instead of matching people to jobs, it would match verified water-related requests with countries or technical experts that have already declared available expertise, equipment, and funding. This would make finding support faster and more targeted, instead of relying on traditional diplomatic outreach.

The financial model also has a practical precedent. Since 1967, the UN Women’s Guild in Vienna has raised funds through its annual International Festivals Bazaar to support small humanitarian projects. A review committee rates applications each year and recommends selected projects for funding, to ensure resources are shared fairly and transparently. AqylSu could adopt a similar approach for water requests that are too small or complex to attract a single sponsoring organization or country, by using a pooled fund overseen by a committee to provide support where it is most needed.

What it would look like in practice

Imagine a country whose water system can no longer hold or provide safe drinking water due to its lack of filtration equipment. Instead of beginning lengthy negotiations, the country submits a request through AqylSu, clearly outlining what is needed and when. The platform verifies the request using independent water data stored in its database, before matching it with a country that has available filtration capacity.

If the country cannot cover the full cost, AqylSu will first look for a state that is willing to help finance the request. If there is no direct sponsor available, the request can be reviewed through a pooled funding mechanism based on the UN Women’s Guild’s model. At every stage, from receipt to approval, this information would be posted on a public dashboard so that international water aid would be both swift and transparent.

Bringing the Shanghai vision home

Tokayev’s message in Shanghai was that AI should not remain the property of a handful of advanced economies — that every country deserves the infrastructure and institutions to use it well. Kazakhstan is now in the unusual position of having said that on the world stage and having, close at hand, the exact problem where it could prove it: a water crisis it cannot out-wait, a digital-government platform that already works domestically, and two very different but equally instructive templates — one Gulf, one Viennese — for how the money and the matching could actually flow. AqylSu is not a rival to the UN’s own water diplomacy; it is the operational arm that diplomacy has never had. Kazakhstan already knows it can build fast, charter-based institutions when it chooses to. The question now is whether it does the same for the resource its own president has called an emerging crisis — before the next round of consultations concludes.

The authors are Jansultan Syrymbet and Jamila Syrymbet, students of the CIS Astana and Corvinus University respectively.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: What Will Drive Next Wave of Investment in Central Asia
World.content:
TASHKENT – Investors increasingly want predictable policies, credible financial regulation, functioning capital markets, digital infrastructure, a talent pool and transparent governance, as Central Asia seeks to strengthen its position as an attractive and resilient investment destination. According to experts, Central Asia now has an opportunity to attract a larger share of global investment flows, but doing so will require not only financial innovation and regional connectivity, but also stronger institutions, transparent regulation and deeper capital markets.

Over the past few years in Central Asia, several factors have been positive for the countries, including high gold prices and very high income flows supporting current account deficits. The question is whether this will last long. External risks also include rising fuel and food prices, as well as climate factors.

The experts agreed that macroeconomic stability is the foundation for attracting investors during the panel session at the Silk Road Forum on Aug. 24.

Central Bank of Uzbekistan Governor Timur Ishmetov said the country will continue reducing inflation toward the 5% target by next year to ensure macroeconomic stability. The exchange rate remains flexible and market-oriented.

“The IMF reclassified our exchange rate regime to floating, and we are keen to continue on that. We will continue on capital account liberalization, but in a gradual and rightly sequenced manner. We drafted the roadmap for sequencing of those reforms. Our aim is, while providing more flexibility, to improve institutions, safeguard requirements, risk management, to make sure that we will not harm our stability issues and to improve our regulation,” he said.

Uzbekistan also reduced the state share in the banking sector from 85% to close to 60% in the last few years, and we will continue this trend.

Foreign investors are looking for growth but also predictability.

“Uzbekistan saw a 6% average growth since 2017 in real terms. There is obviously a demographic dividend, which is pretty high in Central Asia overall and Uzbekistan in particular, which will help the market to grow. We have seen consistent policy making in Uzbekistan. In fact, our upgrade of the sovereign credit rating in 2025 was very much linked to this consistent track record of policy making and coordination between the authorities on that front,” said S&P Global Ratings Director Roman Rybalkin.

The country’s first major international equity transaction is being presented as a signal of investor confidence. The National Investment Fund of Uzbekistan (UzNIF) was listed on both the London Stock Exchange and the Tashkent Stock Exchange. The transaction raised $692 million, with demand exceeding $2.9 billion. The fund was trading at a significant premium to its net asset value.

“We continue to bring companies to the market from our portfolio, because through the successful listing of the UzNIF, it shows the global interest in Uzbekistan, and we want to take advantage of this window of opportunity over the next few years and list a few of our assets including Uzbekistan Airways, UzTelecom, the hydropower business, and I think our successful IPO should also pave the way for very attractive private businesses that will be coming to the market over the next few years,” said Marius Dan, Chief Executive Officer for Central Asia at Templeton Global Investments.

Uzbekistan is also advancing its fintech ecosystem. UzCard and Humo are successful examples of networks that build fintech ecosystems around their payment networks. The country has 100 fintech startups, and the government seeks to double that number by 2030 and attract 1 billion investments in this sector.

Tashkent is hosting the Silk Road Finance and Technology Forum 2026. The Central Bank of Uzbekistan and Singapore-headquartered Global Finance and Technology Network (GFTN) support the event, which Ant International co-hosts on Aug. 24-26.

The event connects more than 4,000 participants from 74 countries in Tashkent. The forum focused on five key themes: digital payments and infrastructure; Islamic finance and new economic corridors; AI and emerging technologies; tokenization and digital assets; and cross-border finance and regulation.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Transport Sector Is Diversifying as Growth Moderates, Experts Say
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s transport sector maintained positive growth in January-July 2026, with the physical volume of transport and warehousing services increasing 7.4% year on year, down from 22.5% a year earlier. The slower pace of expansion, alongside diverging trends across transport modes, may signal a gradual shift in the structure of the country’s logistics system, experts say.

The latest figures from the Bureau of National Statistics’ Aug. 12 report show that Kazakhstan’s transport sector is still expanding, with freight transportation up 0.9% and freight turnover increasing 1.0%. Passenger transportation grew 4.5%, while passenger turnover rose 6.1%.

However, the slower pace of growth does not necessarily indicate a weakening of the sector, according to financial economist Rassul Rysmambetov. He said the comparison with last year’s 22.5% growth should be viewed in the context of a high base effect.

“The slowdown from 22.5% to 7.4%, if calculated correctly, can’t be explained as a crisis in transportation. Partially, it is a higher base effect, because last year’s high growth rate cannot be sustained for long,” Rysmambetov told the Astana Times.

He described the current rate as still representing “robust expansion,” with the sources of growth becoming more diversified.

“Now we have domestic trade, road transportation, and Caspian shipping growing instead of high-volume transit and pipeline,” he added.

Different modes reflect different parts of the economy

The overall figures conceal significant differences between individual segments. Road freight transportation increased 6.2% year on year, accounting for 37% of the sector’s total freight volume. Freight turnover in the segment rose 6.5%.

Maritime freight transportation increased 7.2%, while freight turnover grew 18%. Inland waterway transportation recorded particularly rapid growth, with freight volumes increasing 68.5% and freight turnover more than doubling, rising 109.6%.

At the same time, railway freight volumes declined 1.7% to 190.1 million tonnes. Despite the decrease in physical volume, railway freight turnover increased 2.5% to 170.1 billion tonne-kilometres, accounting for 57% of total freight turnover.

The combination of lower volumes and higher turnover may indicate that goods are being transported over longer distances. Pipeline transportation recorded a 2.6% decline in freight volumes, to 148.5 million tonnes, while freight turnover decreased 2.9%.

According to Rysmambetov, however, comparing the performance of different transport modes too directly can be misleading.

“The figures for different transportation means should be compared very cautiously. For example, a 2.6% decline in pipeline transportation reflects changes in oil production and export schedules rather than the same cargo, oil in this case, simply being moved to trucks, ships or rivers,” he said, noting that different modes serve different parts of the economy.

This distinction is important for interpreting the latest statistics. The decline in pipeline transportation coincides with an 8.9% year-on-year decrease in Kazakhstan’s oil production during the first seven months of 2026, meaning that lower pipeline volumes cannot automatically be interpreted as evidence that oil cargo is shifting to alternative modes.

Diversification rather than replacement

The strong growth recorded by maritime and inland waterway transportation nevertheless raises questions about the changing role of alternative logistics routes. Rysmambetov cautioned that the particularly high growth rates in Caspian shipping and inland waterway transportation also partly reflect a low comparison base.

“In general, the country is building diversified transportation options rather than replacing its traditional routes. Railways and pipelines will stay the backbone of the system, while road, maritime and river transport are becoming more and more important as complementary channels,” Rysmambetov said.

This distinction could be important for Kazakhstan’s long-term transport strategy. A more diversified system would not necessarily mean moving away from railways or pipelines, which remain critical for large-scale freight and energy exports. Instead, it would give businesses additional options for moving goods and accessing different markets.

Warehousing emerges as a critical part of the logistics system

The development of transport infrastructure is also creating demand for another part of the logistics chain: warehousing. Evgeny Vinokurov, chief economist of the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB), said the bank’s research has identified warehousing infrastructure as a major structural issue for Eurasia.

“One of EDB’s flagship studies last year focused on warehousing infrastructure, which the Bank describes as a turning point for Eurasia this decade,” Vinokurov said.

He noted that warehouses should no longer be viewed simply as storage facilities, but as an increasingly sophisticated component of modern logistics. He also identified Almaty, Astana and Shymkent as three major logistics nodes with strong potential for warehouse development.

The development of these nodes could become increasingly important as Kazakhstan seeks to strengthen its role as a regional transit and distribution hub. Greater cargo flows alone, however, do not guarantee greater economic benefits. The country needs sufficient infrastructure to store, process and redistribute goods efficiently.

Growth is becoming more diversified

The passenger segment also remained broadly positive. Road passenger transportation increased 4.6% year on year, with 1.11 billion passengers transported during the period. Passenger turnover grew 6.8%.

Air passenger transportation increased 2.8%, with 9.2 million passengers transported and passenger turnover rising 8.1%. Maritime passenger transportation increased 138.3%, while inland waterway passenger transportation grew 7.0%.

Railway passenger transportation, meanwhile, declined 3.5% to 11.1 million passengers, although passenger turnover edged up 0.1%. The decline was less pronounced than the 6.3% decrease recorded during the same period last year.

The mixed performance reinforces the broader pattern: Kazakhstan’s transport sector is not moving uniformly in one direction.

For now, experts caution against interpreting the latest figures as a wholesale transformation of the transport system. The data instead point to a sector that is continuing to grow while gradually developing a broader range of logistics channels and infrastructure around its traditional backbone.

World.title: Tokayev Meets US Congressional Delegation in Astana: What Deeper US Engagement Means for Kazakhstan?
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is becoming increasingly important to Washington not only as a source of energy and critical minerals, but also as a key partner in developing alternative trade routes and strengthening U.S. engagement across Central Asia. A meeting between President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and a delegation of the U.S. House of Representatives on Aug. 25 highlighted the expanding scope of that relationship, as both sides emphasized economic cooperation ahead of Tokayev’s planned participation in the G20 summit in Miami.

The delegation was led by Jason Smith, chairman of the U.S. House Committee on the Budget and Taxation, and included Congress members Greg Murphy, Carol Miller, Ronny Jackson, Wesley Bell and Edward Case.

Tokayev highlighted the timing of the delegation’s visit, which came shortly after Kazakhstan’s first elections to the new unicameral Kurultai. According to him, parliamentary diplomacy would become an important area of activity for the new legislature.

“Constructive and meaningful dialogue between members of the U.S. Congress and the Kurultai is important for further deepening mutual understanding, promoting common priorities and strengthening the Kazakhstan-U.S. partnership,” Tokayev said.

The meeting also comes ahead of Tokayev’s planned visit to Miami for the G20 summit, following an invitation from U.S. President Donald Trump.

From political dialogue to economic interests

The discussion reflects a broader expansion of the Kazakhstan-U.S. relationship, which increasingly extends beyond traditional diplomatic cooperation. Tokayev briefed the delegation on Kazakhstan’s political and socioeconomic reforms and outlined the country’s modernization priorities.

Smith emphasized the economic dimension of the delegation’s visit. According to him, Trump asked to convey his warmest greetings and expressed his appreciation for the trusting and constructive relationship that has developed between both leaders.

“He also said that he looks forward to your visit to Miami to participate in the G20 summit,” Smith said.

“One of the main goals of our visit is to explore opportunities for further expanding economic ties between the U.S. and your wonderful country. We are firmly committed to meaningful dialogue on strengthening bilateral cooperation,” Smith added.

This emphasis is significant because the relationship is increasingly being driven by practical economic interests rather than diplomacy alone.

Kazakhstan’s strategic position

The growing U.S. interest in Kazakhstan also reflects the country’s position within a rapidly changing Eurasian environment. A discussion held Aug. 21 by the CFive Intellectual Platform and the Hudson Institute brought together experts from the U.S., Kazakhstan and Switzerland to examine the changing dynamics across Eurasia.

The discussion highlighted different interpretations of Kazakhstan’s emerging role. Ken Moriyasu, senior fellow at the Hudson Institute and an expert on Greater Asia, Central Asia and the Caucasus, described Kazakhstan as the “most important swing state in the world.”

His argument places Kazakhstan within the broader competition between the U.S. and China. He said Central Asia, the Caucasus and Türkiye could become increasingly important in that competition.

His framing, however, raises a broader question: should Kazakhstan’s importance primarily be understood through the competition between larger powers?

The growing U.S. engagement therefore does not necessarily indicate a shift away from a balanced foreign policy. Instead, it could strengthen Kazakhstan’s ability to maintain a diversified network of international partnerships.

The G20 invitation

Tokayev’s upcoming participation in the G20 summit in Miami provides a particularly visible example of this expanding engagement. The latest invitation is significant because it comes from Washington at a time when the U.S. is showing greater interest in Central Asia and the wider Trans-Caspian region.

Iskander Akylbayev, CEO of Xander Group and chairman of CFive, described the upcoming summit as a practical opportunity for Kazakhstan.

“My expectation is that the Miami G20 will be highly pragmatic and transaction-driven,” he said, identifying economic growth, secure energy supply chains and technological innovation as likely priorities.

The invitations extended to Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan can be also an evidence that Washington’s engagement extends beyond Kazakhstan. Thus, Kazakhstan’s growing importance to the U.S. can be viewed both as recognition of its individual economic and strategic weight and as part of a broader American effort to strengthen ties across the Trans-Caspian region.

A partnership with room for expansion

During the Aug. 25 meeting, Tokayev also emphasized cooperation between Kazakhstan and the U.S. in multilateral formats, including efforts to promote global and regional stability. He highlighted Kazakhstan’s support for U.S. initiatives, including the Board of Peace and the Abraham Accords, as well as cooperation on nuclear security and non-proliferation.

Smith, for his part, said Trump had expressed appreciation for the relationship and looked forward to Tokayev’s participation in the G20 summit. The upcoming meeting in Miami could therefore provide an opportunity to translate the growing political relationship into concrete economic agreements.

But the long-term significance of the partnership will depend on whether increased diplomatic attention results in sustained investment, technology cooperation, expanded trade and infrastructure development.

The latest meeting in Astana, the upcoming G20 summit and the expanding focus on economic cooperation suggest that Kazakhstan-U.S. relations are entering a more pragmatic phase – one in which the strength of the partnership will increasingly be measured by concrete economic outcomes rather than diplomatic rhetoric alone.

World.title: Lawyers call prison ban on Lasha Bugadze’s novel The Observer act of censorship
World.content:
The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA) says the refusal to allow writer Lasha Bugadze’s novel The Observer into a prison violates freedom of expression and amounts to censorship.

According to GYLA, the arguments put forward by the Special Penitentiary Service to justify the ban run counter to international human rights standards, including case law established by the European Court of Human Rights.

In early August, reports emerged that the Rustavi prison administration had refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel The Observer to be delivered to Nana Sander, a prisoner convicted of taking part in a 4 October 2025 protest.

The Special Penitentiary Service’s response to a request from lawyer Giorgi Chkheidze, dated 24 August, later circulated in the media and on social networks. The agency explained why it had refused to allow the book into the prison.

The service referred to an annex to Justice Minister’s Order No. 1166 of 21 January 2026. Under the rules, prisoners and detainees may receive parcels containing books, but publications that could pose a threat to their safety or the normal operation of a prison are excluded.

According to the Penitentiary Service, the title The Observer creates uncertainty about the novel’s content and does not allow it to be interpreted unambiguously. The authorities therefore deemed it inappropriate to allow the book into the prison.

GYLA says this justification amounts to an arbitrary restriction of prisoners’ right to receive information.

GYLA argues that freedom to receive information forms part of freedom of expression. It covers not only receiving information itself, but also accessing it in different forms, including through literature. Imprisonment does not in itself mean that a person loses their rights, although certain restrictions may apply because of the conditions of detention.

However, GYLA says such restrictions can only be justified if they serve a lawful, legitimate and necessary purpose.

Under European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) case law, when authorities refuse to deliver publications to prisoners, they must provide sufficient and specific reasons. These may include incitement to or justification of violence, threats to prison security and order, or facilitating communication between members of criminal organisations.

Under ECHR standards, however, the grounds for a ban must be directly linked to the publication’s content. Authorities must identify the relevant passages and demonstrate a connection between the specific text and the threat that the restriction seeks to prevent.

GYLA says the argument that the book has a “vague” title clearly fails to meet these requirements. In the case of fiction, the organisation says, such a factor cannot provide sufficient grounds for a ban.

The Observer is a dystopian novel depicting almost half a century of rule by a despot in Georgia. In March 2026, the book, along with other publications, was targeted in an act of vandalism at a bookshop.

GYLA says the Penitentiary Service’s decision is particularly concerning in this context, as it suggests that the book was censored because of its anti-repressive and political content.

About Lasha Bugadze’s novel The Observer

World.title: ‘We pray together’: Georgian and Russian Orthodox churches to exchange hundreds of icons
World.content:
The Georgian diaspora in Russia has announced the launch of the “We Pray Together” project, which will involve creating hundreds of icons and exchanging them between the Orthodox churches of Georgia and Russia.

The icons created as part of the project will depict Saint Gabriel and Saint Seraphim of Sarov. The organisers say the icons will share the title “Friendship of the Peoples of Russia and Georgia”.

According to the Federal Georgian National-Cultural Autonomy in Russia (FGNCA), the first batch of icons has already been painted in Georgia and is ready to be handed over to the Russian Orthodox Church.

In a statement, the FGNCA said the project would “serve as a major civilisational response to the challenges of our time” and bring the peoples of Russia and Georgia closer through their shared faith and centuries-old traditions.

The head of the Georgian diaspora in Russia, David Tsetskhladze, described the project as “one of the largest Orthodox initiatives” in the history of Russian-Georgian relations.

“We are not simply exchanging gifts. We are bringing together the patron saints of our peoples to show that spiritual kinship is stronger than any political circumstances. The exchange of hundreds of Orthodox icons will create a historic precedent,” Tsetskhladze said.

The idea of creating the icons came from a group of volunteers led by journalist and filmmaker Konstantin Tsertsvadze.

The statement also says that the initiative received the blessing of the late Catholicos-Patriarch of All Georgia Ilia II in 2018.

Georgia-Russia icon exchange

World.title: Tourism support package: Can Azerbaijan reach its target of 3.8 million visitors?
World.content:
State support for tourism in Azerbaijan

A new state programme, approved by a decree from President Ilham Aliyev, sets out plans to develop the tourism sector in the coming years, attract more foreign visitors and expand tourism beyond Baku.

The programme comes into force as the tourism sector faces declining figures. In the first half of 2026, 1.09 million foreigners and stateless people arrived in Azerbaijan. This was 10.3% fewer than in the same period last year. Arrivals from the Gulf countries fell by 31.4%, while hotel stays declined by 8.3% and hotel revenues by 3.8%.

Target for 2030: 3.8 million tourists

Under the State Programme, the value added generated by industries directly linked to tourism — in other words, the sector’s actual contribution to the economy — should rise from 6.96 billion manats (about $4.1 billion) in 2025 to 8.51 billion manats in 2027 and 12.17 billion manats (about $7.2 billion) in 2030.

The programme targets real growth of around 40% in the tourism sector by 2030. “Real growth” means an actual increase in the volume of production and services, rather than a nominal rise caused by higher prices.

The government plans to increase the number of foreign arrivals from 2.57 million in 2025 to 3.8 million by 2030.

The target for 2026 is 2.42 million arrivals. Given the 10.3% decline recorded in the first half of the year, the figures will need to improve significantly in the second half to meet this target.

Competition is also intensifying. Azerbaijan ranks 56th among 119 countries in the World Economic Forum’s 2024 Travel and Tourism Development Index. Georgia ranks 45th, Kazakhstan 52nd and Uzbekistan 78th.

In 2025, Georgia reported 5.5 million tourist trips, Uzbekistan 11.7 million foreign tourists and Kazakhstan 15.7 million foreign visitors. The countries use different methods to count tourists and visitors, so these figures cannot be compared directly. Nevertheless, they show that Azerbaijan’s tourism sector faces strong regional competition.

Subsidies, new flights and easier visa rules

The programme provides for extensive government support. Authorities plan to offer subsidies to local tour operators that bring tourists to Azerbaijan, as well as to micro and small businesses operating in the tourism sector.

The measures also include partial compensation for charter flight costs, incentives to open additional scheduled flights to Azerbaijan from priority markets, and financial support for concerts and other entertainment events.

Another area concerns easier entry into the country. The programme provides for expanding visa-free access to citizens of 34 target markets, widening access to e-visas and introducing a “digital nomad” visa in 2027-2028. It will target people who work remotely and want to live in another country for an extended period.

The plan also calls for the development of regional tourism zones, walking routes, health tourism and gastronomic tourism. These measures could help reduce Azerbaijan’s tourism sector’s dependence on Baku, expensive hotels and major international events.
