A 2026 World Bank analysis also highlights shortcomings in transport links, accommodation infrastructure, local tour operators and the quality of services in the regions.

At least on paper, therefore, the programme correctly identifies many of the sector’s existing problems.

The problem is not just a lack of subsidies

The key question is whether government support alone can make Azerbaijan a more affordable and competitive tourist destination.

The State Programme itself also highlights the high concentration of the air travel market, meaning that a relatively small number of companies provide most of the services. It also points to limited hotel supply, high prices, and problems with hygiene and service quality.

At the same time, budget airlines have expanded their presence in Baku compared with previous years. In July, Heydar Aliyev International Airport said that around 20 low-cost and hybrid airlines operated flights from Baku to more than 20 international destinations.

The problem can therefore no longer be reduced to the claim that “Azerbaijan has no budget airlines”. Other questions have become more important: how frequently do these airlines operate, which cities do they serve, and does competition between airlines actually affect ticket prices?

The position of major business groups in the tourism and hotel markets also matters in this context.

According to publicly available information from PAŞA Holding, whose shareholders include the president’s father-in-law and daughters, its wholly owned subsidiary Absheron Hotel Group operates hotels including Four Seasons Baku, JW Marriott Absheron and Ritz-Carlton Baku. Another group company, PAŞA Travel, brings tourists to the country, books hotels and provides transport services.

This means that companies belonging to the same business group operate at different stages of the tourism chain. Economists call this model “vertical integration”.

Vertical integration is not in itself illegal or necessarily harmful. However, even without complete public data on market shares, an important question remains: what rules will govern the distribution of subsidies among companies of different sizes?

The main question is this: will government support help new and small companies enter the market, or will it mainly benefit companies that already have significant resources?

Who will receive the money, and for what?

Under the presidential decree, the Cabinet of Ministers must develop rules for awarding subsidies within three months. So although the programme has already been approved, one key question remains unanswered: which companies will receive public funds, according to what criteria and in return for what results?

The Centre for Analysis of Economic Reforms and Communication has been tasked with monitoring and evaluating the programme.

However, effective oversight will depend not only on which institution is responsible for it. It will also depend on how accessible information is to the public about the companies receiving subsidies, the amounts they receive and the results they achieve.

Previous audits of other government support programmes by the Chamber of Accounts have identified problems such as insufficient justification for spending on individual projects and a lack of data needed to assess their results. These findings do not directly concern the tourism programme, but they highlight the importance of building the new subsidy mechanism around clear and measurable criteria from the outset.х.

A tourist’s decision is not based on price alone

Entry requirements also directly affect the competitiveness of the tourism sector.

At present, travellers can enter Azerbaijan by air, while crossing the land border remains largely restricted and subject to special rules. Since 25 May, exceptions have applied to rail travel with Georgia for Azerbaijani citizens and some foreign nationals who can enter the country without a visa.

The country’s overall reputation also affects tourists’ choices. The UK Foreign Office generally considers crime levels in Baku to be low, but notes that there are occasional reports of foreign nationals being asked for unofficial payments.

In Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index, Azerbaijan ranks 171st out of 180 countries. In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, it ranks 130th out of 182 countries.

These rankings do not directly determine whether tourists will visit Azerbaijan. However, they form part of the broader picture that shapes international perceptions of the country, assessments of the predictability of its legal and business environment, and investors’ perceptions of risk.

State support for tourism in Azerbaijan

World.title: Azerbaijan confiscates cryptocurrency in favour of state for first time
World.content:
Cryptocurrency confiscated in Azerbaijan

The Yasamal District Court in Baku has sentenced two people arrested by the State Security Service, B.H.R. and I.R.F., and ordered the confiscation by the state of virtual assets identified as the proceeds or subject of the crime.

Details of the case

The defendants were found guilty under Article 206-1.3 of the Criminal Code. The article provides for criminal liability for organising the illegal covert transfer of particularly large sums of money out of Azerbaijan or into the country using set-offs and other forms of settlement.

According to the court’s ruling:

B.H.R. received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of 3,623,568 manats (about $2.13 million);

received a two-year-and-five-month restriction of liberty and a fine of (about $2.13 million); I.R.F. received a three-year restriction of liberty and a fine of 31,399,709 manats (about $18.47 million).

The court also ordered the state to confiscate 830 units of cryptocurrency held in an account on the international virtual-asset platform Binance. Investigators had frozen the assets during the preliminary investigation.

Official reports do not specify which cryptocurrency was involved, whether Bitcoin, Ethereum or another asset.

Legal basis

Under Article 99-1 of the Criminal Code, special confiscation involves the compulsory and free transfer to the state of tools and means used to commit a crime, as well as property obtained through criminal activity.

The Law on Combating the Legalisation of Property Obtained through Crime and the Financing of Terrorism also classifies virtual assets as property obtained through criminal activity.

The court has therefore applied the same legal regime to digital assets as it does to physical property for the first time in practice.

Context and significance

In 2025, the State Security Service had already secured a court order to freeze cryptocurrency in a similar criminal case. At the time, Baku’s Sabail District Court ordered the assets to be frozen. On 24 August, the process moved to the next stage: the authorities confiscated the assets.

Azerbaijan does not yet have a separate law governing virtual assets. The Central Bank previously said it expected the relevant draft law to be adopted by the end of 2026. Against this backdrop, the court ruling shows how authorities are addressing the existing legal gap in practice and could set a precedent for future regulation.

Experts note that international exchanges generally comply with court orders promptly. However, the authorities have not yet disclosed what will happen to the confiscated assets, including whether they could be sold at auction, transferred to state reserves or used in another way.

The case marks a new stage in Azerbaijan’s fight against digital crime and expands law enforcement agencies’ ability to track and confiscate virtual assets. At the same time, it highlights the real risks faced by people operating in the unregulated cryptocurrency market.

Cryptocurrency confiscated in Azerbaijan

World.title: Is Georgia expecting a new wave of migrants from Russia?
World.content:
Upper Lars checkpoint, 2022. Photo: Mediazona

While rumours of a possible mobilisation circulate in Russia, Georgia is bracing for a new wave of Russian migrants. However, current data from the Upper Lars checkpoint on the Russian-Georgian border do not yet indicate a mass exodus from Russia.

In mid-August, Russia’s Customs Service said that Upper Lars had seen a “record flow” of travellers. The agency said more than 20,000 people crossed the border in passenger cars on 18 August.

Georgia’s Interior Ministry disputed the Russian figures. According to its data, 7,880 citizens of various countries entered Georgia from Russia between 8 and 19 August, while 8,406 people left Georgia for Russia. In total, 16,286 people crossed the border in both directions.

Russia’s customs authorities later clarified their figures, also saying that more than 16,000 people had crossed the border in both directions. This time, however, they did not describe the figure as “record-breaking”. They noted that more people were travelling towards Russia as the tourist season came to an end.

The figures nevertheless caused concern in Georgia. Many people remembered September 2022, when tens of thousands of Russians entered Georgia after Moscow announced a partial mobilisation.

That large influx drove up property prices significantly. Many people in Georgia now fear that the situation could happen again.

Why are people expecting a new wave of migrants?

Reports of a new mobilisation in Russia remain unconfirmed, but they are spreading widely. The reports claim that mobilisation could be announced after September’s State Duma elections. The Russian authorities have made no official statements to that effect.

Nikoloz Urushadze, managing partner at the consulting company G. Miller International Georgia, says that even these rumours could prompt some Russian citizens to leave the country.

“Even if Russia ultimately does not announce mobilisation, the expectation of it still affects people. They are afraid, and fear is often a powerful factor driving people to move,” he told BusinessPressNews.

Urushadze believes Georgia remains one of the most accessible destinations for Russian citizens and could face a new influx of migrants if Russia announces mobilisation.

The experience of 2022

In September 2022, immediately after Russia announced its partial mobilisation, the queue at the Upper Lars checkpoint stretched for 20-30 kilometres on the Russian side. Around 5,500 cars were waiting at the border. Authorities even set up a mobile military recruitment office in North Ossetia, where the checkpoint is located.

According to Georgia’s then-interior minister, Vakhtang Gomelauri, around 10,000 people crossed the border each day. Before the mobilisation announcement, the figure stood at about 6,000.

As a result of the influx, around 100,000 Russian citizens lived in Georgia for a period. Some local residents called on the authorities to introduce a visa regime for Russian citizens.

How could a new influx affect property prices in Georgia?

According to Nikoloz Urushadze, a new wave of Russian migrants would primarily affect the property market. Increased demand would push up rental prices again. Georgia experienced this in 2022-2023, when the arrival of large numbers of Russian citizens sharply increased rental costs in Tbilisi and Batumi.

Russian citizens, along with Ukrainians and Belarusians, are also actively buying property in Georgia. In the first half of 2026, they accounted for 18% of all buyers. A year earlier, their share stood at 13%. During the same period, the share of Georgian citizens among apartment buyers in the resort city of Batumi fell from 43% to 33%.

Urushadze points to another problem. In his view, some Russian citizens do not integrate into local society and the economy. Instead, they create their own closed infrastructure.

“Georgia is a country where 300,000 Russians could come and create a little Russia here, with their own schools and universities. They would not need the Georgian language or anything else at all,” he says.

At this stage, the situation on the Russian-Georgian border does not resemble the mass exodus of 2022. The queues in August were mainly linked to the tourist season and a temporary border closure due to bad weather. Many people were leaving Georgia rather than entering it, returning to Russia.

The real scale of any new influx will become clearer later. The decisive factor will be whether the Russian leadership officially announces mobilisation.

Russian migrants in Georgia

World.title: ‘Ice cream’ and cold showers: Keeping cool on hot days at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
As summer temperatures rise, Tbilisi Zoo switches to a special routine. The keepers’ main task is to help the animals cope with the heat and protect them from overheating.

A range of measures is used, from cooling the enclosures to providing special diets. The first and most important rule is to ensure that all the animals have a constant supply of clean, cool drinking water.

The water is refreshed several times a day, while keepers provide additional ways for the animals to cool down in their enclosures when needed. One method is to spray the enclosures with water. Zoo staff regularly hose down the floors and surrounding areas to maintain humidity and lower the temperature.

Large animals require particular attention. For elephants, for example, water treatments are a real treat. Keepers hose them down all over their bodies, helping them cool off quickly.

The zoo also creates mud wallows specifically for the elephants and the rhinoceros. As the mud dries on the animals’ skin, it forms a protective layer against strong sunlight, possible sunburn and insects. The layer also helps keep their bodies cool.

Summer heat also affects the animals’ daily care. Keepers adjust feeding methods so that the animals receive both physical and mental stimulation. Seasonal juicy fruits are added to their diets, providing another way to help them cool down.

For primates and herbivores, keepers freeze fruit and vegetables. For the animals, this is a kind of “ice cream”, but it serves more than just a cooling purpose. The animals have to make an effort to get to the frozen food, providing both physical and mental stimulation. It also allows them to display natural behaviour.

The same principle applies to predators, for which keepers freeze meat. “Meat ice cream” helps lions and tigers cool down while also providing sensory enrichment.

It is also important that the doors to indoor enclosures, where temperatures are lower and it is cooler, remain open at all times. This allows the animals to choose where they want to stay.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

The heat at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: South Ossetia residents name region’s main problems ahead of presidential election
World.content:
South Ossetia presidential election

South Ossetia election. Illustration created by Caucasian Knot using AI

A report by Caucasian Knot

Population decline, low wages, unemployment, queues at the customs checkpoint and poor public transport. Residents of South Ossetia named these as the main problems ahead of the snap presidential election.

Murad Valiev, Kazbek Kodoev, Marat Kambolov and Zurab Kokoev have been cleared to stand in the election. The Central Election Commission plans to print 40,000 ballot papers. Khokh Chochiev, leader of the Iry Farn party, who was denied registration, called the election a sham.

On 23 August, a Caucasian Knot correspondent spoke to residents of the region. The survey is not representative and reflects individual views.

“There is no trust left in anyone”

Fatima, 45, works as a kindergarten teacher in Tskhinval. She sees the lack of jobs as the main reason people are leaving the region.

“Young people mostly leave because of this. Graduates of Russian universities return home but cannot find work. If jobs become available here, they will come back,” she says.

Fatima also wants to see higher wages. She says incomes remain low while prices continue to rise. She also names queues at the customs checkpoint as another major problem.

“They said the situation improved after Kambolov visited the customs checkpoint. But there are still queues. I am not following the campaign. There is no trust left in anyone. I have not come across any campaigning either,” she said.

Karina, 23, is unemployed and lives in Dzau. She lists wages, unemployment, environmental problems and the state of agriculture among the region’s main challenges.

Public transport is a particular concern for her. The last bus leaves Dzau at 17:00, while the last bus from Tskhinval leaves at 18:00.

“I would like buses to run at least until eight or nine in the evening. I do not have a car and cannot afford to buy one. It is also practically impossible to get a loan or mortgage in South Ossetia,” Karina says.

In her view, unless these problems are addressed, the population decline will become irreversible.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions”

Karina is not following the election campaign and believes the outcome has already been decided.

“I am used to Russia’s authorities making all the decisions. They would benefit from making Kambolov president. The election is just window dressing. People have not had a choice for a long time,” she said.

Karina says she has not seen campaign posters or activists in Dzau or Tskhinval.

World.title: Why has Georgia’s government revived debate over Treaty of Georgievsk?
World.content:
In recent days, Georgian government officials have made a series of similar statements about the 1783 Treaty of Georgievsk.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the agreement with Russia saved Georgia and the Georgian nation. He argues that it laid the foundations for today’s sovereign state and helped preserve its European prospects.

Several days later, other leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party began speaking about the Treaty of Georgievsk in similar terms. They repeat not only the main conclusion but also the same arguments: Georgia faced the threat of destruction, an agreement with Russia was the only option, and that decision saved the Georgian nation, Christianity and Georgian statehood.

This level of coordination suggests that the discussion has moved beyond a spontaneous debate about history. The positive assessment of the Treaty of Georgievsk sounds more like a unified political message from Georgian Dream.

But what is the purpose of this message?

The Treaty of Georgievsk was an agreement under which eastern Georgia (the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti) came under the protection of the Russian Empire. The parties signed the treaty in the summer of 1783 at the fortress of Georgievsk. The treaty protected Georgia from external threats but ultimately led to the complete loss of its independence.

Opposition figures say the government is preparing the public for a possible new agreement with Russia. Former president Mikheil Saakashvili, who is currently in prison, has even referred to specific draft agreements.

Other political commentators see the renewed focus on the treaty as an attempt to divert attention from important current issues. Against the backdrop of what they describe as the Georgian government’s increasingly pro-Russian course and anti-Western rhetoric, the Treaty of Georgievsk is a particularly sensitive issue for politically active Georgians and can easily provoke a strong reaction.

According to this view, the government deliberately sparked a historical debate to draw attention away from corruption within the administration. At the same time, the authorities have intensified the charges against former prime minister Irakli Garibashvili. His case goes beyond the actions of an individual official and raises questions about the scale of systemic corruption itself.

Russian media have already described Kobakhidze’s remarks as another sign that Tbilisi’s attitude towards Moscow is changing.

So why has a treaty signed 243 years ago suddenly become one of the main topics of Georgia’s current political debate?

What Prime Minister Kobakhidze said

Irakli Kobakhidze has made several statements about the Treaty of Georgievsk. His main argument is that King Erekle II’s decision ultimately ensured the physical and political survival of the Georgian nation.

On 18 August, Kobakhidze described the signing of the treaty as a “civilisational choice”. He said Christian Georgia, surrounded by Muslim states, chose fellow Orthodox Russia.

“The fact that today we are an independent, sovereign state based on traditional European values and traditional European culture is precisely the result of this pragmatic decision taken by Erekle II,” the prime minister said.

Kobakhidze has also argued that Erekle II’s decision was not only justified, but the “only correct and only possible” choice at the time. In his account, Russia honoured the terms of the agreement during Erekle II’s lifetime:

“While Erekle II was alive, he ensured that the agreement was upheld to the end. Almost 20 years passed between the Treaty of Georgievsk and the annexation of Georgia. For two decades, our country was effectively saved.”

Kobakhidze presented Russia’s abolition of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti as a process that became possible only after the Georgian king’s death: “When Erekle II died, unfortunately, events took a different course.”

Georgian Dream leaders have also drawn parallels between this historical episode and modern Georgian-Russian relations.

Kobakhidze compared the Treaty of Georgievsk with the August 2008 war and said that “under Mikheil Saakashvili’s leadership, all the agreements, whether signed or unsigned, were torn up over our heads.”

Other party leaders have expressed similar views. MP David Matikashvili, for example, called the Treaty of Georgievsk a “smart and wise” decision.

“Ultimately, despite the many negative consequences, Georgia and the Georgian people managed to survive physically. The genius of King Erekle is obvious here,” he said.

More about the Treaty of Georgievsk

The Treaty of Georgievsk was signed in 1783 between the Russian Empire and the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. It was not an agreement between a united Georgia and Russia. At the time, the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia were not parties to the treaty.

Under the agreement, Kartli-Kakheti came under Russian protection. In return, Russia undertook to protect its territorial integrity and the Bagrationi dynasty.

Historian Beka Kobakhidze strongly disputes Kobakhidze’s claim that Russia honoured the treaty during Erekle II’s lifetime. He writes that the period from 1783 until Erekle’s death was instead one of the most difficult periods of his reign.

In 1785, an army led by Avar ruler Omar Khan invaded Kartli-Kakheti. Beka Kobakhidze says Erekle had warned Russia about the planned attack and requested the assistance provided for under the treaty. Russia did not provide it.

Agha Mohammad Khan’s 1795 campaign had even more devastating consequences. After the Battle of Krtsanisi, his forces captured and looted Tbilisi. Thousands of people were killed or taken captive.

Beka Kobakhidze draws on these facts to write:

“Irakli Kobakhidze is falsifying history. The period from 1783 to 1798, from the signing of the Treaty of Georgievsk to Erekle’s death, was the most difficult and destructive period of his reign.”

In 1801, the Russian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. The Bagrationi royal family lost power, and some of its members were exiled to Russia. The Russian Empire later conquered and annexed the kingdoms and principalities of western Georgia as well.

Was Georgia “on the brink of extinction”?

Another key element of Georgian Dream’s new historical narrative concerns demographic survival. The prime minister says the Georgian nation faced a “real threat of extinction” at the end of the 18th century. MP Matikashvili has also referred to the “physical survival” of the Georgian people.

This view is not new. The Russian imperial narrative, and later the Soviet version of history, often portrayed the annexation of Georgia as a painful but necessary step to save the country.

Historian Giorgi Ugulava wrote in a 2025 article for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty that this representation was one of the main products of Russian imperial propaganda. The argument was that Georgia could not survive independently and that Russian protection was the best option available.

Why has Erekle II become a political symbol for Georgian Dream?

Georgian Dream’s political campaign around Erekle II began well before August 2026.

In 2023, literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili criticised Erekle II over the Treaty of Georgievsk. Georgian Dream leaders responded with fierce criticism of the scholar. That same year, the pro-Russian Conservative Movement disrupted one of Berdzenishvili’s lectures. He was later attacked in the street.

At the time, Georgian Dream chairman Irakli Kobakhidze said violence was unacceptable. At the same time, however, he accused Berdzenishvili of acting against Georgian identity.

In August 2024, Kobakhidze announced plans to erect a new monument to Erekle II in Tbilisi. The monument opened on 24 September 2025. At the ceremony, Kobakhidze described Erekle II as a symbol of “patriotism”, “love of the homeland” and “pragmatism”.

Kobakhidze also claimed that foreign diplomats had criticised Erekle II during meetings with Georgian Dream representatives. He did not name any of the diplomats or specify which countries they represented. However, according to his account, criticism of Erekle II formed part of coordinated actions by Western diplomats and the Georgian opposition.

Erekle II has therefore gradually evolved from a historical figure into a symbol of the current political confrontation. On one side stands the “pragmatic” king who reached an agreement with Russia. On the other are his critics, whom the government portrays as agents of Western interests.

“A new treaty”: what do pro-Russian forces in Georgia want?

While Georgian Dream highlights the positive historical significance of the old Treaty of Georgievsk, openly operating pro-Russian forces in Georgia are already calling directly for a “new treaty”.

One of the main figures in this campaign is Russian-Georgian citizen Mamuka Pipia, leader of the Solidarity for Peace party.

In July 2025, Pipia called for the signing of a “Treaty of Georgievsk 2” and an alliance treaty with Russia. His proposals included restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and removing Article 78 from Georgia’s Constitution. The article requires constitutional bodies to take all measures to ensure Georgia’s full integration into the European Union and NATO.

Pipia said: “Given today’s geopolitical situation, Russia and Georgia need to support each other, and they need to formalise an alliance treaty on equal terms.”

In August 2026, Pipia described Kobakhidze’s statements as a success for his own political agenda.

“I am glad that the country’s leadership now recognises the reality that we have been speaking about openly for the past two years,” he said.

Pipia says his idea of a “new Treaty of Georgievsk” means “a completely new, comprehensive and, most importantly, equal treaty with the Russian Federation”.

“We are working in this direction, and Moscow will make an appropriate statement very soon,” he added.

Georgian Dream denies coordinating with pro-Russian groups. However, Pipia’s political network maintains open contacts with Russian officials. He has appeared in public at various times with Russian State Duma deputies and other senior Russian officials.

In May 2025, former Georgian prosecutor general Otar Partskhaladze, who is under US sanctions, was also in Red Square with Pipia. The US Treasury Department has described Partskhaladze as a Georgian-Russian oligarch and said Russia’s FSB used him to influence Georgian society and politics.

How closely do the two narratives align?

Mamuka Pipia’s and Georgian Dream’s ultimate political demands do not currently coincide. Georgian Dream is not officially calling for an alliance treaty with Russia, a “new treaty” or the repeal of Article 78 of the Constitution. This is a significant difference.

However, the similarities in their rhetoric are clear. In both cases, the main arguments for closer relations with Russia are “pragmatism”, peace, security and national interests. In both narratives, the West is increasingly portrayed not as a security partner but as a source of threats or pressure.

The rhetoric around the “deep state” also overlaps. For years, Pipia has spoken about Western forces allegedly trying to use Georgia against Russia. A similar conspiracy theory has become part of Georgian Dream’s official political messaging in recent years.

Now another important element has entered this shared vocabulary: the interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk as an agreement that saved Georgia.

What does the opposition say about a possible new agreement?

Against this backdrop, Georgian opposition figures suspect that the historical debate may serve to prepare public opinion for a more concrete political decision.

Mikheil Saakashvili said that the government was carrying out “ideological preparations for signing a treaty of betrayal”. He claims that Russia has even given ruling-party founder Bidzina Ivanishvili drafts of several agreements.

Saakashvili referred to restoring diplomatic relations with Russia and separate agreements on Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region. He also claims that Irakli Kobakhidze is expected to travel to Moscow in the coming weeks.

There is currently no independent confirmation of this information. Neither the Georgian nor the Russian authorities have officially announced preparations for such agreements.

Former diplomat Ghia Japaridze also sees the government’s rhetoric as preparation for possible changes in foreign policy. He says the government is using the Treaty of Georgievsk to “justify a change in Georgia’s foreign policy course”.

What is the Russian media saying?

Irakli Kobakhidze’s statements have also attracted attention in Russia.

On 21 August, the Russian publication Vzglyad published an article headlined “Georgia has taken an important step towards normality”.

The article links several issues: the Georgian government’s campaign against so-called “Russophobia”, accusations against the West and the new interpretation of the Treaty of Georgievsk.

The publication places particular emphasis on the “restoration of respect for the Treaty of Georgievsk — an alliance with Russia that saved Georgia”.

In other words, what Georgian officials present in Tbilisi as a historical interpretation and an assessment of Erekle II’s decision is already being read by Russian media as a sign of changing political attitudes towards modern Russia.

A day earlier, even more far-reaching claims circulated in Russian Telegram channels. INSIDER-T, citing unofficial sources, claimed that Tbilisi had offered Moscow a behind-the-scenes deal: “full geopolitical loyalty” from Georgia in exchange for Russia publicly abandoning the annexation of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

These claims are also not supported by reliable evidence.

What matters, however, is the political expectations now emerging in the Russian information space in response to statements by Georgian officials.

A historical dispute or an ongoing political process?

There is currently no publicly confirmed evidence that the Georgian authorities are preparing to sign a “New Treaty of Georgievsk” or another alliance agreement with Russia.

However, it is difficult to describe what is happening as merely a dispute among historians.

On one side is a government that has sharply worsened relations with Georgia’s main Western partners in recent years and has effectively frozen the country’s EU accession process.

On the other are pro-Russian groups openly calling for a political alliance and security ties with Russia. They see the prime minister’s new rhetoric as a victory for their position.

This is accompanied by the reaction of the Russian information space, where Georgian government statements are increasingly seen as a sign that Tbilisi is turning towards the Kremlin.

Against this backdrop, the significance of the Treaty of Georgievsk is no longer confined to the 18th century. The key question now is why the government needs to convince the public that a historical agreement with Russia, which ultimately led to the annexation of the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti, saved Georgia.

And, more importantly, what modern political choice might this version of history be intended to justify?

Debate over the Treaty of Georgievsk in Georgia

World.title: Emine Erdoğan makes phone call to First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. On August 26, First Lady of the Republic of Türkiye, Emine Erdoğan, made a phone call to the First Vice-President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Mehriban Aliyeva.

This was announced by the press service of the President of Azerbaijan.

Emine Erdoğan congratulated First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva on her birthday and wished her robust health and continued success.

First Lady of Türkiye Emine Erdoğan emphasized that Mehriban Aliyeva’s charitable activities are highly appreciated around the world.

First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva expressed her gratitude for the attention and congratulations.

During the phone conversation, First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva and First Lady of Türkiye Emine Erdoğan fondly recalled their warm meetings.

First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva and First Lady of Türkiye Emine Erdoğan expressed confidence that the brotherly relations and strategic alliance between Azerbaijan and Türkiye will continue to develop successfully.

World.title: Zahra Pezeshkian congratulates First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Zahra Pezeshkian sent a congratulatory letter to the First Vice President of Azerbaijan, Mehriban Aliyeva, on the occasion of her birthday.

''My dear and kindhearted sister.

On the occasion of your birthday, it is my distinct honor and pleasure to convey my sincerest congratulations and best wishes to you.

Your outstanding, visionary, and tireless efforts across the social, cultural, and international spheres have always served as an inspiration and a source of pride.

I am extremely delighted that the deep roots of friendship and brotherhood exist between the friendly, brotherly and neighborly countries of Iran and Azerbaijan, and that the women of both our nations play a vital role in preserving this shared cultural heritage.

On this remarkable and joyous day, I sincerely wish you a happy and long life, robust health and continued success, as well as progress and prosperity to the friendly and brotherly Republic of Azerbaijan,'' the letter reads.

World.title: Halyk Finance becomes first KASE digital assets platform participant
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Halyk Finance has become the first participant of the digital financial assets (DFA) and digital assets (DA) platform of the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE), the exchange’s press service said.

"This is an important stage in the development of Kazakhstan’s digital financial market and the formation of modern infrastructure for the circulation of digital instruments," KASE said.

In late July 2026, KASE introduced the digital assets platform (DAP), an infrastructure for the issuance, recording and trading of digital assets and digital financial assets.

The platform provides for two types of clients - issuers and trading participants. KASE clients that meet established licensing, regulatory and compliance requirements will be eligible to participate.

Halyk Finance was established by a decision of Halyk Bank of Kazakhstan No. 93 dated August 3, 2004, and was officially registered on November 10, 2004.

In June 2018, Halyk Finance Astana was registered as a branch in the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) to ensure the company’s presence within the financial hub. The AIFC licenses held by the company allow it to conduct activities in the AIFC similar to those carried out by Halyk Finance under a license issued by the National Bank of Kazakhstan.

Halyk Bank of Kazakhstan is the sole shareholder of Halyk Finance.

World.title: First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva, her daughters Leyla Aliyeva and Arzu Aliyeva visit the Scientific Research Institute of Pediatrics (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. On August 26, First Vice-President of the Republic of Azerbaijan and President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation Mehriban Aliyeva, together with her daughters Leyla Aliyeva and Arzu Aliyeva, visited the Scientific Research Institute of Pediatrics.

Minister of Health Teymur Musayev briefed First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva on the institute’s activities.

The Scientific Research Institute of Pediatrics has been serving the important and noble cause of protecting children’s health for more than a century.

Currently operating as a scientific and methodological center, the medical facility was established in 1925 on the basis of a 200-bed children’s hospital and reorganized in 1927 into the Institute for the Protection of Mother and Child. Alongside the treatment and prevention of childhood diseases, the institute provides training for professional medical personnel in pediatrics, conducts scientific research, and contributes to the improvement of medical education. The institute has clinical departments with a total capacity of 255 beds, as well as scientific and numerous paraclinical divisions. Its 60-bed neonatal resuscitation and intensive care department serves as a central facility for the republic.

During the visit, the First Vice-President and her daughters viewed the conditions created at the institute. Medical equipment, including mechanical ventilation devices, was also presented to the institute to support its future operations.

World.title: Meta to pay $23 billion to settle teen social media addiction cases
World.content:
Meta has agreed to pay $US17 billion (AUD$23.6 billion) and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by 47 states, state attorneys general have announced.

California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were among 29 states that sued the tech giant in 2023, but the deal cuts short the trial, which was expected to see CEO Mark Zuckerberg take the stand before a jury in federal court in California.

The agreement is worth $US353 million in Virginia alone and is one of the biggest in state consumer protection history, Attorney General Jay Jones said in a statement.

"For years, Meta intentionally deceived the public about the addictive and harmful design features that have wreaked havoc on youth mental health," Mr Jones said.

The settlement "will put an end to these dangerous practices and deliver meaningful relief that will protect children from online harm".

A protest against social media platforms outside the US Courthouse. (AP: Noah Berger)

Meta did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The $US17 billion settlement is a fraction of the company's 2025 revenue of $US201 billion.

The lawsuit accused Meta of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by deliberately designing features that addict children to its platforms and hiding them from the public.

It also argued Meta violated federal laws by routinely collecting data on children under 13 without their parents' consent.

The trial kicked off last week in Oakland, California, with US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers overseeing the proceedings.

Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, began his testimony late on Tuesday and defended Meta's record and progress on child safety and privacy.

The cases in other states had been expected to go to trial later. In addition, nine attorneys general filed lawsuits in their respective states.

Under the proposed settlement, Meta agreed to adopt a series of safety features, including a "hard cap" on daily time limits and pauses for children using Instagram and Facebook.

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg was expected to take the stand. (Reuters: Brendan McDermid)

It will eliminate push notifications during weekday school hours and bring in "robust" age assurance measures and "age-appropriate" content controls to prevent bullying and harmful material about eating disorders and self-harm.

There will be stronger and more user-friendly parental controls and limits on social comparison features such as "like" counts.

The federal lawsuit was the result of an investigation led by a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general from California, Florida, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New Jersey, Tennessee and Vermont.

It followed newspaper reports, first by The Wall Street Journal in 2021, that found that the company knew about the harm Instagram can cause teenagers — especially teen girls — when it comes to mental health and body image issues.

Meta has since added a host of safety features to Instagram, including separate accounts for teenagers with stronger protections around messaging and privacy, along with content restrictions.

But child safety experts, along with some former Meta employees, have long contended that the features are little more than window dressing.

Former Meta engineering director Arturo Béjar, said during his testimony last week that Meta consistently prioritised profits over safety in designing its products, focusing on how often and for how long people used them, even if it was detrimental to their mental well-being.

"If you step away from the product, they are not going to make any money," he said.

While the four states in the Oakland trial did not officially say how much they had been seeking, Meta said in a court filing that financial penalties in the case could amount to as much as $US1.4 trillion — a figure legal experts said was unlikely, if not impossible.

AP

World.title: Prince Harry and Meghan arrive back in UK
World.content:
Prince Harry and his wife Meghan arrived back in the United Kingdom on Wednesday, six years after they moved their lives to California amid simmering tensions within the royal family.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex last week made a surprise announcement they would be relocating back to Britian with their children.

UK media reported a private jet landed at Birmingham International Airport around noon local time (9pm AEST) — a claim backed up by publicly available flight-tracking data.

It has been speculated the couple will live at a private residence in the picturesque Cotswolds region outside of London.

The couple's two children, seven-year-old Archie and Lilibet, five, have already been enrolled in a British school.

Harry and Meghan gave up their royal duties at the start of 2020 and moved to the exclusive seaside area of Montecito, near Santa Barbara, as relations with his family soured.

They pursued their own independent careers but never left the headlines as they did tell-all interviews with Oprah Winfrey, produced Netflix series and continued to take on the press in court over breaches of security.

What's behind Harry and Meghan's UK return While a move to London now brings Meghan and Harry in closer proximity to the royal family, it does not solve the Windsor's complicated dynamics or the deep rift between two brothers.

In the last couple of years of Queen Elizabeth II's life, the couple made allegations against palace staff as being insensitive to Meghan and levelled allegations of racism at members of the royal family.

After losing his fight for government funded security protection last year, the Duke of Sussex told the BBC he could not see a world where he would feel safe returning to the UK with his family.

The prince's relationship with his father King Charles, who is living with cancer, is said to have improved in recent times, in particular after a visit last month.

The Duke visited the UK in July for his charity work with the Invictus Games and also brought the family across from their Portugal holiday home for a surprise visit, allowing the King to see his grandchildren for the first time in four years.

Prior to that, the last time the entire Sussex family was in the UK together was for the Queen's funeral in 2022.

But it's widely reported Harry is not on speaking terms with his brother and heir-to-the-throne, Prince William.

The announcement of their return came a day before a London court ruling meant Harry could be liable to pay millions of pounds to the publisher of the Daily Mail newspaper after a failed privacy lawsuit.

Meghan is reportedly in talks about a return to acting although neither her agent nor the speculated TV drama have commented.

World.title: Ukraine awards Elon Musk Order of Freedom for Starlink support
World.content:
Elon Musk has been awarded Ukraine's Order of Freedom, one of the country's highest state honours, for his "outstanding personal merits" in protecting human life and freedom and strengthening ties between Kyiv and the United States.

Mr Musk — the founder of SpaceX — has become one of the most influential and contentious private sector figures in Ukraine's war effort.

His decision to provide Ukraine with access to Starlink, SpaceX's satellite internet network, was critical. It remains a communications lifeline for Ukrainian forces and civilians after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

There was no immediate comment from Mr Musk on the award, which was announced by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Musk has restricted Starlink access in Russia

Ukraine's president is hoping Mr Musk will reconsider allowing Starlink to operate over Russian territory.

Starlink has become deeply embedded in Ukraine's military operations, with commanders and soldiers relying on satellite connectivity to communicate and coordinate operations.

The technology has been integrated into Ukraine's drone operations, helping operators maintain links with drones and navigate them over longer distances.

Ukraine's first-ever drone parade It was not soldiers marching down Kyiv's main parade to mark 35 years of Ukrainian independence, but robots designed to take their place on the frontline.

Ukraine's access to Starlink is the main reason its middle-strike drone campaign, which caught Russian forces off guard and undermined their logistics lines earlier this year, reported early successes.

Mr Musk has allowed the Ukrainians to use Starlink inside their own territory, including in Ukrainian regions occupied by the Russians, but has restricted use of the satellite system inside Russia.

SpaceX's decision earlier this year to accept Kyiv's pleas and block unauthorised Starlink terminals being used by Russian forces in occupied territory also strengthened Ukraine's position.

The campaign has put pressure on Russian logistics in Crimea, giving Ukrainian forces a degree of battlefield momentum that Kyiv has not enjoyed since its successful counteroffensives around Kherson and Kharkiv in late 2022.

Ukraine's president is hoping Mr Musk will reconsider allowing Starlink to operate over Russian territory so Ukrainian forces can maintain satellite connectivity for longer-range drone attacks targeting Russia's military and economic infrastructure.

Musk's outsized influence over Ukraine

Starlink has become embedded in Ukraine's wartime communications. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

Mr Musk is both a crucial partner for Kyiv and a potential source of vulnerability and dependence.

As Starlink has become embedded in Ukraine's wartime communications, Mr Musk and SpaceX have significant influence over how the technology can be used.

Mr Musk's decisions can have direct consequences for Ukraine's military capabilities, making it important that Kyiv preserve a positive relationship.

Pentagon denies reports of clash with SpaceX The Pentagon has denied claims that the department has been clashing with Elon Musk's SpaceX over costs to use its satellite internet network.

Mr Zelenskyy has sought US help in persuading Mr Musk to permit Ukraine to expand its ability to use Starlink beyond Ukraine.

Mr Musk has said he believes that would be a significant and dangerous escalation, Mr Zelenskyy told reporters last week.

Meanwhile, a reported mix-up over whether SpaceX had approved Ukraine's use of Starlink for operations inside Russia contributed to tensions between Mr Zelenskyy and then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who was the government's main interlocutor with Mr Musk.

Mr Zelenskyy said inaccurate information from the Defense Ministry that SpaceX had approved the bid had contributed to an awkward exchange with US President Donald Trump, who accused the Ukrainian president of deceiving him. He did not say when that occurred.

That contributed to "some of the steps" taken against Mr Fedorov, Mr Zelenskyy told reporters last week without explicitly accusing him of deliberately providing false information.

Mr Fedorov was dismissed in July as part of a broader government shake-up. His dismissal also highlights the political element of Mr Musk's role in Ukraine's war effort.

AP

World.title: At least 95 dead in Nepal floods, Australian among hundreds missing
World.content:
At least one Australian is missing after a deadly flash flood hit the Tibet-Nepal border, according to local authorities.

The torrent of water swept through the Himalayan border region on Wednesday morning, local time, killing at least 95 people in Nepal, according to local police.

Nepal's tourism board said at least 340 foreign nationals had been reported missing.

The list of foreigners unaccounted for, which has been seen by the ABC, includes one Australian.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade has yet to respond to the ABC's questions.

A survivor is transported out of the flood zone in Nepal. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

People from India, the United Kingdom, the United States and Malaysia are also among those reported missing.

At least 28 local police officers were also unaccounted for, while South Korean authorities said eight of its citizens who were working on a hydropower plant were missing.

On the Tibetan side of the disaster, Chinese officials said they feared "major casualties" in the the county of Gyirong after a mudslide hit a land crossing.

An earthquake caused an avalanche that triggered the flood along the Bhote Koshi river in Rasuwa, Nepal's foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, told parliament on Wednesday.

Broadcast images showed crumbled homes, floating cars and a metal bridge being washed away in the Nepal flood waters.

"There could be heavy casualties or loss of property," said district administrator Narendra Pariyar, who urged dwellers on the banks of the Bhote Koshi river to move to higher ground, after reports of villages and project sites being swept up.

A flooded road in Galchhi in the Dhading district. (Reuters.)

'All-out' rescue operation underway

Nepal's rescue helicopters would be unable to land in the affected areas until the waters recede, army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet said.

Chinese President Xi Jinping urged "all-out" search efforts for the missing as well as stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.

Houses have been washed away or buried under the mud following the flash flood. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

Chinese state media said access to the the area was cut off and communication channels were down.

Devendra Subedi, the senior editor at Nepal Television, told ABC's The World the flood came from nowhere.

"It was sunny weather...all of a sudden with a massive roar, there's a river flooding and washing away some of the settlements," he said.

He said "almost everything has been washed away" in up to five districts and it had been hard to get exact information about what had happened.

Nepal's foreign minister said an earthquake caused an avalanche that triggered the flood along the Bhote Koshi river in Rasuwa. (AP: Niranjan Shrestha)

"The damage has been so unprecedented, it can take a few days to come up with the exact details," he told the ABC.

"The government has mobilised all its mechanisms, including Nepal's army, private choppers.

" The worst part is the communication has been difficult because most of the lines have just been washed away by the floods. "

Mr Subedi said people were being rescued every hour with many survivors being brought to local hospitals for treatment.

A survivor is airlifted following a flash flood in Nepal. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

Nepal tourism board officials said most of the missing were likely tourists from India and the Indian diaspora on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in the Chinese autonomous region of Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus.

He said the flood occurred near the Langtang National Park which was also a popular place for international tourists to go hiking.

Australia urges tourists to follow local safety advice

The Australian Embassy in Nepal has issued a joint statement with other nations, including the UK, encouraging its citizens in the affected areas to follow guidance and safety advice of local authorities.

"Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster," it said.

"We express our solidarity with the people of Nepal during this difficult time."

The UK's Foreign Office said it was "deeply saddened by the loss of life and devastation".

Mud has covered roads and houses after the flash flood in Nepal. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

India begins evacuations as authorities warn of another flood

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has offered "humanitarian assistance" with the rescue and recovery after speaking with Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah.

Authorities in India's Bihar state have begun evacuating up to 12,000 people from six districts fearing floods in that region.

The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development has warned a second flood may also be imminent.

"With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur," Qianggong Zhang, the centre's head of climate and environmental risks, told AFP.

A street and houses are covered in mud in Nepal's Nuwakot district. (Reuters: Navesh Chitrakar)

The Nepal Electricity Authority said about 430 megawatts of production capacity, including from hydropower and solar facilities, had also been damaged in the flood.

"The disaster has damaged the production, transmission and distribution facilities of the Authority… resulting in disruption of electricity supply," it said.

Major highways and roads have also been closed in both Nepal and Tibet.

Traffic authorities in Tibet's Shigatse said roads in the area were "at risk of mudslides and unsafe for passage".

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah has urged people to "be patient" and "stand together".

"The government takes full responsibility for your rescue, treatment, food and shelter," he said in a statement.

World.title: The home of the Ford Falcon may soon become Australia's AI engine room
World.content:
For more than half a century, Ford's Broadmeadows manufacturing plant was known as the home of the iconic Falcon.

"That was the manufacturing heartland of Australia," said Basem Abdo, the federal member for Calwell in Melbourne.

" I always say that we didn't just make Australian-made products — that site helped make Australia. "

Now, 10 years after the plant shut its doors, there are plans to turn the former Ford site into the engine room of Australia's AI boom.

Zoe and John live across the road from the former Ford factory in Broadmeadow and are worried about a data centre potentially moving into the site. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)

The $1.1 billion proposal for a massive data centre by Singaporean digital infrastructure firm Zerra DC — dubbed "Project Dune" — is predicted to draw 336MW of power across six buildings and will take 12 years to build.

Zoe, who lives across the road from the site and is a former employee at the Ford plant, is concerned about having the data centre on her doorstep.

"I had to ask my children what it is," she told 7.30.

"They said something to do with batteries, and they will be working 24 hours a day.

"I don't think it's a good idea. I don't know how long we're going to live but it's still not a good idea for us to live in this area [during the construction] and having all those things in and out every day.

"It's terrible."

Fears of a 'pathway to nowhere'

The final car rolls off the production line at Ford in Broadmeadows in 2016. (Supplied: Ford Australia)

At its height, the Broadmeadows factory — which covered the size of 10 MCGs — employed more than 5,000 local workers who were producing generations of Ford vehicles.

In contrast, Zerra DC said 407 jobs would be created annually during the construction phase and 670 jobs created annually once the data centre was fully operational, boosting the Victorian economy by $158 million.

But Mr Abdo said many residents in his diverse community were concerned about the long-term job prospects from the data centre.

"People need to see that it offers a pathway to employment, a pathway to good, secure, well-paying jobs that offer them a career, which was what this site was about and which is what this site should be about," he told 7.30.

Basem Abdo says people in his community are concerned the data centre will not offer many long-term jobs. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

"I will only support a project that is in line with our national standards that we've put forth clearly on a national level.

" At this stage, I'm not satisfied that that proposal meets those standards. "

Mr Abdo said the project was yet to make the case for the same kind of long-term employment pathways that the region's manufacturing industry provided.

"Are they good, secure jobs that provide long-term careers for people in our area?" he asked.

"This must not lead to a pathway to nowhere in terms of jobs and skills."

'Why is it being fast-tracked?'

An artist's impression of part of the proposed Zerra DC data centre. (Supplied)

State governments in Australia, particularly New South Wales and Victoria, are competing to capture billions of dollars in data centre investment.

An Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) report released this week shows the number of Australian data centres in development has more than doubled since 2025, from 97 to 225 this year.

AEMO's report also predicted data centres would account for 13 per cent of the nation's energy consumption by 2035.

But communities are asking whether the speed of approval for these projects is coming at the expense of scrutiny.

Campbellfield resident Anastasia Drapaniotis has taken a leading role in opposing the Project Dune proposal.

Anastasia Drapaniotis is critical of the planning process for the data centre. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)

"I think a lot of the residents feel like they can't do anything about it and I think that's really horrible," she told 7.30.

" It's really awful to feel like you don't have a say in what comes to your area. "

She told 7.30 she was not against data centre developments but was critical of the planning process.

"I would have to say … OK, bring these in, sure, but have stricter regulations," she said.

"Why is it being fast-tracked? Why are they being approved so quickly when something like this would ordinarily take a very long time to get approved?"

Community members protest against the proposed data centre in Broadmeadows. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Zerra DC lodged the development application for the Campbellfield project in April directly with the state government under special planning provisions for big projects and expects the "fast-tracked" decision within four months.

Victoria's Environment Protection Authority lodged a formal objection to the proposal with the Department of Transport and Planning, citing "concerns over potential noise risks and the cumulative impacts associated with the overall site layout and development".

Zoe and her husband John received the letter informing them of the proposal four days before the date on which Victoria's planning minister was permitted to decide on the project.

At the bottom of the letter, it said: "The responsible authority will not decide on the application before: 28 July 2026."

The planning minister is yet to announce a decision on the proposal.

"I think we could fight against it, but as far as it stopping, I don't think so," Zoe said.

"Not when you get a big overseas company coming in with billions of dollars."

Company says it engaged with community

A map showing the proposed Zerra DC project in Broadmeadows. (Supplied)

Zerra DC declined an interview with 7.30 but said in a statement: "We understand that a proposal of this scale can raise genuine questions and concerns for nearby residents and businesses, and we recognise that some people feel they have not had enough opportunity to be heard."

The company said it began its community engagement program in late May and distributed information "to approximately 1,080 nearby households and 470 industrial businesses, supported by translated information, a dedicated project website, community survey, telephone and email channels, and direct visits to neighbouring businesses".

Zerra DC said the redevelopment of the former Ford site represented "a highly-productive long-term use of industrial land", adding that it had "carefully reviewed the issues raised through community feedback and lodged a detailed response to submissions with the Department of Transport and Planning on 7 August".

"No amendments to the proposal have been made at this stage," it said.

Victoria's Minister for Planning Sonya Kilkenny. (ABC News: Maddison Cutajar)

Victoria's Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny also declined an interview with 7.30, but a Victorian government spokesperson said in a statement: "Every proposal is considered on its merits — as this proposal is under consideration it would be inappropriate to comment further.

"Submissions from the community and nearby businesses can be provided up until a decision is made."

The proposal bypassed local government and prompted Hume City Council, which includes the suburb of Broadmeadows, to pass a motion calling for a moratorium on data centre approvals in Victoria.

A further three councils, Melton, Brimbank and Maribyrnong, have since joined Hume in calling for a temporary halt on these types of projects.

Attracting data centres to Australia

Anthony Albanese says Australia wants to attract data centres but "maintaining social licence will be essential". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

While state governments court data centre investment, the federal government increasingly has its own expectations for what large data centres will deliver for Australia and the communities they are built in.

In a speech to business leaders yesterday, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said "Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential".

"That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained, and locations are appropriate," he said.

Today, the prime minister took his plan to implement national mandatory standards for the industry to National Cabinet.

Under these legislated rules, the biggest facilities will be required to fund and use renewable energy, pay their share of grid and water infrastructure and meet community expectations.

World.title: Notes allegedly written by woman accused of killing parents released
World.content:
A woman standing trial accused of murdering her elderly parents allegedly scrawled notes — which a court has released — including a reference to police waiting to see if she would "get cocky and slip up".

Raelene Polymiadis, 65, of Craigmore is standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court, after pleading not guilty to murdering her parents, Brenda and Lynton Anderson, by injecting them with her own insulin in 2022 and 2023.

Prosecutors previously told the jury a set of notes were allegedly found during a search of Ms Polymiadis's house and car and detailed what she should be saying to police when she spoke to them.

Brenda and Lynton Anderson, both aged 94, died a year apart. (Supplied: Nine News)

Supreme Court Justice Sandi McDonald, who is presiding over the trial, approved the release of handwritten notes, which prosecutors alleged were penned by Ms Polymiadis.

One note written on the top corner of a piece of paper said: "What they will do is wait for a few weeks months year to see if I think I got away with it and I get cocky and slip up. Hang on buddy, it could be a long ride."

A handwritten note tendered in the Raelene Polymiadis murder trial. (Supplied: Courts SA)

In another note, the author posed questions to authorities.

"Who are you sorry?" the note read.

"What's this about?

"Are you from the Coroner's office?

"Why only now are you speaking with me and it's only a few days after the funeral!!"

One of the handwritten notes released by the Supreme Court lists questions. (Supplied: Courts SA)

Prosecutors previously told the court Ms Polymiadis wrote to herself to "sob here", saying that matched a point in the police interview where she started sobbing.

One of the notes released by the court discussed events occurring in hospital.

"We went to see dad, they were keeping him warm," part of the note said.

"He was out to it — unconscious I guess but breathing with help of oxygen I 'think' — I'm sorry this is really hard relieving all this — is it absolutely necessary."

Another handwritten note prosecutors allege Raelene Polymiadis wrote. (Supplied: Courts SA)

The note went on to say, "… just holding his hand, talking to him, but I got no response (sob)".

The trial previously heard police listening devices captured Ms Polymiadis in her car praying to God, confessing to the crimes.

Ms Polymiadis's lawyer, Marie Shaw KC, previously told the jury the context of the alleged confession would arise during the trial.

"The issue about the alleged confession is: was my client admitting she was responsible for the deaths or was she telling her god she felt responsible for their deaths because if they died of insulin administration, they must have accessed her insulin?" Ms Shaw said.

Another of the handwritten notes tendered in the Raelene Polymiadis murder trial. (Supplied: Courts SA)

Another note made references to Ms Polymiadis's father.

"Then I burst into tears, thinking my God he got into my stuff, it's my fault."

The trial continues.

World.title: Canberra childcare centre ordered to close as provider enters administration
World.content:
The childcare regulator has ordered Edge Early Learning in Charnwood in Canberra's Belconnen area to close for three months.

The notice of suspension, issued by Children's Education and Care Assurance (CECA), comes about a month after an Edge Early Learning centre in nearby Higgins was forced to shut immediately over its response to a serious medical incident involving a child.

The reasons behind the Charnwood centre's notice of suspension remain unknown, with its closure due to begin on September 3.

In a statement, CECA said:

"Edge has the right to appeal the decision and is legally required to communicate the suspension to families. "Under administration, the administrator can also exercise the right to appeal."

The ABC has spoken to parents who said they were unaware that CECA had ordered the Charnwood centre to close for three months from next Thursday.

Edge Early Learning also has a centre operating in Ngunnawal in the Gungahlin area.

The Edge Early Learning centre in the ACT that was forced to close suddenly in July. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

'Business-as-usual'

It comes as the childcare provider, which runs dozens of childcare centres across South Australia, Queensland and the ACT, went into voluntary administration.

In a statement from Edge Early Learning, it said administrators had been appointed to "review the business and work with key stakeholders to determine the best path forward", and that the process would allow the company "to assess its financial position and consider options for its future".

" We understand that this may be a confusing and stressful development for families who rely upon Edge Early Learning to provide care for their children. "

Canberra childcare centre ordered to close A Canberra mother had concerns for her daughter's safety at Edge Early Learning in Higgins long before the ACT regulator ordered the centre to close.

Edge Early Learning said it was continuing to operate all centres "on a business-as-usual basis".

"There will be no change to your care arrangements, centre opening hours or staffing. Families should continue to attend their centre as normal," it told parents.

"Our immediate focus is to maintain the safe and ongoing operation of each centre while this urgent review is undertaken."

World.title: Body found as police investigate shooting of Melbourne father
World.content:
Homicide detectives have found a body in their search for a Melbourne father who went missing after allegedly being shot.

A desperate search has been underway for Khaled Malas, 37, who has not been seen since he was allegedly attacked at a home in Wildwood, north-west of the city, on August 19.

Police allege he was shot after a dispute, which is understood to involve a significant debt, and there were grave fears for his welfare.

Police last week searched near a waste facility at Sunbury for missing man Khaled Malas. (ABC News)

Mohammed Aboueid, 56, has been charged with intentionally causing serious injury.

On Wednesday afternoon, investigators found human remains covered in grass on Havelock Road in Clarkefield, about 15 kilometres from Wildwood.

The coroner has been notified, and an autopsy is expected to take place.

Victoria Police said it would consider alternative charges upon receiving the results of the autopsy.

The dog squad was involved in the search near the Sunbury landfill site. (ABC News)

Remembered as a loving father

Omar, a long-time friend, said Mr Malas would be remembered as a family man who was deeply respected by his community.

He said Mr Malas, who arrived in Australia 14 years ago, "loved his young family and kids to death".

"We remember him as a hard, honest worker that came to this country ... to achieve a dream," Omar said.

"He was the sole son that was also providing for his parents overseas as well."

He said the community was in shock.

"[They're] in disbelief ... how can a beautiful soul vanish in such [a] horrible way," he said.

World.title: Australian among hundreds missing after avalanche triggers deadly flash floods in Nepal
World.content:
Breaking WorldAsiaTragedy Australian among hundreds missing after avalanche triggers deadly flash floods in Nepal Niranjan Shrestha and Sibi Arasu Updated August 27, 2026 — 12:11am ,first published 8:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains graphic content. Hundreds of people, including an Australian tourist, were reported missing after an avalanche of ice and rock triggered massive flash floods that swept through parts of Nepal on Wednesday, killing at least 95 people and causing widespread damage to villages and infrastructure. The Nepal Tourism Board reported 384 tourists were missing as a result of the flash flood, including one Australian. The 291 foreign nationals listed also include visitors from India, the United States, the United Kingdom, South Africa and Malaysia. Loading Local police confirmed 95 bodies have been recovered from the wreckage so far.



The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9am on Wednesday (around 1pm AEST), destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. They issued warnings to residents of several of Nepal’s districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. Torrential floods swallowed roads, bridges, houses, and power projects in the border areas of Nepal, and triggered a mudslide that hit Gyirong Port, a major land crossing with neighbouring Tibet, cutting roads, communications, and power links to the area. CCTV footage shows the moment the Chinese and Tibetan side of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing, known as Gyirong Port, is enveloped by the mudslide. Social media It is suspected that an earthquake struck the region and triggered an ice-rock avalanche on the Lhende Khola river in Nepal, causing the floods. The river runs through both Nepal and Tibet. Police and military personnel were engaged in rescue efforts, although officials have said rescue helicopters would not be able to land in the affected areas until the waters recede.



Damaged houses stand precariously near the swollen, debris-choked banks of the Trishuli River after flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha “We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts,” said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government. China has deployed at least 574 rescuers to the land crossing, and India says it was coordinating closely with Kathmandu on rescue and relief efforts. People living in low-lying regions were being moved to safer places, and those along the river have been advised to remain alert, as authorities warn that a second flood may occur since a blockage is still lodged upstream. View post on X



Flood alerts have also been issued in the Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, which border Nepal, since several rivers flow down the Himalayas into their plains. The worst-affected area, Rasuwa district, witnessed similar flash floods to those in August last year, when a glacial lake in neighbouring Tibet overflowed as a result of high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people lost their lives, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting the two countries, was damaged at the time. Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday’s flash flood. Rescuers use an earthmover to carry a victim of flash flooding to safety along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, witnessed maximum flooding Wednesday, they said.



“The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group. “In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation,” he added. The Himalayan region, which crosses Nepal and several nearby countries including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rains, floods and landslides because the area is warming up faster than the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Research has shown that extreme weather events, including heat waves, heavy rains and melting glaciers, have become more frequent in the region. Members of the Kathmandu research group found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000 primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change.
