Product Price (MSRP) Wi-Fi Version Bands Ports Suggested Coverage Best Router: Asus RT-BE58U $150 Wi-Fi 7 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN, 1x Gigabit WAN/LAN, 3x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB WAN 2,000 square feet Upgrade Pick: Asus RT-BE96U $550 Wi-Fi 7 6 GHz, 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz 1x 10-Gbps WAN/LAN, 1x 10-Gbps LAN, 4x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB 3.2, 1x USB 2.0 5,400 square feet Best Midrange Router: Netgear Nighthawk RS300 $300 Wi-Fi 7 6 GHz, 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN/LAN, 2x 2.5-Gbps LAN, 2x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB 3.0 2,000 square feet Best Budget Router: TP-Link Archer BE230 $120 Wi-Fi 7 5 GHz, and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN, 1x 2.5 Gbps LAN, 3x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB 3.0 2,000 square feet Best Router for Large Homes: Netgear Orbi 770 Series (2-Pack) $550 Wi-Fi 7 6 GHz, 5 GHz and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN, 3x 2.5 Gbps LAN (main), 2x 2.5 Gbps LAN (satellites) 5,500 square feet Best Travel Router: Asus RT-BE58 Go $160 Wi-Fi 7 5 GHz and 2.4 GHz 1x 2.5 Gbps WAN, 1x Gigabit LAN, 1x USB-A 3.0 1,800 square feet Best 5G Router: Netgear Nighthawk M7 $500 Wi-Fi 7 5 GHz and 2.4 GHz 1x USB-C, SIM slot 2,000 square feet

This is how the throughput compares on different bands averaged over multiple devices and tests in the same room with a clear line of sight to the routers.

CHART: Simon Hill

Other Routers I Tested and Liked

I have tested many other models and have several more in the queue. These aren’t as great as the picks above, but they are worth considering.

Photograph: Simon Hill

TP-Link Archer BE600 for $250: This standalone router supports Wi-Fi 7. I don’t love the design, but the six adjustable antennas allow for tinkering, and TP-Link has been very generous with the ports (one 10 Gbps, four 2.5 Gbps, and a USB 3.0), though it’s a little annoying that the USB is on the side. This model also offers excellent close-range speeds on the 6-GHz band, and solid speeds on both the 5-GHz and 2.4-GHz bands, though TP-Link’s dual-band BE260 slightly outperformed it on those two bands. But it does offer a pretty expansive range (up to 2,600 square feet).

Photograph: Simon Hill

TP-Link Roam 7 (BE3600) for $130: This dual-band, Wi-Fi 7 travel router was my pick, but the Asus RT-BE58 Go above is a slightly better performer for around the same money. This is still a good, portable device, capable of keeping you online in your hotel room or modest apartment. It also supports mobile tethering, VPN, and can serve as a Wi-Fi range extender. There’s a USB-C for power that works with portable chargers, and a USB-A for file sharing or backup.

TP-Link Archer BE260 for $110: This dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5 GHz) Wi-Fi 7 router runs close to our top pick on performance and is a solid alternative. This router offers a slight upgrade over the BE230 above, with improved 5-GHz performance, an extra antenna, and a coverage boost up to 2,400 square feet. It also sports a 2.5-Gbps WAN, a 2.5-Gbps LAN, three Gigabit LAN, and a USB 3.0 port. Throw in EasyMesh support and a relatively low price, and the BE260 is a tempting option. But if you want enhanced security and parental controls, you have to subscribe, which takes the shine off the value.

Asus RT-BE86U for $207: The new Wi-Fi 7 version of the Asus RT-AX86U, this dual-band (2.4- and 5-GHz) router is similar to the Asus RT-BE88U below. It lacks the 6-GHz band but brings all the other improvements that Wi-Fi 7 offers. The RT-BE86U proved reliable in my tests and performed extremely well on the 5-GHz band, matching the slightly more expensive RT-BE88U. It is slightly smaller but still has one 10-Gbps and four 2.5-Gbps Ethernet ports, alongside a USB 2.0 and a USB 3.0 port.

AVM FRITZ!Box 5690 Pro Photograph: Simon Hill

AVM FRITZ!Box 5690 Pro for £500: AVM has dominated the German router market for years and is expanding across Europe and the UK, so I tested the FRITZ!Box 5690 Pro. AVM’s range is distinctive in white and red plastic, but there's a focus on functionality. This tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router boasts a 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN, four gigabit LAN, and a USB 3.1 port. It’s fast, scoring mid- to high-table results in my tests, and it proved reliable. It also has DSL or fiber-optic modems, an integrated DECT base station for cordless phones, built-in storage (NAS), and support for Zigbee to connect smart home devices. You don’t need an account to set it up or configure it. There’s a firewall and guest network option in the straightforward web interface (you can use the mobile app if you prefer). AVM’s routers are developed and manufactured in Europe, making them an interesting, privacy-focused alternative to routers from China or the US. The company also has a strong track record of supporting its products for years after release. Folks in the UK and Europe looking to upgrade to Wi-Fi 7 should consider this router. My fingers are crossed that AVM expands into the US next.

Asus RT-BE92U for $290: After a simple setup and a trouble-free week of speedy, stable internet across the 2.4-, 5-, and 6-GHz bands, I can recommend this router. It has Wi-Fi 7 benefits like MLO and 320-MHz channels, support for a guest network, VPN services, free security software, and parental controls. It also boasts a 10-Gbps WAN/LAN, a 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN, three 2.5-Gbps LANs, and a USB 3.2 port. This tri-band Wi-Fi 7 device came perilously close to claiming the midrange spot above, but was a smidge slower on the 5-GHz and 6-GHz bands and had a considerably shorter range. However, if your home is around 1,500 square feet and you’d rather avoid a subscription, the RT-BE92U is an excellent alternative. Customer reviews suggest some folks have had trouble with this router, but the latest firmware was rock solid for me.

Asus RT-BE88U for $335: This dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router is an odd prospect because it does not offer the 6-GHz band at all, just 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz. But you can still combine those bands with MLO and enjoy features like 4K QAM, and this router will be fast enough for the average home. It has ports galore (two 10 Gbps, four 2.5 Gbps, four Gigabit, and one USB 3.0). It outperformed several more expensive routers on the 5-GHz band, and that’s likely what most of your devices are using most of the time right now. Asus also offers free security software and parental controls with its routers, so there’s no need for subscriptions. But when I consider that you can snag the Netgear Nighthawk RS300 listed above for less, I find it tough to recommend this router to folks in the US. If the 6-GHz band is unavailable or nerfed in your country, the RT-BE88U is for you.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Netgear Nighthawk RS700 for $600: Although I had setup issues that required a factory reset, there’s no hiding the top-notch performance of this router. It’s a Wi-Fi 7 tri-band router with two 10-Gbps Ethernet ports, four gigabit ports, and a USB 3.2. The tower design is new for the Nighthawk line, and it looks great. This router will blend in far better than our bulky Wi-Fi 7 pick above from Asus, and it was slightly faster on the 6-GHz band, though not the 5-GHz or 2.4-GHz bands. It mainly misses out on a recommendation because it is more expensive. We’re already seeing discounts on the RT-BE96U, and Asus offers free security software and parental controls. If you get the Nighthawk RS700S, the “S” at the end denotes a free year of Netgear Armor, which costs $100 a year thereafter. If you need parental controls, that’s another $70 a year.

TP-Link Archer BE800 for $500: With a fresh design that’s more desktop PC than router, the BE800 tri-band beast came out high up in my tests on the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands, proving impressively swift for file transfers and downloads. It also boasts speedy ports galore, a cool but kind of pointless customizable dot-matrix LED screen, and the Tether app offers a guest network, IoT network, VPN server or client, EasyMesh, QoS for device prioritization, and remote management.

Netgear M3 for £450: I was very impressed by this mobile 5G router. Slip a SIM in there, and it connects to 4G or 5G networks to deliver Wi-Fi to your devices. It’s a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 model that’s speedy on the 5-GHz band. The M3 had no trouble handling multiple connected devices (up to 32) and served a stable internet connection for around 10 hours. You can charge via the USB-C port, and there’s a 2.4-inch LCD color screen for configuration. It’s a solid hot spot for business or personal travel. Sadly, the M3 doesn’t seem to be available in the US, but folks in the UK can save some money and snag this instead of the M7 above (it's frequently discounted).

Firewalla Gold SE for $519: This quirky portable device is perfect for people who worry about security and privacy. It offers comprehensive tools for monitoring all traffic in and out of your house, robust and detailed parental controls, ad-blocking, and enhanced security with a built-in firewall and VPN option. It serves as a router, but you will want to pair another router in access point mode for Wi-Fi in your home. It’s expensive and may prove intimidating for inexperienced folks, but it offers deep insight into your network and an impressive depth of security features without an additional subscription. The Gold SE has two 2.5-Gbps ports and two gigabit ports and is suitable for folks with up to 2-gigabit connections. If your internet is only one gigabit, try the more affordable but slightly less capable Firewalla Purple ($409).

What About Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 6 Routers?

While I recommend buying a Wi-Fi 7 router if you’re upgrading, there are loads of Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 6 routers that will serve the average family well. With Wi-Fi 6E you still get the faster 6-GHz band. The bulk of household traffic still likely uses 5 GHz, and you can save a lot of money by sticking with Wi-Fi 6 for a bit longer.

Best Wi-Fi 6E Router

Netgear Nighthawk RAXE300 for $369: The curvy spaceship design in matte black is a little more stealthy than your average gaming gear, but those wings contain antennas for a strong signal throughout your home. The Nighthawk RAXE300 is a tri-band router with Wi-Fi 6E support, covering the 2.4-GHz, 5-GHz, and 6-GHz bands. It served seamless, speedy Wi-Fi during two weeks of testing, with zero issues while handling a revolving mix of four simultaneous gaming and video streams. A single 2.5-Gbps WAN/LAN port, five gigabit LAN ports, and a USB-C 3.0 port will be enough for most folks.

The Nighthawk app is excellent and offers band splitting, guest network options, and a host of analytical tools. The Premium Smart Parental Controls ($8/month or $70/year) and Netgear Armor ($100/year) are slick, but the extra expense is hard to swallow when many competitors offer cheaper or free alternatives with similar features. This is discontinued, but a few places still have stock, and it’s still a great router.

Best Wi-Fi 6 Router

TP-Link Archer AX55 for $90: This affordable Wi-Fi 6 router is still a decent pick for the average home. The slick black finish is attractive, and there are four antennas to direct Wi-Fi to every corner (it is worth tweaking and testing different positions). Performance was solid throughout my two-floor, 1,600-square-foot home but dropped off slightly in the back garden. Stability was excellent over a couple of weeks of testing, and this router ticks many feature boxes (MU-MIMO, beamforming, WPA3). It has four Gigabit Ethernet LAN ports, a single Gigabit WAN port, and a USB 3.0 port on the back, which is enough for most people.

I’m a fan of TP-Link’s Tether app, where you can review traffic, split bands, create a guest network, schedule reboots, set automatic updates, and even tell the LED to turn off at night. TP-Link’s basic free HomeShield tier offers network scanning, QoS (Quality of Service) for device prioritization, and basic parental controls so you can filter and blacklist websites and set the same bedtime every day. If you want a variable schedule, time limits, downtime, and real-time security protection, you must upgrade to HomeShield Pro (30-day free trial, then $6 per month or $55 for the year). If money is tight, you may even consider the next system down, the TP-Link Archer AX21 ($70). Performance is slightly weaker, but the experience is broadly similar.

Routers I Don’t Recommend

These are the internet routers we had issues with or can't recommend for one reason or another.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Acer Connect X6E 5G: This is an interesting Wi-Fi 6E model with a 5G SIM card slot capable of keeping you online using a mobile network should your main broadband connection fail. It has two Gigabit Ethernet ports, a WAN/LAN, LAN, and an RJ-11 port for a phone line. It’s easy to set up and offers an NFC connection option, so you can just wave your phone over it to connect. This unusual blend of features could be good for business travelers. Performance was solid when it worked, and you can get a very fast connection at close range on both the 6-GHz and 5-GHz bands. Sadly, the range was limited, and the Connect X6E 5G was intermittently unstable during my testing, dropping devices randomly and cutting out repeatedly.

Photograph: Simon Hill

D-Link AX3000 DBR-330: This lightweight, rectangular travel router from D-Link is aimed at business professionals who travel for work. It’s a dual-band Wi-Fi 6 router that can also serve as a hot spot, with a connection via USB. There’s even a potentially handy microSD/TF card slot for up to 2 TB of storage for file sharing or backup. Setup via the browser is easy, and there’s built-in VPN support. It proved nice and fast at close range, but it dropped off quickly, and I couldn’t get a signal two rooms away. It will work fine for a hotel room, though. You can get our TP-Link travel router pick above or the Asus RT-AX57 Go for similar money, and I prefer both of them.

Netgear Nighthawk RS200: The RS200 is Netgear’s dual-band (2.4- and 5-GHz) router and the cheapest in its Wi-Fi 7 lineup. After the tri-band RS300 won a recommendation, I expected this router to perform decently, but I encountered several issues, including random drops and poor range. After turning the router off and on again, many devices, including my Pixel and iPhone, struggled to reconnect. Perhaps I have too many devices in my home for it, though Netgear suggests it can handle up to 80. It has two 2.5 Gbps ports, three gigabit Ethernet ports, and a USB 3.0 port. Test results were OK, but significantly slower than the RT-BE86U.

TP-Link Archer AX5400 Pro: This dual-band Wi-Fi 6 model is almost identical to the Archer AX73, except for the 2.5-Gbps WAN port. It delivers relatively fast speeds on the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands and boasts a 160-MHz channel width on 5 GHz. The range is good, easily covering my home and garden, but the performance was inconsistent. It was also relatively slow at moving files locally. There’s support for TP-Link OneMesh, VPN, and QoS, but you only get basic parental controls and network security unless you subscribe.

What Features Should I Look for in a Router? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron My How to Buy a Router guide answers a lot of questions on the terminology you'll come across when shopping for a new router. Still, here are a few other considerations. Wi-Fi Standards: All my main picks are now using the latest Wi-Fi 7 protocol. That doesn't mean Wi-Fi 6 or Wi-Fi 6E routers aren't worth having, necessarily. But with cheaper dual-band Wi-Fi 7 routers available, there's not much reason to buy anything older. Only Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 routers offer extra bandwidth and faster speeds on the 6-GHz band, but devices like phones and laptops must also support Wi-Fi 6E or 7 for you to take advantage. The 6-GHz band is also short-range compared to the 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz bands. Internet Speeds: Your maximum internet speed is set by your ISP and depends on your internet plan. It will likely fluctuate, depending on the time of day. Some ISPs guarantee a minimum download and upload speed. While your router can’t provide an internet connection that exceeds that speed, it can potentially go faster when you stream from a server in your home or move files from one device on your local network to another. Coverage: It’s worth checking a prospective router’s coverage and speed, but understand that your home Wi-Fi mileage may vary. Construction materials in your house, your neighbors’ activity and Wi-Fi networks, your devices, and the position of your router are just a few of the factors that will impact your wireless performance. Ports: Ethernet ports offer stable connections and are essential for some smart home setups that require a hub for lights or security cameras. Some network-attached storage (NAS) for backups or media will plug into your main router via USB. Ensure that the model you are considering has all the ports you need. What Is the Difference Between a Modem and a Router? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron A modem (modulator-demodulator) connects your home to your internet service provider (ISP) and the external internet. A router connects the devices within your home to that internet connection wirelessly via Wi-Fi or with Ethernet cables. Check out my Router vs. Modem guide to learn more. Can a Single Wireless Router Cover Your Entire Home? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Manufacturers usually suggest a coverage range for a router in square feet, but every home is different, and the real-world range is likely to be shorter. Walls and other obstructions will weaken and block wireless signals. Ideal placement would be in the center of the home near the ceiling of the ground floor without any obstructions. A well-placed single router is generally enough to cover a typical two-floor home up to 2,000 square feet. For larger homes, it's worth considering mesh systems to create a reliable home network. Where Should You Put Your Router? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Physically moving your router can make a real difference to Wi-Fi speeds. It should be central, out in the open, and high up. Walls, cupboards, and even bookshelves can interfere with your Wi-Fi signal, as can fish tanks, TVs, or microwaves. Even changing the angle or moving the antennas can impact the strength of the Wi-Fi around your home, so don't be afraid to experiment with different positions. Can I Add Routers or Extenders to Make a Mesh? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Many manufacturers allow you to create a mesh network by adding more routers or devices like Wi-Fi extenders, but check what is supported before you buy. For example, Asus AiMesh enables you to link multiple routers, while TP-Link’s OneMesh only allows you to add power-line adapters or range extenders. EasyMesh is a standard certification by the Wi-Fi Alliance that hopes to allow the mixing and matching of devices from different manufacturers to form a mesh, but few devices support it so far. You can also buy single mesh routers, like an Amazon Eero, and then add more later if you find that you need them. Based on my testing, a mesh is always better than an extender. How Do Ethernet Cables Compare? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Running an Ethernet cable to create a wired connection between your home router and device will provide a faster and more secure link than Wi-Fi. But running Ethernet cables everywhere can be tricky. Read my Ethernet guide to learn more. Wireless connectivity makes life easy and is often fast enough for most tasks, such as browsing the web or streaming video. What About the US Ban on Foreign-Made Routers? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The Federal Communications Commission has banned new consumer internet routers manufactured outside the US because of national security concerns. The ban doesn’t affect any routers already in American homes or currently on sale in the US, but all new routers aimed at the consumer market must be approved. The way the ban is described, it will likely apply to every new Wi-Fi router, because there are no companies manufacturing routers or the components they are assembled from in the US (except maybe some Starlink Wi-Fi routers). But companies can apply for exemptions. All new models of foreign-produced routers will require Conditional Approval from the Department of Defense and the Department of Homeland Security before the FCC can clear them for sale in the US. Read “Everything You Need to Know About the Foreign-Made Router Ban in the US” to learn more. What About Firmware and Security Updates? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron While the FCC initially published a waiver covering software and firmware updates until March 1, 2027, it has now extended that waiver “at least until January 1, 2029.” What happens after that date is not clear, but if the FCC were to block further updates for the routers folks already own, it would exacerbate the very issue it is trying to address. The majority of routers that are compromised and used in cyberattacks are usually older devices that no longer receive security updates. Should You Buy a Router Now? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron This is tricky. If you live in the US and need a router, you should maybe still buy one, but I wouldn’t blame you for waiting to see how a potential router ban pans out. All the major manufacturers I asked who responded or have released a statement, including Asus, TP-Link, Netgear, and Synology, are confident about getting exemptions, but whether they will is impossible to say for sure. So far, only Netgear, Adtran, and Eero have been granted a Conditional Approval, though an FCC spokesperson told me, “We expect approvals to be granted in a timely manner.” How I Test Routers AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron To find the top Wi-Fi routers, I use each one for at least a week (usually longer) in a busy family home of four with lots of video streaming, gaming, and video calls. I also test the mobile apps and web interfaces to see how easy it is to change settings, set up parental controls, and access security features. My priority is to learn how well the router works in real-life rather than a lab, but I do also run a set of standardized tests, so that I have numbers to compare. I run speed tests (downloads and uploads). I transfer files on the network on multiple devices (including iPhones, Android phones, Windows PCs, and MacBooks) from different spots around my home. I use NetSpot to survey signal strength throughout the house and create heat maps for comparison. I run the TamoSoft Throughput Test. I turn the power and modem off and on to find out how each system recovers. How Did I Select Products to be Reviewed AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron I try to test as many routers as I can. It’s not possible to test every device, so while I will typically test flagship releases, I also call in more affordable routers and try to find models to suit the average family home in terms of budget and performance. We are brand agnostic, so we will test routers from any manufacturer, provided we can get ahold of them. But we do lean toward testing more systems from the most popular brands. All the routers we test are provided by the manufacturers or their PR companies. Most are loaned for a month or so and then returned. A handful of our recommended picks are kept for longer term testing. The remainder are donated to charities. I recently dropped off a batch to Reusing IT and have donated several devices to Oxfam and Shelter.

Tech.title: AI Slop Is Ruining Cute Animals on the Internet
Tech.content:
AI-generated videos and pictures are destroying one of the largest and most enduring sources of joy and compassion on the internet: animals. Whether the imagery features sailors rescuing a polar bear, baby cows separated from their mothers, or a lost pet that was miraculously found, many people have reached the point where they can’t take the creatures on their feeds at face value anymore. The explosion of deepfakes and AI slop over the past few years has led to widespread frustration among viewers, creators, and organizations that support animals, forcing everyone to hunt in the pixels for glitches or other telltale signs of AI.

Mibbby Butler was overjoyed one day in April when she received a text message that her lost cat, Brooklyn, had supposedly been found. Her roommate’s boyfriend had allegedly taken the cat and dumped him 30 minutes away in the Los Angeles suburbs the day prior. Butler quickly posted a missing poster on social media, and she was driving around with her roommate searching for Brooklyn when a stranger sent her a photo. In it, he is sitting on a kitchen counter while being embraced by a girl.

“My baby is OK!” Butler exclaimed to her roommate. But if she wanted to get him back, the person said, she would have to pay money up front for Brooklyn’s purported temporary care. That’s when Butler sensed she was being scammed and began looking closer at the photo.

Brooklyn was posing the same way as he had in the picture Butler used for the missing poster. In both images, a Torani syrup bottle and a microwave can be seen in the background, except in the new photo, the label text was garbled, a classic sign that it was AI-generated. A disheartened Butler didn’t pay up. “I didn’t know people scammed for lost pets,” she says, noting she also didn’t report the incident to police because she wasn’t sure a crime had occurred. Four months later, Brooklyn is still missing.

The flood of fakes has been no easier on the creators of authentic content. The nonprofit We Animals has published the work of 175 photojournalists who have documented alleged animal abuse and other harms at farms, circuses, and scientific labs. The material can be shocking, which naturally invites skepticism, says Eva von Jagow, the group’s marketing manager. For instance, drone footage We Animals shared of rows and rows of hutches allegedly used to shelter calves separated from their moms on a dairy farm in Arizona looks almost too mesmerizingly perfect to be real.

In the past, people have claimed We Animals’ work is staged or photoshopped. It’s no surprise, then, that some viewers have begun accusing the group of relying on AI, even though it bans the photographers it works with from using the technology. “How to prove it's not AI?” an Instagram user commented earlier this month on the dairy farm video.

To convince audiences that its content is authentic, We Animals expects it will have to start sharing behind-the-scenes clips and more details about the steps staffers take to verify submissions. It also plans to adopt technology that embeds the provenance and editing history of photographs and videos into digital files. Victoria de Martigny, the group’s director of visual content, says preserving trust is crucial, or else it could “open up the door to people questioning all of the work,” and “we don’t ever want to be in that position.”

Real, evocative images often pull on viewers’ heartstrings and are an important way for conservation and welfare projects to attract donations. But for the owners of AI slop accounts, synthetic imagery can be a convenient path to collecting likes and ad revenue. Since fakes are much cheaper to produce, they appear to be drowning out real clips in social feeds and search results, says Oscar Horta, a philosopher and leading animal activist who recently helped direct a short film on how AI could affect wildlife.

Tech.title: Green Chef Meal Kit Review (2026): Great Ingredients, Layered Flavor
Tech.content:
At $14 a serving, Green Chef ranks among the more expensive meal kits (HelloFresh runs around $10–$12), and the 42-deep selection of meals doesn't match middle-of-the-market meal kits like HelloFresh and Marley Spoon, which each offer 100-plus. But the recipes are thoughtful, and the care taken with its ingredients—especially for those with eating restrictions—makes it one of the tastiest meal kit options I've tried, without requiring long cook times.

Here's my experience with Green Chef, and how it works.

Cost per meal $14 per serving on most plans, plus $12 shipping per week Meal plan options Three to eight meals per week; sized for two, four, or six people Lowest-cost plan at full price $96 (including shipping), for three meals for two people Size of weekly menu More than 40 options, plus salad-kit, protein, and smoothie add-ons Gluten-free meals? More than half the menu is certified gluten-free Plant-based meals? About a third of dishes are vegetarian. The vegan selection is more limited. Other dietary plans/restrictions A third of meals are dairy-free. A third are listed as low-calorie or low added sugar. Five to 10 keto offerings a week. Produce and eggs are organic unless otherwise specified. Allergens are clearly marked. Prep time 20 to 45 minutes

The Nuts and Bolts

Like many other meal delivery services, Green Chef is subscription-based. After selecting your diet preferences, whether Mediterranean or gluten-free, you'll be asked how many people you're serving and how many meals a week you'd like to receive. Cost is straightforward: It's $14 a meal, plus $12 shipping per week. Generally, for first-time customers, you'll get 50 percent off the first week.

Also, as with HelloFresh's other meal kits, you can choose which day of the week you want your meals delivered. On the appointed day, a well-organized green box will arrive with recipes and most of the ingredients you need to prepare the meals. The exceptions are basic staples like oil, butter, salt, and pepper. Each recipe comes clearly marked with allergens, whether sesame or tree nuts.

Tech.title: How Ikea Turned a Controller Thumbstick Into the Star of Its Xbox Gaming Range
Tech.content:
Ikea has taken another swing at a gaming gear collection, but this time it brought in a ringer: Xbox. The new nine-piece range, revealed at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany, came about not through whiteboard marketing brainstorms, but a meeting between the Xbox and Ikea design teams at Milan Design Week in 2024.

Hearing the Xbox team—including Carl Ledbetter, head of Xbox devices design—was in Milan at the same time, Ikea product design developer Philip Dilé wanted to show off the company's latest creations, the Brännboll gaming collection, that pleasingly stepped away from sharp edges, RGB lighting, and a black color palette.

“That was a bit of an icebreaker," Dilé tells WIRED. "We were exploring gaming, so we wanted to team up with experts who really understand how people play. We know a lot about life at home, but we wanted to specifically understand how you design for gamers.”

Two years on, Ikea's new Yxstaby range is the fruit of that Milan meeting. The collection takes the ethos of 2024's Brännboll, where gaming gear sits well within home decor and doesn't look like it belongs in a bachelor's basement. But it also moves it forward by taking liberal inspiration from Xbox design cues.

Aimed at making it easier to bring gaming into living rooms and tuck everything away afterwards, the range includes a side table on wheels that can store controllers while charging them at the same time behind sliding doors; a toolbox that keeps cables and hardware under a lid that doubles as a laptop stand; a gaming lounge chair with a webbed pocket underneath to stow controllers out of sight; and even a rollable TV stand for a set of up to 55 inches, one that has a split level shelf for consoles.

Overtly Xbox-inspired pieces include a green gaming D-pad cushion and a surprisingly elegant D-pad controller platter, originally designed as a stool. Johan Ejdemo, Ikea's head of design, removed the base and played with the seat, eventually deciding it would make a fine plate or tray.

Tech.title: A Mutation Is Making It Easier for Drug-Resistant Malaria to Spread
Tech.content:
The main drug that has been in use for decades to combat malaria in sub-Saharan Africa is running into a problem: In recent years, researchers have become increasingly concerned that parasites are becoming less sensitive to treatment. Identifying the underlying genetic factors has become an urgent priority.

In an attempt to identify the reason for drug-resistant malaria, a team led by Brown University researchers conducted whole-genome analysis of 157 malaria parasite samples selected from specimens collected in Uganda between 2016 and 2024. The work, published in Nature Medicine this week, shows evidence that mutations in a gene that encodes a protein called px1, which had previously received little attention, is likely responsible for the rise in drug resistance.

“Malaria still is a major killer, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa,” Jeffrey Bailey, an associate professor at Brown University specializing in pathology, says in a press release. “As drug resistance continues to emerge, we worry it will undermine control of its spread and result in even more deaths for a large number of people there and beyond.”

When Bailey’s research team examined the px1 gene in detail, they found that a set consisting of three amino acid mutations and two deletions—the loss of a portion of a chromosome or DNA sequence—was being passed down through generations. The researchers named this cluster of mutations PIN.

Genes undergo recombination with each generation, causing their sequences to gradually break down. However, malaria parasites carrying the PIN mutation were found to have passed on a large region surrounding the px1 gene to multiple individuals almost entirely intact. This suggests that not enough time has elapsed since the PIN mutation emerged for genetic recombination to occur, indicating that it has spread rapidly in recent years.

Tech.title: AI Detectors Are Being Used to Discipline Students. I Tested Whether They Should Be
Tech.content:
Academic integrity offices across the country are making disciplinary decisions based on AI detection scores. Students are appealing grades and fighting academic misconduct charges on the strength of what those scores say. And the tools producing those scores, like Turnitin, GPTZero and the others, are operating with a confidence that my testing didn’t find them to have earned.

I submitted both AI-generated text and human-written text to every major detector I could access, documented the results, and reached a conclusion that anyone using this technology to evaluate student work should probably read before they do it again.

Detectors, homework helpers, essay writers, AI math wizards and even sneaky backdoor test assistants have entered the student-focused chats on cheating in a big way. Here’s a roundup of all the biggest tools and how they’re being used to get around old-school schooling.

Have AI write, and then rewrite it again

The big names like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook) still appear to be the gold standard for getting away with skipping out on writing in school. I spent an afternoon slinging assignments in PDF format into all these tools and each generated polished, accurate responses in the form of persuasive and well-researched essays.

Most students and educators already know about these use cases, but what is surprising is the closed loop created by AI and plagiarism-detection tools. In essence, the cops are helping the culprits get away with the heist. These companies are having their cake, eating it, throwing it up and selling it again as a muffin-of-the-month subscription.

I tried a number of AI text humanizers and tested them against AI detector tools, and after being “humanized,” every single blurb passed with flying colors.

There’s a lot of talk in and out of academic circles about whether AI-detection tools are accurate or useful. From my research for this piece, I can confidently say they are worthless. Unless you’re a student who used AI to write your work and want to prove you didn’t use AI to write your work.

Do your homework, but don’t

The idea that students are at least absorbing some part of the materials in assignments or school work when they use AI, because they have to copy and paste things and put together a cohesively structured output that illustrates learning outcomes they can review, has reached One Wish Willow levels of delusion.

I threw a PDF of an assignment that’s supposed to be AI-proof into Claude — one of those “make something out of your work” assignments that educators like to point to as a better outcome, even if AI is involved.

The only instruction I gave the tool was: “Do this assignment. Complete all the required elements, including the visual elements, and put them into a standardized, cohesive format for submission. pdf please.”

The tool produced a couple of slick infographics that looked good enough to be made by someone using a Canva template and not slick enough to raise any alarm bells on the part of an educator.

Created by Rachel Kane using Claude

This is just the right level of mediocre that passes classes, and at no time did I ever read the assignment or review the generated work. These types of deliverables from assignments were actually the most difficult to pin down as AI within the confines of my research. I used several AI image detectors, and the results were mixed.

In one case, a tool called Winstonai flagged my AI created infographic as 100% AI, but it also flagged a graphic I created long before generative AI was available to the masses as 100% AI.

Another AI image detector, AI or Not, determined my entirely AI infographic was just 1% AI.

AIorNot/Screenshot by CNET

So it’s not a foolproof method, and a student looking to get away with passing this work off as their own just has to point to conflicting detectors to shut down an argument.

Hard problems call for easy solutions

There were exactly zero AI apps, tools and services used in the research for this piece that claimed to be “cheating apps.” Instead, words like “study guide,” “homework helper,” and even the bold promise to provide an “A+ result” were used to advertise each tool’s capabilities.

That didn’t mean any of them balked at being asked for outright solutions to complete problems. or stop them from highlighting features like the Advanced Assignment Solver right next to Homework Helper. I wonder which appeals to a student using these tools.

Services like Gauth AI, a paid study helper, and Studocu, a free study helper with a paid tier that starts at $7 a month, either explicitly offered to do student work wholesale, or put up zero resistance to solving multipage, complex assignments when simply prompted with “do this assignment.”

I used Studocu to generate answers to a complex, five-page astronomy assignment (PDF) from the University of Northern Iowa that included explicit instructions to use a dataset unique to each student based on their student IDs.

Studocu/Screenshot by CNET

In a matter of seconds, the tool used the unique data given and the five-page assignment to generate customized answers to every problem. Gauth AI was also more than up to the task, for a price ($12 a month, or $100 for a year).

Gauth/Screenshot by CNET

Not bad, considering you could probably pass the class without ever having to look at an HR diagram, or even learn what one is.

Test taking when you didn’t study

Testing is supposed to be the time-honored, proven ground for measuring competency, but in the age of AI tools, it’s just another hurdle to limbo under.

Some universities are now doing testing differently, using randomization of questions from large pools and more in-person testing.

For those schools still testing with lockdown browsers and through timed digital, students can get around protections with a variety of easily available tools that utilize “stealth” or discreet windows and integrate AI software, like ChatGPT, to provide on-demand answers.

Tools like Hiding AI even use data on how test scores improved using their subscription-based software that claims to provide an undetectable experience ($192/year).

Hiding AI/Screenshot by CNET

Another covert AI tool that advertises itself as an exam helper, Pluely (starting at $15/month and up to $120 for a lifetime subscription), is particularly adept at call-and-response. All a student needs to do is read out the questions to the exam they’re taking, and Pluely will provide the answers in a discreet, undetectable window. All the student has to do is click.

The bottom line

For every AI app, service or tool designed to build and generate all the different mediums and modes educators are asking students to demonstrate competency, there is an equal and opposite AI app, service or tool designed to help them argue that the work was done by a human.

It’s a marketplace of double dips where the primary customer — the thousands of people keeping investors interested in a growing consumer base — is the student, not the educator.

No matter what it says in the marketing materials, these tools aren’t made to help teachers teach or students learn. They’re made to serve the core customer who most likely just wants to get it over with.

Correction, July 31: A previous version attributed tools and functionality to Turnitin that do not exist on that website.

Tech.title: Meta to Pay Up to $16.68 Billion to Settle With US States on Teen Social Media Addiction
Tech.content:
Instagram and Facebook’s parent company, Meta, has struck a deal with the 29 US states currently suing the tech giant for intentionally designing its social media platforms to be addictive and harmful to children and teens. Reuters first reported the settlement Wednesday, saying the company could pay up to $16.68 billion, which is less than 10% of its 2025 annual revenue ($201 billion).

The settlement allows CEO Mark Zuckerberg and the company to avoid a high-stakes trial, whose consequences could have remade how the tech industry operates. The proposed agreement will need to be approved by the court, but it brings 52 US attorneys general into the deal, not just those who were party to the original lawsuit.

Under the new rules, Meta will enforce default daily usage limits, including blocks during school hours and at nighttime. It will also implement more rigorous age-verification measures, court filings on Wednesday show.

“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of difference for children and their families,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the case, said in a statement Wednesday.

Social media giants like Meta and Google-owned YouTube have been under intense scrutiny in recent years for how well (or poorly) they protect their youngest users. In two separate landmark cases preceding this one, Meta was ordered to pay $375 million to the state of New Mexico after a jury ruled the company enabled child exploitation online. A day later, a Los Angeles court ordered Meta and Google to pay a combined $3 million in damages for similar claims.

In a blog post, Meta calls on TikTok and YouTube to join its efforts. “While this is an important step, the fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day. All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place, because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another,” the company wrote.

Meta did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment.

This is a developing story.

Tech.title: Ring Gave Itself a Security Makeover Called TAKE. Here’s What’s Actually Changing
Tech.content:
Starting this September, Amazon’s Ring security brand is clarifying how it encrypts customer data on cameras, including security video data used for AI analysis, like turning it into video descriptions on your phone. This begins with a unique Ring standard called Throw Away the Key Encryption.

Previously, Ring’s cloud practices were a bit of a black box. We knew the sort of encryption used, but not how easily or frequently Ring could access videos for analysis. Privacy concerns quickly followed, especially as Ring has come under scrutiny — and lawsuits — for features like its AI familiar face technology.

Now Ring has redefined the process and outlined several encryption practices made to give customers more protection or at least more information. Here’s how TAKE works.

A tale of two keys

Ring’s cloud storage is typically necessary to save videos and use intelligence features. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

TAKE is a new approach and a significant jump in transparency for Ring. When TAKE is used and a Ring camera records a video, that video is encrypted with rotating encryption keys, which means the keys are periodically updated with new versions.

One copy of the key is held in the cloud by Ring, in what Ring describes as a “secure enclave,” which requires specific permissions and situations to access. If you have any Ring artificial intelligence features enabled for your Ring device, like video descriptions and summaries, familiar face detection, advanced object recognition and so on, then Ring takes the key out of its vault and uses it — once — to analyze your video footage.

After Ring uses its copy of the key to analyze your video and use the data gathered, it deletes the key and can no longer access that video for any purpose. The company says, “Ring can only receive access to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account,” but I’m not sure if that includes analysis for Ring’s own purposes, like AI training, too. Either way, it seems like it can only happen for one instance.

Meanwhile, you keep the master key for your Ring video, so you can access your cloud storage clips whenever and how often you want, until the cloud storage limit runs out. (Ring’s storage starts at 180 days.) If you have Shared Users on your Ring account who you’ve enabled to access videos, they’ll have this master key, too.

Jamie Siminoff, founder and chief inventor at Ring, told CNET, “We wanted to provide E2EE-like security while allowing customers to continue using all the features they expect from their Ring devices.”

What about end-to-end encryption?

Ring has excellent cameras, but you may want to turn off certain features. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

In the past, Ring has offered an end-to-end encryption mode for users to enable with a password. The video is automatically encrypted and can only be viewed by those who have the password. This option will remain with TAKE, offering the highest level of privacy for Ring security videos — but at a cost.

With the end-to-end encryption mode on, most of Ring’s cloud-based features won’t work. That includes all its AI features. However, you’ll still be able to use live view, access videos in cloud storage and share videos as long as you have your password. It’s a give and take that benefits anyone worried about Ring’s AI or analysis and wants to skip that part of the cameras altogether.

What if I don’t have a Ring subscription at all?

You can get local storage on Ring devices, but it will disable a lot of features. Julie Snyder/CNET

Without a Ring subscription, you can’t store videos in the cloud, so none of this really applies. There are ways to get local storage with Ring, notably using a Ring security hub, that can act as a local storage device if you add a microSD card. But much like end-to-end encryption, you won’t get any of Ring’s extra cloud features.

Getting Ring’s TAKE standard

The new TAKE approach is free for users, although you’ll have to pay a Ring subscription in the first place to access any of this cloud storage. Ring subscriptions start around $5 for a single camera, but you’ll need a $20 subscription to start accessing more advanced AI features and 24/7 professional monitoring.

Ring told me the TAKE standard will start rolling out in September, but the company didn’t give me any indication of how long it would take to update for all users. When it comes to your camera, TAKE will be turned on by default. I’ll keep an eye on my Ring app and let you know if I notice significant differences, although most of this update is behind the scenes.

Tech.title: The Google Pixel 11 Pro Still Has the Best Display for Gaming, but Other Troubles Emerge
Tech.content:
In 2025, I lauded the Google Pixel 10 Pro for its bright, vibrant display that was great to game on. Now, its successor has arrived, and although it looks identical — with some slight hardware changes — the luster has worn off. The Google Pixel 11 Pro feels underpowered when it comes to gaming, and odd glitches that emerged while playing make it harder to recommend for gaming on the go.

The Google Pixel 11 Pro is unquestionably the best phone Google has ever released, with its AI-powering Tensor G6 chip, a trio of great cameras with refined photo software and an expansive list of generative AI features. With all these advantages, the 11 Pro is one of the best phones out there for taking pictures. But its hardware and software edge doesn’t extend as much to gaming as other phones do, such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 and its Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip.

In practice, the Pixel 11 Pro struggles with higher graphics settings within games, and will pop up warnings about overheating and battery drain when I pump it up above the lowest resolution, frame rate and detailing. It’s a bit surprising given the phone’s premium price.

Unfortunately, that price has gone up, though in a roundabout way. Google got rid of the 128GB entry option for its entire lineup, so the $1,099 starting price for the Pixel 11 Pro with 256GB of storage is the same price as last year at that storage level — you just can’t pick up a lower-storage configuration for under $1,000 anymore. That’s especially limiting for mobile gamers, since installing multiple titles can quickly eat through the available storage. The action RPG Genshin Impact alone takes up 55GB.

When reached for comment, Google confirmed that the raised storage and price reflects the impact of the RAM shortage, driven by AI, which has made components more expensive across consumer tech. But it bites the Pixel 11 Pro phones in another way: That new entry model comes with only 12GB of RAM. You’ll still get 16GB with the 512GB and 1TB storage options ($1,219 and $1,499 respectively, $50 higher than last year’s prices), but it’s a bummer after last year’s 10 Pro series all shipped with 16GB.

Google says that this reduction in RAM doesn’t matter as much, since its 11 Pro phones are faster and smoother than last year’s thanks to optimizations in silicon and software. I wasn’t able to test this claim, as the Pixel 11 Pro review unit Google sent me had 512GB of storage and 16GB of RAM, but it’s worth keeping in mind.

With those considerations, the Pixel 11 Pro starts off with compromises, which progressed as I spent more time gaming on the phone.

The Pixel 11 Pro’s svelte design made it easy to handle while gaming, though not everyone may be comfortable with the sizable camera block on the back side. David Lumb/CNET

What it’s like to play games on the Pixel 11 Pro

As with last year’s Pixel 10 Pro, the new Pixel 11 Pro stands out among other phones with its 6.3-inch OLED display. Details are crisp with its 2,856×1,280-pixel resolution and colors are vivid with HDR10 Plus support.

Once again, the 3,600-nit maximum brightness sets the Pixel 11 Pro’s screen apart from competitors, allowing me to play in direct sunlight and brightening up dark rooms. Other phones are catching up, with screens on this year’s Samsung Galaxy S26 at 2,600 nits and the iPhone 17 Pro Max at 3,000 nits. But the Pixel 11 Pro keeps its lead, showing a stunning array of colors and details from games of all genres.

The phone itself is comfortable enough to hold and play. While it’s physically identical to the Pixel 10 Pro from last year, the metal frame ringing the sides feels slightly more polished, leading my fingers to slip on it while gaming — perhaps the tiniest nitpick I’ve ever had with a phone. The wide camera bump on the back of the Pixel 11 Pro rises up enough to make for a decent finger hold, though unavoidably touching the bump’s metal rim and glass becomes a problem when the handset heats up during high-graphics gaming (more on that later).

The dual speakers at the top and bottom of the device pump out admirable sound. Like a lot of phones, the speaker on the bottom edge of the phone can be easily covered by a finger when holding the handset sideways to play games, which cuts off half the audio — unfortunate, but not uncommon.

What is extremely rare in gaming are the sound issues I ran into while playing the action RPG Diablo Immortal, in which the audio occasionally switched into an echoing, garbled mess. I’d never experienced this before.

Most games have touchscreen controls in the form of parts of the screen converted to digital buttons, which are suitable, if clunky, necessities when playing on an all-glass display. The Pixel 11 Pro had suitably responsive touch controls, and the only trouble was with my own fat thumbs incorrectly pressing one part of the display instead of another. A physical wrap-around controller is a big upgrade for most games, and I relished using my Backbone One to play Dead Cells and others that rely on fast responses with a range of options to dodge or attack.

Unlike some other premium Android phones, the Pixel 11 Pro has magnets embedded in its rear cover (playfully called Pixelsnap) that makes it compatible with a lot of accessories, including wireless chargers. I was able to snap on an official Apple MagSafe charger and play while juicing it back up, which was convenient — and helpful. The phone’s 4,850-mAh battery lasted awhile through gaming, but its wired charging maxes out at 30 watts, which is slower than other phones, but I worry about the heat buildup if it were any faster. Its Qi2.2-supporting wireless charging tops out at 25 watts. Being able to top up in the middle of a play session was nice, even if it doesn’t match the faster 45-watt ability of a phone such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus or even the 60-watt charging of the Galaxy S26 Ultra.

The Pixel 11 Pro is truly plug-and-play with the Backbone One after the Backbone app is installed — slide it in, pull it out and the game continues either way. David Lumb/CNET

The Pixel 11 Pro’s gaming problems are in the present Tensor

While the Pixel series’ Tensor chips power superior AI features such as Magic Eraser and live translation, they’ve been underpowered compared to other silicon in benchmark testing, with Pixel phones routinely coming in lower than devices running Snapdragon chips such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 series. Silicon makes a huge difference in graphically intensive tasks, like gaming.

It stands to reason that the Pixel 11 Pro’s Tensor G6 chip is what keeps it from mustering the higher-tier graphics capabilities that other premium phones achieve. When I loaded up Diablo Immortal, the game defaulted to the lowest graphical setting possible, and even just ratcheting that up to medium with a faster framerate, a pop-up warned me that I was risking overheating and battery drain.

Typical play, even with higher graphics settings, got the phone warm but not toasty, only reaching dangerous levels of heat when I had it plugged in to recharge and was downloading more game content. The camera block on the back of the phone became uncomfortable to touch with its metal rim and glass atop the cameras. Most games didn’t do this, and it was only in specific circumstances that the heat hit concerning levels, but it still leads me to conclude that the phone’s heat management isn’t quite as good as other premium phones during graphically heavy tasks.

It’s worth mentioning that, with heat management concerns, I removed Google’s official case off the phone to ensure heat could escape off the back and sides. This made the warm metal on the sides of the phone less comfortable to hold, but hopefully would keep it from cooking within the case.

Supposedly, this is Genshin Impact. Things still happened on-screen, but I couldn’t see what was going on. David Lumb/CNET

Then there’s the field of pink. I loaded up Genshin Impact, an older Hoyoverse game that’s presumably more optimized than more recently released titles such as Wuthering Waves. Yet when I booted up Genshin (after downloading the aforementioned 55GB of content), I loaded into the game’s world to find it awash in pink, a layer of obfuscating color that made it impossible to tell what was going on. Clearly, it was a graphical glitch, but one I reproduced over and over. Perhaps this will be ironed out in a patch, but I’ve never had a major mobile game become unplayable just when dropping in.

Combined with the odd audio issues on Diablo Immortal (again, something that hasn’t happened when loading the game on other phones), I’m unsure whether this is just post-launch glitching that’ll be fixed in immediate patches or a deeper issue with the phone’s hardware. It’s bothersome for sure, though thankfully the only bizarre issues I ran into across the half-dozen games I played.

Overall, the Pixel 11 Pro remains a good gaming phone for its fantastic display, which also shines when you’re taking photos and watching films and TV shows. Other concerns keep it from being a top recommendation for playing games, but if it’s a secondary or tertiary priority above photography and AI, the Pixel 11 Pro would serve you well — and hopefully those glitches won’t affect the games you want to play.

Tech.title: NASA Astronaut Christina Koch’s Secret Trick to Decompress After Artemis II
Tech.content:
How do you recover from 10 days of traveling through outer space and around the moon? If you’re astronaut Christina Koch, you disconnect from being online and just journal.

“I spent that first week journaling about the mission without looking at any photos from the mission,” Koch told CNET on Monday during a visit to her alma mater, North Carolina State University, where an engineering building was being named after her. “I knew that, one day, the photos might define my memories, but initially, it was important to remember things as they were [with] fresh memories.”

Koch’s latest mission was NASA’s Artemis II, which sent her, commander Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover and Canadian mission specialist Jeremy Hansen on a 10-day voyage in early April beyond the far side of the moon and back, becoming the first astronauts to go that distance in more than 50 years.

The NASA astronaut said she really “kept the blinders on” for the first two weeks. “The biggest fear I had when I landed was that I would forget it all so quickly.”

“The process of coming home is such an important one, whether you’ve done 328 days or nine days,” Koch said. She compared it to a kind of military deployment. “Reentering to Earth is a process, physical and mental. You’re coming back and, in some cases, coming into a routine [that] has gone ahead without you.”

Koch said she also came home to “quite a few” text messages, all congratulatory. But any emails she got from April 1 to April 10 are still unread; “I think people understand why,” she said with a laugh.

After a few weeks, Koch did look at the photos, and by then, the snaps were already world-famous. The photos the Artemis II team took — on off-the-shelf iPhones and Nikon cameras — came to be how the world experienced Artemis II. More than 18 million people tuned in to watch the crew’s takeoff, and their photos and live TV appearances spread in what became known as “Moon Joy.”

The Artemis II crew — (clockwise from left) Christina Koch, Jeremy Hansen, Reid Wiseman, and Victor Glover — take time out for a group hug inside the Orion spacecraft on their way home. NASA

It was a record-breaking trip. As a whole, the Artemis II crew broke Apollo 13’s record for the furthest space travel, traveling over 700,000 miles total. Koch became the first woman to go beyond low Earth orbit; Glover, the first Black person; and Hansen, the first Canadian.

Koch also holds the record for the longest-ever single spaceflight by a woman from her 2019 stint on the International Space Station, as well as taking part in the first all-female space walk.

One of the most popular photos from the trip is of Koch looking out the Orion spacecraft window, the planet Earth a bright sea of blue and green, her hair braided and iconic curls lit up. The image quickly went viral and became a rallying cry for women interested in science, technology, engineering and math, known as STEM.

Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch looks out the window at Earth. NASA

Launching an aerospace career

Being a role model isn’t new to Koch, and she considers it a big part of her job now, especially for women and girls.

“I had an experience meeting Sally Ride once,” Koch said, referring to the astronaut who became the first woman in space in 1983. “And in one moment, shaking my hand and her looking into my eyes, I felt like she said so much. She said, ‘Your dreams are valid. I see you. I believe in you.’ And I think that that’s really the job that’s before me, is to just look at people that might be looking after me, to tell them I see them, to tell them that their dream matters.”

A big part of Koch’s hometown visit was highlighting how her education was a launchpad for her aerospace career. Koch is a three-time NCSU grad, earning her Bachelor of Science degrees in electrical engineering and physics and a Master of Science in electrical engineering in the early aughts.

But it wasn’t just the technical know-how that aided her on the moon mission. Koch said her time working for NCSU’s student newspaper, the Technician, sharpened her photography skills. She recalled learning how every photo should tell a story, something she thinks about “every single time I raise a camera to my eye,” whether the subject is the moon or her friends.

The young engineers and space enthusiasts who turned out in droves to see Koch this week have more reason than ever to aim for the stars, literally. In many ways, Artemis II kicked off what space enthusiasts hope will be the beginning of a new space age.

Four Artemis missions are slated to run before the end of the decade; Koch’s team was the first crewed mission. They stress-tested the new Orion spacecraft (which they named “Integrity”) and the Space Launch System that will be foundational to other missions.

North Carolina State University, led by Chancellor Kevin Howell (left), renamed one of its engineering buildings in honor of its alum, Christina Koch. Koch is making the university’s “Wolfpack” hand symbol. Katelyn Chedraoui/Rene Ramos/CNET

Artemis III is the next mission, slated for 2027. It plans to test docking procedures in a low Earth orbit, with NASA commander Randy Bresnik, mission specialists Andre Douglas and Frank Rubio, and European Space Agency pilot Luca Parmitano. Astronauts won’t step foot on the moon’s surface until Artemis IV in early 2028.

Koch said she won’t be part of Artemis IV but will cheer on her friends who are. She spoke briefly about the “revolutionary” role of new technology in powering these future explorations and discoveries, specifically generative AI. But she also called out the need to address fundamental issues with the tech.

“I think the biggest challenge with AI is still preserving truth in our world,” Koch said. “If you find the thing that you can do the longest, for the slowest, and still love every day, you’re doing the right thing, no matter what people predict about AI or what it may do or not do.”

The upcoming Artemis missions have already stirred controversy. The all-male Artemis III crew sparked outrage and criticism, particularly after so many women and girls watched Koch break new records with Artemis II. The name “Artemis” even comes from the Greek goddess of hunting. NASA’s 2025 astronaut class also had, for the first time ever, more women than men (six versus four).

NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said in an X post in June that staffing decisions “tak[e] into account many factors, including the background and expertise of the astronauts,” and that the Artemis III astronauts are “experienced, qualified and deserve to be celebrated.”

Koch remains steadfastly optimistic that there will be room for many young people as we invest in future aerospace missions and science, both at NASA and with “commercial ventures” like Blue Origin and SpaceX. She hopes to be an active role model for students, ones like she was at NCSU and beyond — in her self-described “ripped jeans [and] pink hair” with an “inexplicable love of rockets.”

“For the students in the fourth row who think they’re the only ones in the room who don’t understand, and maybe haven’t been told yet, that’s not a disqualification,” Koch said. “Students of every kind, walking by and into this building, are my ‘why.’ Because it’s not the record for miles you travel away that really matters. It’s the impact you make, we make, right here at home.”

Tech.title: Before Splurging on a $500 Vitamix, Consider This Cheaper Model. It Works Just as Well
Tech.content:
CNET’s key takeaways

If you want a great Vitamix blender, you don’t have to spend $500 for a great model. Go for the VX1 instead and save yourself $120.

The VX1 has self-cleaning and pulse modes, a sleek, modern design and doesn’t compromise on power.

The VX1 is a larger blender at 64 ounces. If you don’t need that much blending space, opt for a personal blender, such as the $130 Ninja BlendBoss, instead.

Certain brands have become synonymous with the products they create. Think Kleenex, Sharpie, Band-Aid and even Vitamix. That notoriety can make it easier for consumers to know which brands to turn to for quality tissues, permanent markers, adhesive bandages or blenders. But choosing becomes tricky when you realize these brands offer multiple versions of their most popular products. So which model should you buy?

In the case of Vitamix, when testing the VX1 and 5200, two of its most popular blenders, for CNET’s best blenders list, I learned that more expensive doesn’t always mean better. Here’s why.

The Best Blenders: Picks for Smoothies, Dips, Soup and More See It

My experience with the Vitamix VX1

Launched as a replacement for the discontinued and beloved Explorian, the VX1 is now one of Vitamix’s most affordable blenders at $380. It’s also CNET’s pick for the best overall blender, since it excelled during our hands-on testing.

Vitamix VX1 vs. 5200

Both the 5200 and VX1 have a 64-ounce capacity, cord storage underneath and 10 speeds, but neither is dishwasher-safe. However, the VX1 has a few extra features, including a pulse mode, a self-cleaning program and 0.2 more horsepower. It also has a slightly smaller footprint than the 5200.

The VX1 (right) measures 9.5×7.8×19.6 inches, compared to the 5200’s 20.5×8.75×7.25 inches. Anna Gragert/CNET

During testing, the 1440-watt VX1 outperformed 10 other models at blending raw almonds into almond butter, taking only 1 minute and 13 seconds. It also excelled at turning chickpeas into hummus in less than a minute.

As for the 1380-watt 5200, it took 1 minute and 51 seconds to blend almond butter and 1 minute and 41 seconds to blend hummus. It also took 12 seconds longer than the VX1 to blend a green smoothie.

Where the 5200 impressed

Although I preferred the VX1’s operation, the 5200 still performed well in two specific tests: blending cubed ice and butternut squash soup. It blended the former in 24 seconds to create snow-like ice, leaving just two medium cubes, while the VX1 took 26 seconds and left several large cubes. When blending the soup, the 5200 required only 12 seconds, which was five seconds less than the VX1.

The 5200 was also a smidge quieter than the VX1 when mixing a green smoothie on high speed, with a max of 93 A-weighted decibels. The VX1 was 95.1 dBA on high. Despite these wins, I don’t think the 5200 justifies such a steep price increase.

While it doesn’t have a pulse mode, the 5200 does have a “high” speed switch, which is nice if you often blend challenging ingredients that require more power and don’t want to fiddle with a speed dial.

I prefer the more modern look of the VX1. Anna Gragert/CNET

The one I’d keep on my countertop

Numbers aside, I prefer the VX1 over the 5200 in terms of design. It has a more modern look and is visually less angular and bulky. I also like that there are three different ways to safely stop blending: an on/off switch under the base, a start/pause switch on its front and a standby mode on the speed dial.

3.5 feet of cord storage. Not too shabby. Anna Gragert/CNET

Vitamix’s 5200 costs $500, $120 more than the $380 VX1. While both models have a limited warranty, you get seven years with the 5200, two years more than the VX1’s five-year warranty.

Overall, based on my testing, I don’t think you need to spend the extra money to get a great Vitamix blender. If you’re stuck choosing between the 5200 and VX1, I’d go with the VX1 and rest assured you won’t miss out on anything.
